Desiring to erect the bright banner to sustain the world and to draw the swift sword to dispel evil, one must first understand the shallow and deep aspects of the True Dharma before being able to shatter the attachments of sentient beings.
The Northern and Southern Tripitakas have circulated for a long time; their ancient and modern commentaries and compilations—
The titles of these works differ from one another. The catalogues of the extant Sanskrit manuscripts (vaṃśa-kośa) preserved today remain rigorous, yet they cannot be entirely free from errors.

During the late Ming dynasty, the catalogs of the Chinese printed editions (shū-bon-zō) were incomplete in their nomenclature; subsequent additions were indiscriminately included, flowing on without end, continuing right up to the present dynasty.
His Majesty Emperor Xian presided over and regulated this undertaking; he gathered the extraordinary and rejected the spurious, restoring it all to a state of new order.

I humbly observe that, throughout the past two hundred years, the vital spirit of our State has inspired manifestations of transformation throughout the ten directions, appearing therein to uphold the orthodox, heal the infirm, remove cataracts, and shatter the vulgar.

Regarding the Śāstra-piṭaka, those who know the way to its ford consider it proximate. The essential meanings presented therein are inherently worthy of contemplation;
however, its shortcomings lie in the confusion of its notations and the fact that various schools have entered it in a disordered manner, leaving their distinct gateways intact.

The recent addition of a table of contents results in more precedents than actual texts, which is unnecessary. Now, following its original sequence and harmonizing its concluding sections, I shall compose the "Water and Land Path."

may those in the rows of the lower hall and throughout the ten directions rejoice together, planting these roots of goodness so that they remain indestructible like a vajra.

Terms such as "Miscellaneous Piṭaka" (Zàzàng) or "Mantra Piṭaka" (Zhòuzàng) are not employed; rather, all are subsumed within the Three Piṭakas. Thus, whether Esoteric or Exoteric, Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, Eastern or Western, earlier or later, the main pillars are raised and the secondary details are displayed.
Regarding retranslations, there is nothing extraordinary. As for non-Buddhist treatises and suspected or spurious scriptures, these shall all be [treated accordingly].
Annotate this to demonstrate its essential points. Now, when masters of repentance and others read the Tripitaka, they will not be confused.

(The term *fangdeng* [vaipulya] is equivalent to *fangguang* [vaipulya]. Among the twelve divisions of the teachings, only this one division does not apply to the Hīnayāna; thus, all sutras from the *Avataṃsaka* downwards are subsumed under the *vaipulya*. However, since the *Ratnakūṭa* and *Mahāsaṃnipāta* do not have many distinct categories, they can be integrated [into the general category].

The *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* have many distinct categories; therefore, they are separately designated. As the ancient masters said: "That which exclusively addresses those of great capacity is named the *Avataṃsaka*; that which integrates and penetrates emptiness is named the *Prajñāpāramitā*; that which opens up the provisional to reveal the real is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. )

That which is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra) is called "Nirvāṇa" because it upholds the Vinaya while discussing the eternal. Those that do not fall within these four categories are designated by the general name "Vaipulya. Because it is difficult to surpass, the *Avataṃsaka* (Flower Ornament) is placed second.

Whenever there is a reduction of two characters, one must kneel and recite them. Rising to stand, one performs a formal greeting (*praṇāma*). In the ritual for the Great Offering of the Dharma Realm for Holy and Mundane Beings of Land and Water, the *Dharmacakra* Jewel Repentance,
the practitioner rises from meditative concentration and enters the hall with composed dignity, chanting "Namo Huayan Haikai" three times.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, greetings.
With all reverence and a single-minded heart, I prostrate to the Huayan Dharma-realm’s Perfectly Interfused Triple Gem (bow; while observing, say):
Manifesting the power of mastery, you preach the Perfect Sūtra; may all immeasurable sentient beings receive the prediction of enlightenment.
May these clouds of Dharma-sound fill the realms of the ten directions, so that the mirror of the minds of sentient beings may be opened.
Each adorned with jewels, complete with the power of radiance, they perfect the body of the Tathāgata.
These incense and flowers of mine pervade the ten directions; their fragrance and full blossoming are all supreme.
Extending and filling the entire Dharma-realm, they transform into subtle clouds of Dharma. Their layered, precious resonance is inexhaustible. Thus it is said:
Mind is itself the body, and the body is itself the world. As the body and world engage with various thoughts, each one reflects the banner of radiant light.
The world-systems and the oceans of worlds, auspiciously revolving, all shine in splendor. The numinous mind universally illumines the ten voids;
not seeing the Sahā world, one sees the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, wherein the myriad phenomena of the forest and the mountains are fully contained within the One.

The constellations shine brightly within the robes; the patterns and textures wind and turn, coalescing into elegant compositions. Through skillful means, they sustain the lives of wisdom for all beings.
Having made these offerings, everyone bows with the utmost reverence (the ritual of bowing and viewing is as described above).
With single-minded devotion, we reverently entreat the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the New Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vaipulya (the manner of prostration and contemplation is as above).
The Dharmadhātu is perfectly luminous; all measures of the emotional mind are utterly shattered. This is the unshared, unobstructed realm of the One Vehicle.
*The Chapter on the Sublime Array of Worldly Rulers, First.* The Buddha was at the site of enlightenment, having attained Buddhahood. The lords of the three worlds had all assembled.
Each attained liberation. The leaders each spoke ten verses. From the lion thrones and the ornaments, bodhisattvas emerged, raising clouds of offerings and speaking verses.
Chapter Two: The Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata. From within the offering articles, the bodhisattvas produced verses inquiring about the Dharma.
The Buddha emitted light from his teeth, illuminating billions of ocean-like lands, and produced verses.
The assembly gathered. A light from the Buddha’s brow manifested and returned beneath his feet, where a great lotus flower appeared before them.

Within the *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair between the eyebrows) of the Buddha, there was the Bodhisattva Sarvadharmaviśeṣaghoṣa, together with a retinue as numerous as atoms of dust, seated upon this lotus flower.
Verses Spoken to the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions. Chapter Three: Samantabhadra’s Samādhi.
Samantabhadra entered the Samādhi of the Body-Treasury of Vairocana Tathāgata, which encompasses all Buddhas; thereupon, all Buddhas appeared before him.
The Buddha stroked [the crown of his head] and bestowed wisdom. Rising from samādhi, the great assembly obtained benefit. Light radiated from the pores of the Tathāgata as he offered praise;
all the bodhisattvas likewise offered praise and entreaty. Chapter Four: The Accomplishment of the World.
Chapter Five: The Flower Treasury World System. Samantabhadra explains ten matters concerning the ocean of world systems:
the various world-system seeds and the names of lands and Buddhas within them. Chapter Six: Vairocana.
Samantabhadra explains the original practices of the Great Majestic Radiance of the past. By means of... [text ends]
The First Assembly, Part One.

Chapter Seven: The Names and Titles of the Tathāgatas. The Buddha sat in the Hall of Universal Radiance and, by means of his supernormal powers, gathered ten bodhisattvas from ten Buddhas of the ten wisdoms across ten worlds of form.
Mañjuśrī then proclaimed the Dharma-gate of the distinctions among these names and titles.
Chapter Eight: The Four Noble Truths. Chapter Nine: Mañjuśrī’s Exposition of the Radiance of the Various Names for the Four Truths in Every Buddha-field.
The Buddha emits light from his feet, illuminating the lands of the ten directions;
in all places, Mañjuśrī speaks in verse. Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Wisdom. Mañjuśrī together with nine [bodhisattvas] who had come with him...
The Questions and Answers of Humans: Elucidating the Essential Points of the Dharma. Chapter Eleven: Pure Conduct. Question by Jñānaśrī;
Answer by Mañjuśrī on the Dharma-gate of Making Vows Amidst All Activities. Chapter Twelve: Worthy Leader.
Mañjuśrī questions the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla on the Dharma-gate of extensively extolling the merits of faith.
This concludes the second assembly.
Chapter Thirteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. The Tathāgata, without departing from the foot of the Bodhi tree, ascends to the abode of Śakra.
Chapter Fourteen: Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru.
Dharmamati and the others came from the world of Daśapuṣpa, located beyond a hundred *rajas-kṣetra* worlds, from the presence of the Tathāgata Daśamāsika. The Buddha emitted light from his toe.
Dharmamati and the others each spoke verses. Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes (*Daśabhūmi*). Dharmamati entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means (*ananta-upāya-samādhi*).
Buddhas bearing the same name appeared before him and touched his head with their hands. Emerging from concentration, he expounded the Dharma of the Ten Abodes.
Chapter Sixteen: The Holy Life (*Brahmacarya*). The Devaputra Samyaksmṛti asked questions; Dharmamati spoke on the contemplation of non-existence.
Chapter Seventeen: The Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment (*Prathamacittotpāda-puṇya-parivarta*). Dharma Wisdom answers the questions of Śakra;
the lands of the ten directions tremble, and Buddhas bearing the same names manifest and offer praise. Chapter Eighteen: Elucidating the Dharma (*Dharmavyakti-parivarta*).
Vīryamati asked, "How does one cultivate the arousal of the mind? Dharmamati replied, "By abiding in ten kinds of non-negligence.
This concludes the third assembly. Chapter Nineteen:
Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. The Buddha did not leave the Bodhi tree; from the palace of Śakra, he ascended to the Yāma Heaven.

Chapter Twenty: Verses of Praise in the Palace of Yama. From the world-system of Ten Wisdoms outside ten thousand lands, the Bodhisattvas such as Guṇakara and others come from the presence of the Buddha Daśanetra. The Buddha emits light from his two feet and speaks in verse.
Chapter Twenty-one: The Ten Practices. Guṇakara enters the Bodhisattva’s Skillful Contemplation.
Samādhi. The same Buddha appears before them and touches their heads. Emerging from concentration, he expounds the Ten Practices.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries. Also spoken by Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha. This concludes the Fourth Assembly.

Chapter Twenty-Three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. The Buddha, without departing from the Bodhi tree, Sumeru, or the Yāma heaven, ascends to the Tuṣita palace. Chapter Twenty-Four: Verses of Praise within the Tuṣita Palace.
Vajradhvaja and others come from the ten Wonderful Worlds beyond ten thousand dust-motes of lands, from the presence of the Buddha Daśadhvaja.
He emitted light from his knees, causing those in the ten directions to see one another. The Bodhisattva Daśaketu spoke these verses. Chapter Twenty-five: The Ten Dedications (*Daśapariṇāmanā*).
The Bodhisattva Vajraketu entered the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s Wisdom-Light; Buddhas bearing the same name appeared before him and touched his head with their hands.
Rising from this meditative absorption, he expounded the Ten Dedications. This concludes the fifth assembly.

Chapter Twenty-Six: The Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*). While the Buddha was dwelling in the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), Vajragarbha entered the Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom (*Mahājñānāloka*).
Buddhas bearing the same name appeared before him and touched his head with their hands. Upon emerging from samādhi, he proclaimed the names of the ten stages.

Vimukticandra requested [the teaching], but he declined twice; only when the great assembly collectively entreated him did the Buddha emit light from between his eyebrows, illuminating the ten directions.

The Buddhas likewise emitted light from between their eyebrows, which came to illuminate [the assembly]. In the void, it formed a pavilion of a luminous net, from which verses were uttered to provide exhortation.
Thereupon, the meaning of the stages was proclaimed. This concludes the sixth assembly.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Ten Samādhis. The Buddha was dwelling in Universal Radiance, having entered the Samādhi of the Momentary Boundary of All Buddha-fields.
Universal Eye questioned Samantabhadra regarding samādhi; the Buddha then instructed him to question Samantabhadra himself.

The great assembly entered various samādhis, yet they could not see Samantabhadra. The Buddha taught them to pay homage to Samantabhadra and to contemplate the ten directions, thereby generating the Great [Vow].
[The Buddha] made a vow. Then Samantabhadra manifested his body and rained down ten thousand clouds; the world shook.
The Buddha himself proclaimed the names of the ten great samādhis and commanded Samantabhadra to speak [them]. Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Supernatural Powers (*Daśābhijñā-varga*).
Chapter Twenty-Nine: The Ten Patiences (*Daśakṣānti-varga*). Both were spoken by Samantabhadra. Chapter Thirty: The Immeasurable (*Asaṃkhyeya-varga*). The Mind...
The King asks; the Tathāgata answers: Chapter Thirty-one, "On the Lifespan"; Chapter Thirty-two, "On the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas"—both spoken by Cittarāja;
Chapter Thirty-three, "On the Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha," spoken by the Bodhisattva Green Lotus Treasury through the empowerment of the Buddha; [Chapter on] the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata.
Chapter Thirty-Four: The Ocean. Samantabhadra explains the ninety-seven marks of a great man.
Chapter Thirty-Five: The Tathāgata’s Minor Marks, Radiance, and Merits. The Buddha addressed Ratnapāṇi:

“When a Bodhisattva is about to descend to be born, his light illuminates the hells and transforms beings into the heavens, leading them to realize the ten stages [of the bodhisattva path]. This is the practice of Samantabhadra.”
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Obstruction of an Angry Mind; the Universal Worthy’s Exhortation to Practice the Ten Dharmas; the Ocean of Lands Raining Various Clouds;
Bodhisattvas of Identical Names Act as Witnesses. Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.

The Buddha’s light from the white tuft between his brows shines universally throughout the ten directions, circumambulates [the assembly], and enters the Wondrous Virtue of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising.

At the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, the Bodhisattva inquired about the Great Dharma. Light issued from the Buddha’s mouth, universally illuminating the ten directions, circling to the right, and entering the mouth of Samantabhadra.
Samantabhadra’s body and seat became increasingly sublime as he proclaimed the name of the Dharma-gate. The great earth shook violently.
As the questions and answers were repeated, Buddhas bearing the same names appeared before him to offer praise, and Bodhisattvas bearing the same names served as witnesses.

The above concludes the seventh assembly, the thirty-eighth chapter, "Leaving the World. The Buddha sat upon the Universal Radiance [Throne], and Samantabhadra entered the Buddha-Flower Adornment Samādhi.
All lands shook in eighteen ways. Emerging from concentration, he engaged in hundreds of thousands of questions and answers with Samantamati.
The Buddhas appear before him and praise him with joy.
This concludes the eighth assembly. Chapter Thirty-nine: Entering the Dharma Realm (*Dharmadhātupraveśa*). The Buddha was in the garden, accompanied by bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and world-protectors.
He entered the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*). The pavilions were magnificently adorned, and [bodhisattvas] gathered from the ten directions like clouds. Samantabhadra...
Entering the gateway of skillful means into the ocean of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations, he brought forth clouds of great majestic adornments.

Mañjuśrī observed this and spoke in verse. The Bodhisattvas attained gateways of immeasurable great compassion; never leaving the presence of the Buddha, they universally rescued those throughout the ten directions.
As Mañjuśrī traveled south, Śāriputra and six thousand others witnessed these sublime events and followed after him.
Traveling southward, he arrived at the eastern side of the City of Blessings and stayed at the site of the Great Stūpa in the Śāla Grove.
There, Mañjuśrī saw the laymen, laywomen, boys, and girls, as well as the hosts of nāgas, who were all most devoted to Sudhana.
The profound [teachings] were set forth, causing [beings] to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

With principal and retinue layered upon one another, they returned to the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and beheld Mañjuśrī once more, continuing even unto Samantabhadra. Therein, verses were spoken with cooling clarity, extending to the end of the future.
Above is the Ninth Assembly, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from Khotan in the Tang Dynasty.
Translated.

A Solemn Invocation for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*, Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Practices and Vows for Entering the Inconceivable Realm of Liberation (Prostrations and viewing as above).
This is an extensive exposition based on the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Gandavyūha*) of the eighty-fascicle *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
It provides clear and detailed instruction and purifies lingering corruptions. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā, a śramaṇa from Kapiśī in the Tang Dynasty.

With one mind, we reverently entreat the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (though previously translated, it was incomplete); the *Tusha Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha (which is a portion of the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas" and the "Chapter on Radiant Enlightenment");
the *Sūtra on the Original Vows and Practices of Bodhisattvas* spoken by the Buddha (which is the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" and the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes");

the *Sūtra on the Original Vows of All Bodhisattvas Seeking Buddhahood* (same as above); the *Sūtra on the Chapter of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Ten Abodes* (which is the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes"); and the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha*.

*The Sutra on the Ten Abodes of Bodhisattvas* (also known as the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes") *The Sutra on the Gradual Preparation of All-Wise Virtue* (i.e., the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds") *The Sutra on the Ten Abodes* (also known as the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds") *The Sutra on the Samādhi Asked by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin* (also known as the *Sutra on the Universal Treasure Bodhisattva’s Concentrated Mind*;

i.e., the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis") *The Sutra Revealing the Merits of Boundless Buddha-Lands* (i.e., the "Chapter on the Lifespan"; this was spoken by the Tathāgata himself) *The Buddha-Spoken Sutra on the Comparative Measurement*
*The Sūtra on the Merits of All Buddha-fields* (also known as the "Chapter on Lifespan," spoken by the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabhā-rāja);

*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata* (i.e., the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata"); *The Sūtra on the Chapter of Delivering the World* (i.e., the "Chapter on Leaving the World," though it lacks the Tathāgata’s responses to questions);

*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Rāmaka* (from within the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-realm," concerning the twelve stages of spiritual friends from the merchant Anupamavijaya to the Night Goddess Samantagambhīra-śrī-vimala-prabhā, including several incantations); *Mahā-* [Sūtra].
The *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm (from Devendraprabha to Guṇākara);
the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-caryāpraṇidhāna-stotra* (the verses from the *Caryāpraṇidhāna-parivarta*, containing the *Tathatā-praṇidhāna-paripūraṇa-samantabhadra-caryā-dhāraṇī*);
the *Mañjuśrī-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (abbreviated like the *Caryāpraṇidhāna* verses, but in five-character meter). [To be viewed as above.]
