He who cut his two breasts to save his child was next reborn as a man and became a king;
he ruled the country with the True Dharma and further gave his body in universal charity to birds and beasts. Thereafter, he was reborn as the son of a Brahmin;
he abstained from food seeking to leave the household life and sacrificed his body to save a nursing tigress.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Past Buddhas’ Almsround Sūtra (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi in the Western Jin Dynasty. The Buddha spoke of his causal ground:
his mother, seeing the Buddha begging for alms, made a vow to give birth to a son who would leave the household life and receive a prediction of enlightenment.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the *Sūtra of the Causes and Conditions of King Wondrous Color* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of Great Jianfu Monastery during the Tang Dynasty. The Buddha was at the Jeta Grove;
the great assembly, with their faculties unmoving, listened to the essential teachings of the Dharma. A bhikṣu asked the reason for this, and the Buddha spoke of the past... [seeking...]
Dharma. Having abandoned his son and wife, and having further sacrificed this very body as food for the yakṣas, he has now obtained this retribution.
With a single mind, he entreats the Buddha to preach the *Moon-Light Bodhisattva Sūtra*. (The protocol for prostration and viewing is the same as above.
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty. The Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, preaching for the sake of Moon-Light.
Regarding the giving of Dharma and the giving of food, one should always make four vows.

Furthermore, it is recounted that in the past, Prince Jñānasthāpana healed a bhikṣu’s illness with the flesh of his own body; this was the practice performed by the World-Honored One in a former life.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Causes and Conditions of King Māndhātṛ (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa and others from North India during the Song Dynasty.

When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, in response to the inquiry of King Jayasena, he recounted how his past acts of giving had caused him to be born upon the crown of a king's head, to rule over the four continents, and to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There he beheld...

The Sūtra on the Virtuous Radiance Prince as Requested by Rākṣasa, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty (as previously noted for the calligraphy). One hundred and fourteen Śakras undergo birth and extinction.
With one mind, they reverently entreated the Buddha to preach this sūtra. The Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa for the sake of Rākṣasa.
O Bhikṣu, I shall explain the seven sets of four dharmas of a bodhisattva, the five sets of four non-dharmas, as well as the matters concerning the auspicious meaning during the time of the Buddha,
the offering to the Buddha by Guṇaprabha-vīrya, and the protection of the Dharma-treasury.
I single-mindedly entreat you to receive the *Tathāgata-dvaya-svayaṃ-vrata-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Buddha-bhāṣita-svayaṃ-vrata-samādhi-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by Dharmarakṣa. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa An Shigao of the Parthian Kingdom during the Later Han Dynasty. Buddha...

While traveling through the kingdom of Jutami, the Mahāsattvas of the ten directions beheld auspicious *ling-shui* flowers. Empowered by that Buddha’s spiritual force, they came here to make offerings to the Buddha.
The Buddha smiled and emitted light; for the Bodhisattva Xianru, he explained the three conditions for smiling, and for Mingjian Guangxian, he preached the Dharma of renunciation.
Brahmā served as the Buddha’s triple witness, and Kāśyapa vowed to attain [realization].
The *Sutra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, respectfully received with single-minded devotion;
and the *Sutra on the Divine Footsteps and Inexhaustible Transformations* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by Zhu Fahu. Second, translated by the śramaṇa An Faqin of the Parthian Kingdom during the Western Jin dynasty.
It contains a section where Maudgalyāyana, having seen all places with his own eyes, harbors doubts and questions the Buddha; [the Buddha] then travels to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The summer retreat was concluded. Both bhikṣus and bodhisattvas were present. The Devaputra of the Yue-zhi asked about the Dharma and received a prediction of enlightenment.

Maudgalyāyana exhorted the various devas to make offerings to the Buddha. Consequently, the Buddha spoke of manifesting his body throughout the ten directions to bestow transformative teachings—a realm unknown to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
He clarified that all Buddha-bodies are like illusions and transformations; for those who make offerings, the merit is likewise equal.
With single-minded devotion, we entreat the Buddha to speak the *Ullambana Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on Repaying Kindness by Offering the Bowl*, translated by Dharmarakṣa (to be viewed as above).
This second [text] is appended to the Eastern Jin records; it is also known as the *Sūtra on the Merit of Offering Images*.
It is considerably more abbreviated than the first. For the sake of Maudgalyāyana, the Buddha spoke of making offerings to the *pravāraṇā* monks on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
The Dharma. He delivered his mother from the realm of hungry ghosts.
With single-minded devotion, he invited the Buddha to preach the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of the Elder Mahābala* (the details of the prostrations are as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhixiang and others of the Western Xia during the Song dynasty. When the Buddha was in the garden, the elder attained awakening in his heart.
For the sake of five hundred elders, he taught the impermanence of the world and the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. They all beheld the Buddha, who briefly explained the skillful means.
The elders sought the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna, and the Buddha spoke of the sublime practice of the six perfections as well as the faults and sufferings of birth and death.
The elders attained supreme patience (*anuttara-kṣānti*), left the household life, and received their predictions of enlightenment.

With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha to speak the *Sūtra on the Elder Guhagupta*, the *Sūtra of the Youth Candraprabha*, and the *Sūtra of the Original Life of Śunika*. (To be viewed as above.
Translated by the Sramana Narendrayaśas of the country of Udyāna during the Sui dynasty. Second, [the works of] the Western Jin dynasty, [by] Yue...
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhú Fǎhù of the Zhī kingdom. Third, translated by the Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra of Central India during the Liu Song dynasty.
[The second] is identical to the first; the third is abbreviated. The Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
A non-Buddhist (tīrthika) exhorted Guṇapāla to prepare fire-pits at each of the seven gates and to place poison in the food. He then invited the Buddha for the month-long [retreat].
The mother and son praised the Buddha’s merits; the thousand court ladies all rejoiced and sighed in admiration. Candraprabha declared that the Buddha could not be harmed.
The Buddha emitted light, universally summoning the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) of the ten directions to receive the offerings together.
Candraprabha, Candrottarā, Guṇadharā, and the youth Jñānadṛḍha all addressed their father with verses in praise of the Buddha. The Buddha manifested his spiritual powers.
[The Buddha] bestowed his power. The elder apologized and repented, whereupon he immediately received a prediction [of enlightenment]. Furthermore, it was said:
"In the age of the Final Dharma, Candraprabha shall become a great king in the land of China, named Mahācaryā (Great Conduct). He shall cause sentient beings to have faith in the Dharma;
through the power of his majestic virtue, he shall offer to the Buddha’s bowl, uphold all dharmas, and construct immeasurable stupas."

With single-minded devotion, I respectfully request the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of King Aśoka*, the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha Admonishing the King*, the *Sūtra Showing the Teaching to King Aśoka*, and the *Sūtra on the Dharma for Kings Spoken by the Buddha to the Devaputra Prabhāsa* (to be consulted as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śīghra from North India during the Song dynasty; secondly, by the layman Juqu Jing of the Liu Song dynasty.
Translated by [Yijing]. Third, translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of Ci’en Monastery in the Tang Dynasty.
Fourth, translated by the Śramaṇa Yijing of Jianfu Monastery in the Tang Dynasty. When the Buddha was at the Garden, he preached the Dharma for King Prasenajit:
"Govern the state with justice; do not covet sensual pleasures. Use the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather sentient beings," and he further spoke of suffering and emptiness.

The *Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* and other such texts are similar to the *King’s Dharma Sūtra*, with the exception that they additionally entrust the *Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī* to kings, ministers, and others.
The *Four Mountains* points to wrong conduct as old age, sickness, and death; this differs slightly from the treatment of old age, sickness, and death in the three aforementioned sūtras.
*The Sutra of the True Treatise on the Dharma for Kings Spoken by the Buddha for King Udayana* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Tang dynasty North Indian śramaṇa Amoghavajra. It sets forth the ten faults and ten virtues of emperors, the five types of decline, and the five dharmas that are delightful.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha to Expound the *Sūtra on the Kingdom of Uraśā* (to be venerated as above).
Appended to the Kaiyuan Catalogue under the Eastern Jin Record. The Buddha went to convert the king and the people of the country, leading them to realize suffering and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Solemnly requested for the Buddha’s preaching of the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* and the *Puṣpa-haraṇa-viruddha-rāja-buddhābhyupagata-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. Second: translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwuchen of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin.
No translation by Wúlán exists; this refers to the incident of "Plucking Flowers and Receiving Prediction" from the aforementioned sutra.

When the Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, King Pradīpa offered a lamp to the Buddha, and a poor woman likewise offered a single lamp and was the first to receive a prediction of enlightenment. Subsequently, the king took flowers to offer to the Buddha.

The King of Cīna first made offerings to the Buddha himself and obtained a prediction [of his future enlightenment]. The king, together with his queen and crown prince, personally fashioned precious flower-offering implements;
however, as soon as they were completed, the Buddha had already entered *nirvāṇa*. The king was filled with grief. Jīvaka said, "The Buddha is subject neither to birth nor to extinction.

If one’s utmost sincerity reaches its limit, the Buddha will appear. The king took the flowers and went to the mountain, where he saw the Buddha exactly as before. The Buddha then bestowed [the prediction upon him].
The record concludes; [the text] then disappears.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha to speak the *Sūtra on the Prophecy of Kṣamāvatī* (as for the ritual of prostration and viewing, it is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Bodhiruci of North India during the Northern Wei dynasty. The Buddha and Maitreya enter the city.
While begging for alms, he arrived at the palace of King Bimbisāra. Queen Śyāmavatī prepared a seat for him with a fine robe.
The Buddha spoke to her concerning the adornment of trees, and she received a prophecy.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha to Expound the *Bhadramukha-sūtra* (to be read with the same ritual prostrations as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin dynasty. The Buddha was expounding this sūtra in the kingdom of Magadha.
The consort of King Bimbisāra was Bhadrasrī; in this region [of China], she is called "Worthy Head" (*Xiánshǒu*). She wished to hear [the teaching] regarding the ten directions.
The Buddha expounded the names of the buddha-lands of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Next, [the disciple] asked about the method for transcending the female body;
the Buddha answered with ten dharmas, increasing from one to ten.
With a single mind, he reverently requested that the Buddha preach the *Sūtra on the Firm Woman* (the protocol for prostration is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Narendrayaśas of the country of Udyāna during the Sui Dynasty.

When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, he taught that women should abandon all faults and resolve upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta). Upon firmly resolving their minds, Śāriputra engaged them in dialogue, and the Buddha bestowed predictions of their future enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) upon them.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha to Expound the *Cittavidyā-sūtra* (Reverently viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Country during the Western Jin Dynasty. When the Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he went on his almsround.
The brahmin’s wife, fearing her husband, offered the Buddha but a single ladle of rice gruel. The Buddha bestowed upon her the prediction of enlightenment (bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa).
Subsequently, she and her husband both left the household life and realized the fruit [of arhatship].
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Sūtra of the Boy Suvarṇaprabha (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Tianxi’ai from Central India during the Song Dynasty. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, a Brāhmaṇa gave birth to a boy endowed with various auspicious signs.
The Buddha went to visit him, recounted his past karmic conditions, and bestowed a prophecy upon him.

With single-minded devotion, I respectfully request the *Buddhabhāṣita-mṛta-śiśu-sūtra*, the *Buddhabhāṣita-gṛhapati-putra-citra-sūtra*, and the *Buddhabhāṣita-bodhisattva-mṛta-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhi Fadu. Second, translated by the Anxi country śramaṇa An [Shigao] of the Later Han.
Translated by An Shigao. Thirdly, translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty.
At the age of sixteen, [the youth] Shi exhorted his mother to give alms to the Buddha. His mother was stingy; the Buddha then manifested his majestic spiritual power.
Shi urged his mother to share her own food and clothing with him to offer to the Buddha and seek the Unsurpassed Way. The Buddha then bestowed upon them a prophecy of enlightenment.
I single-mindedly entreat you to recite the *Buddhabhāṣita-nāgadattā-dārikā-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-nāgadatta-bodhisattva-pūrvayoga-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty. Second, [the version] from the Yuezhi country during the Western Jin dynasty... [Scribe's signature].
Translated by Zhu Fahu of the Later Han. While the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Nādikā, there was a daughter of the elder Suvīra named Nāgadattā.
While bathing, she saw the marks of the Buddha from afar and gave rise to the bodhicitta. Māra transformed himself into the likeness of her father and exhorted her to practice the Hīnayāna;

however, her resolve remained firm and unshakable. Māra then instructed her to throw herself from a tower. Nāgadattā then transformed her body into that of a male and received a prediction of enlightenment.
The second is the self-narrative of Nāgadatta. In the past, he was a venomous snake who served a practitioner of the Way.
When the practitioner departed, [the snake] climbed a tree and threw himself down to his death. He was reborn in the fourth heaven, and subsequently descended as the daughter of Sūfu.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Wife of the Householder Dharmavatsa (to be venerated as above).
This work is excerpted from Master Dao’an’s *Record of the Liang Region*. When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, he entered the city to beg for alms;
there, he transformed the wife of Dharmavatsa and her female servant into men and bestowed upon them the prediction of the Way (*vyākaraṇa*).
I single-mindedly entreat you to recite the *Buddhabhāṣita-kṣīraprabhāsabuddha-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-vatsa-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi in the Western Jin dynasty; secondly, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi in the Wu dynasty.
Regarding the matter of begging for milk, there is a brief passage on the Dharma taught by Vimalakīrti. Because of this, the Buddha...
The Buddha suffered from a wind ailment and instructed Ānanda to beg for milk from the house of a brahmin.

The brahmin reviled and disparaged him, but Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma and awakened his mind. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, transformed himself into a young cowherd tending a mother cow and her calf;

they joyfully offered them as an act of almsgiving. Ānanda informed the Buddha of this, and the Buddha recounted the past causes regarding the cows and bestowed upon them the prediction of attaining the Way.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Elder Jyotiṣka (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra of Central India during the Liu Song dynasty.
The Buddha spoke of how this elder, having in the past made offerings to a sick mendicant, now enjoys celestial blessings among humans that no king can deprive him of.
A Solemn Invocation to the *Bodhisattvacaryānirdeśa-sūtra* of Ratnadatta Bodhisattva (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Central India during the Song Dynasty. The Buddha, while begging for alms in the city of Vaiśālī, manifested supernatural transformations.
Ratnadatta was three years old when he offered a golden lotus to the Buddha. He engaged in mutual dialogue with Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, deeply clarifying the meaning of the Dharma.
He also engaged in dialogue with Mañjuśrī. Furthermore, eight bhikṣus vomited blood and passed away.
He fell into Avīci. The Buddha prophesied that after he emerged from hell, he would receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Ratnadatta offered a single vessel of food and drink to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and it was never exhausted. The Buddha then bestowed a prediction upon him.
A Solemn Invocation for the Scripture on the Exposition of the Profane and Sacred Vocations (to be viewed as above).

Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin. The Buddha, for the sake of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, taught that there are three treasures for the laity and three vocations for those who have left the home life; these are precisely the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
A Solemn Invocation for the *Upāsikā-śīla-viśuddhi-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* (to be venerated as above).
Transmitted from Master Dao’an’s *Liangtu lu*. Chapter on Practice. The Buddha was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, within the Hall of Joy (*Nandana-kuṭāgāra*).

There, the Mother Viśākhā, together with fifteen hundred faithful female lay disciples (*upāsikā*), inquired about the purification of conduct. The Buddha then related the causes and conditions of the past.

Next, nineteen practices of purity are shown; furthermore, ten dharmas of practice, fifty-eight dharmas, three great practices, four practices for attaining the Buddha-ground, four meditations on abiding, thirty-two meditations on impurity, and seven fetters are explained.
The three types of wholesome conduct; the eight recollections of a great person (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*); the chapter on training, which demonstrates fifty modes of training;
the sixfold training in luminosity; the thirty-two marks with their twenty modes of practice; and the chapter on auspicious responses, which demonstrates the eighty minor marks;
it further demonstrates the sixteen wonders at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth, as well as the thirty-two omens.

The *Pusa daoshu jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva at the Tree of Enlightenment), translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty; also known as the *Sigahami jing*. (For the ritual of reverent viewing, see above. Also known as...
The Samādhi of the Tree of the Path. Also titled the *Sihaka-samādhi Sūtra*.
When the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove, the elder’s son Sihaka-mei, together with five hundred disciples, saw the marks of the Buddha from afar. He asked: "How does one give rise to the bodhicitta?
How many kinds of joy of intention are there? How many merits lead to rest? What dharmas should be practiced? And by what means does one attain the Unconditioned?"

Regarding the patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*): by how many matters does one attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)? By how many dharmas does one abide? By how many dharmas does one attain parinirvāṇa?
After extinction (*parinirvṛta*), how many merits are there? What constitutes the truths (*satya*)? The Buddha answered each of these with six dharmas.
Consequently, he made a vow and received a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
A Solemn Invocation to the *Bodhisattvajanmabhūmi-sūtra* (to be venerated as above);
the translator is the same as above. The son of a wealthy elder of the Śākya clan, Kṣema, asked: "How may one quickly attain Buddhahood?"

The Buddha answered with two kinds of four matters: the offering of a pearl necklace to the Buddha, which transformed into a jeweled canopy; the manifestation of five hundred emanated beings to present offerings;
and the single-minded invitation for the Buddha to preach the *Pratītyasamutpāda-āryamārga-sūtra* and the Buddha’s own account of his contemplation beneath the Peṭaka tree.
*The Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*. *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Parable of the Old City* (to be consulted as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang of the Great Ci'en Monastery during the Tang Dynasty. Second, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi in Wu;
also titled *The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Heard at the City*. Third, [translated] in China during the Song Dynasty... [Middle India...]

Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharma-xian of the Tang Dynasty. The Buddha sat beneath a tree and contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*)—their forward progression and their cessation—and thereby attained perfect enlightenment. The second analogy concerns an old city:
contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both their direct and reverse orders is like traveling an ancient path to reach an old city.
I single-mindedly entreat you to peruse the *Vibhaṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra* (to be viewed as above),
translated by Xuanzang. Second, the translation by the South Indian śramaṇa Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty, consisting of ten [fascicles].
Because of one kind of excellence, ignorance is taught as the causal condition at the beginning of dependent origination. This excellence is sixfold: first, excellence of the object;
second, excellence of the aspect; third, excellence of the causal condition; fourth, excellence of the motivation; fifth, excellence of transformation; and sixth, excellence of wrong practice.
1. Seven characteristics; 2. Eight activities; 3. Nine obstacles; 4. Ten subsequent fetters; 5. Eleven remedies; 6.
One should single-mindedly entreat [the Buddha] for the *Mahāśrīparamārtha-sūtra* and the *Buddha-bhāṣita-pūrvajanma-saṃsāra-sūtra*.
The *Śālistamba Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha; the *Mahāyāna Śālistamba-upama-pratītyasamutpāda Sūtra* Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva (to be venerated as above). Part One:
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dānapāla from North India during the Song Dynasty. Part Two: [Translated by] the Upāsaka from the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Wu Dynasty.
Translated by Zhi Qian of the Saisai (Western Regions). Śāriputra spoke this for the bhikṣus. Three [versions] are appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin. Four:
translated by the North Indian śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Tang dynasty. The Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one can perceive and understand dependent origination through its twelve links, this is called seeing the Dharma and seeing the Buddha. Śāriputra...
For the benefit [of others], he requested Maitreya to explain the profound meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination.
With single-minded devotion, he entreated the Buddha to preach the *Dharmakāya-sūtra* (the ritual of prostration is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Fǎxián of Central India during the Song dynasty. This work explains the two kinds of merit: those of the *dharmakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The *Dharmakāya-saṃgīta-ekottarika-dharma-saṃkhyā-sūtra*.
A single-minded invocation for the Buddha to expound the Sūtra on the Ten Epithets (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Tian Xizai from Central India during the Song dynasty. Spoken by the Buddha for Ānanda.

With single-minded devotion, I respectfully entreat you to receive and praise the *Sūtra on the Merits of the Mahāyāna* and the *Sūtra on the Determination of Karma-obstructions in the Sublime Dharma*. (To be consulted as above.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang of the Great Ci'en Monastery during the Tang Dynasty. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta of the Kingdom of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty.
The Buddha was dwelling in the Palace of the Dharma-realm Treasury. The Bodhisattva Guṇavicitra asked: "By what causes and conditions..."

These are the evil friends of newly initiated bodhisattvas. The Buddha said that those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) would rather fall into hell than give rise to the mental orientation of the two vehicles.
This clarifies the sin of slandering the Mahāyāna and explains the meaning of the name and the significance of the Great [Vehicle].
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Sūtra of the Four Dharmas. *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation of the Four Dharmas* (to be venerated as above).
Translated for the first time by the Śramaṇa Divākara from Central India during the Tang Dynasty. This is the second translation; it differs only slightly.
The Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, preaching to the bhikṣus: First, not abandoning the bodhicitta; Second, not abandoning...
Good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Third, not abandoning the joy of endurance (*kṣānti*). Fourth, not abandoning the forest hermitage (*āraṇya*).
With a single mind, I reverently entreat [you to recite] the *Mahāyāna-caturdharma-sūtra* (the ritual for viewing is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty. When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, Mañjuśrī, with...

The Chapter on Praise, which is established through one hundred and eighty dharmas; the Chapter on Entrustment, consisting of Ānanda’s verses of praise;
and the ten dharmas for upholding this sutra: writing it down, making offerings to it, and so forth, up to practicing these ten dharmas.

It contains incantations spoken by each of the seven Buddhas, incantations spoken by various bodhisattvas, and incantations spoken by various celestial immortals and stellar deities.
It includes the vows and verses spoken by the bodhisattvas, as well as the Five Doubts, the Five Faiths, and the Twenty-five Kings of Samādhi spoken by Vajragarbha. [It provides] protection.
The *Sūtra on the Great Divine Incantations Spoken by the Eighteen Deities Who Protect the Saṃghārāma and the Four Heavenly Kings*, who take refuge in the precepts;
the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Heart-Seal of the Secret Casket of the True Dharma of All Tathāgatas*;
and the *Dhāraṇī of the Jewel Casket Seal of the Heart-Secret Whole-Body Relics of All Tathāgatas*. (I prostrate and gaze upon them with single-minded devotion.)
(As above) Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Hu of North India during the Song dynasty. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Wisdom from North India during the Tang dynasty.
When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha, [he addressed] the Brahmin Vimalaprabhā...
He was invited through the gate. On the way, he saw an ancient stūpa; he circumambulated it and made offerings, weeping with tears falling like rain.
The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise all shed tears. Vajrapāṇi asked for the reason, and the Buddha then spoke this heart-mantra, exhorting people to build stūpas and make offerings.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the *Ārya-jyotirmātā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Fa-tian of Central India during the Song Dynasty. The Buddha was dwelling in the great city of Aṇakāvatī.
Vajrapāṇi requested the recitation of a mantra to protect sentient beings from being harmed by malevolent stars and constellations.
*The Sūtra of the Holy Invincible Vajra-fire Dhāraṇī*, translated by Fǎtién (to be read with the same ritual as above).
When the Buddha was on Mount Sumeru, he commanded Vajrapāṇi to recite the mantra to comfort the devas and nāgas.
The Yakṣas and others, with single-minded devotion, requested the Buddha to preach the *Mahāvajragandhā Dhāraṇī Sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śīlagupta of North India during the Song Dynasty. It contains a single mantra for subduing all devas and lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
There is no ritual manual.

With single-minded devotion, I reverently invoke the *Buddhabhāṣita-jñānaprabha-sarvakarmāvaraṇa-viśodhana-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-jñānolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (the procedure for prostration and viewing is as above).
Translated by Shi Hu. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Ti-yun-ban-ruo and others from the Kingdom of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty.
When the Buddha was in the palace of the Sun and Moon Devas, he spoke the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as well as mantras. Samantabhadra said:
"If one recites [the mantras] six times daily for twenty-one days with a sincere heart and repents, one can destroy the Avīci Hell. He further spoke...
One incantation to protect it. Second Translation. The Buddha was dwelling in the Palace of the Sun and Moon. Buddhas from the four directions assembled there.
The Son of Heaven of the Sun and Moon requested the dhāraṇī. All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas spoke the incantation with one voice.
Samantabhadra praised and exhorted its reception and upholding.

I single-mindedly entreat you to accept [these copies of]: the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra on the Assembly of All Buddhas*, the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra on the Vajra Life Span Spoken by All Tathāgatas*, and the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra for Averting Premature Death* (to be viewed as above), translated by Ti-yun-po-luo (Tibhyanapra).
Second, those by the Śramaṇa Vajrabodhi of South India during the Tang dynasty and [Amoghavajra].
Translated from Tibetan. Thirdly, translated by Shi Hu. When the Buddha was on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, he removed the fear of death for sentient beings.
With a snap of his fingers, he summoned the Buddhas of the ten directions, who spoke the mantra with one voice. Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada and the Four Heavenly Kings [also joined].
Each also recites its own mantra. Next, the methods for the altar (*maṇḍala*) are explained; the latter two do not require an altar.

[These include] the *Sūtra on the Comparative Merit of the Twelve Buddha Names, Divine Mantras, and the Elimination of Obstacles and Destruction of Sins* through Single-Minded Invocation, and the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Divine Mantra Praising the Merits of the Tathāgata* (the protocols for worship are the same as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta of Northern India during the Tang Dynasty. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Great Jianfu Monastery during the Tang Dynasty.
[This text contains] the Buddha’s discourse to Maitreya on the three Buddhas of the eastern direction, the names of one Buddha for each of the remaining nine directions, and the dhāraṇīs.
With single-minded devotion, we invoke the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East to assist in upholding and protecting the *Lokapāla-mantra-sūtra*,
the *Buddhabhāṣita-padadhara-mantra-sūtra*, the *Buddhabhāṣita-dhāraṇī-pātra-sūtra*,
and the *Ārya-paramottama-pradīpa-tathāgata-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (the ritual of prostration is as described above).
Translated by the Sui dynasty North Indian śramaṇa Jñānagupta; second, translated by the Wu dynasty Yuezhi lay devotee (upāsaka) Zhi Qian;
third, translated by the Eastern Jin dynasty Western Region śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Hu of Northern India during the Song Dynasty. The second [version] is also titled the *Dhāraṇīpada Sūtra*.
When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King from the East dispatched a supreme Bodhisattva to this place to recite the mantra.
Next were the Bodhisattvas Ajita, Mañjuśrī, and Śākya, as well as four others...
The Heavenly Kings likewise each recited mantras.
With single-minded devotion, they entreated the Buddha to preach the *Sutra on the Dhāraṇī of the Flower-Arrayed Pavilion*, the *Sutra on the Divine Mantra of the Flower-Cluster Dhāraṇī*,
the *Sutra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin*, and the *Buddha-Spoken Sutra on the Flower-Cluster Dhāraṇī*.
*Zhòujīng* (To be consulted as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śīladharma of Northern India during the Song dynasty. The second [version] was translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi kingdom during the Wu dynasty.
The third and fourth are appended to the catalog of the Eastern Jin. When the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta with the Dragon King...
In the palace, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita questioned the Buddha regarding the merits of [the Dharma] and the merits of making offerings.
The Buddha analyzed these for him and also spoke a dhāraṇī, exhorting him to uphold it.
The Sutra of the Dhāraṇī for Solemn Invocation to Relieve Suffering and Calamity (to be read as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang of the Great Ci'en Monastery during the Tang Dynasty.
When the Buddha was at the Jetavana Grove, the Bodhisattva Inexpressible Array asked about the method for saving sentient beings from suffering. The Buddha then expounded upon the Tathāgata Acala.
The two dhāraṇīs of the Tathāgata Nirmāṇarāja;
with single-minded devotion, I reverently entreat the *Buddhamātṛ-mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-māyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra on the Great Peacock Spell-King Spoken by the Buddha*. *The Sūtra on the Divine Spell of the Great Peacock King Spoken by the Buddha*.
*The Sūtra on the Miscellaneous Divine Spells of the Great Peacock King Spoken by the Buddha*. *The Sūtra on the Spell of the Great Golden Peacock King* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Tang dynasty North Indian śramaṇa Amoghavajra. Second: [Translated during the] Liang dynasty from Funan.
Translated by the Sramana Sanghapala of the [Former] Liang dynasty. Third, translated by the Sramana Shi Yijing of Da Jianfu Monastery in Tang China;
the Chinese and Indic pronunciations differ slightly. Fourth, translated by the Sramana Bo Shilimiduoluo of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Fifth, the translation is identical. Sixth, translated by the Sramana from Northern India during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated by Kumārajīva. These three [texts] are all small portions of the aforementioned sūtra. When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, the bhikṣu Śariputra (Śa-ti) was bitten by a snake;

Ānanda sought help, and the Buddha preached the Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī (Great Peacock Spell), along with the names of various spirits, devas, buddhas, and bodhisattvas, as well as divine mantras, to rescue him. This sūtra was translated by Ān Shìgāo.
The divine spirits were presented with abundant offerings; thus, the means by which they comforted the myriad souls was most profound.
Consequently, they were able to universally eliminate all harm and affliction, each exhausting their merit and fully manifesting the divine power of great compassion.
The Ritual Manual for the Altar of the Painted Image of the Great Peacock Wisdom-King Spoken by the Buddha (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Tang Dynasty North Indian Śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
A Solemn Invocation to the *Bodhimaṇḍālaṃkāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be venerated as above). Translated by the Great and Vast Wisdom Amoghavajra.

When the Buddha was dwelling in the Vast and Expansive Garden (*Vipula-vana*), he preached this dhāraṇī for the sake of the brahmin Viṇhudatta, who sought a son, so that all roots of goodness might be planted and all aspirations fulfilled.
The Sutra of the Dhāraṇī of the Tathāgata Holy King of the Decisive Radiance of Immeasurable Life (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Fātian of Central India during the Song Dynasty. The Buddha spoke to Mañjuśrī concerning Immeasurable Life.
Dhāraṇī. It can increase one’s lifespan and bring great benefit.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha to speak the *Tathāgata-alaṃkāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra of the Unconquerable Banner King*. (The ritual for prostration and viewing is as above.)
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Hu of Northern India during the Song Dynasty. When the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Śakra was defeated by the asuras.
The Buddha then preached this dhāraṇī; if it is written upon banners and flags, no enemy whatsoever shall be able to prevail.

With single-minded devotion, I entreat you to recite the *Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of Supreme Adornment* and the *Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Precious Girdle* spoken by the Buddha (to be venerated as above), translated by Shi Hu.
At that time, the Buddha was in the city of Kapilavastu. While the youth Rāhula was lying down, he was afflicted by an evil rākṣasa...
Afflicted by the *kṣetra-dāruṇa* (harmful spirits), the Buddha preached a mantra to protect them, and further taught the *dhāraṇī* for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
Maitreya and the Brahma King likewise each preached mantras.
With single-minded devotion, one should reverently invoke the *Mahā-śubhārtha-mantra-sūtra* (as for the ritual of worship, see above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanyao, Chief Administrator of the Xiaozhuan Office of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
First, it explains the rites for taking refuge, burning incense, and inviting the Triple Gem, as well as the respective dhāraṇī methods for devas and nāgas.

Next, it clarifies how Śakra-devendra was defeated by the asuras, and how the Buddha then preached the Great Boundary-binding Dhāraṇī. Following this, there are all the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, listed in successive order.
Assisting the Buddha in the recitation of mantras, the Buddha then expounded the dharma for its accomplishment.
*The Sutra of the Dhāraṇī of Vajrajvālā for Stilling Wind and Rain* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Bodhiruci of South India during the Tang Dynasty. [Concerning] the Buddha and the Mahākāya Nairṛta.
Together with the various heavenly kings, each spoke of the methods for subduing evil nāgas and ceasing wind and rain.
With single-minded devotion, they entreated the Buddha to preach the *Āryatārā-bodhisattva-sūtra* (the ritual of prostration is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Central India during the Song dynasty. When the Buddha was on Mount Gandhamādana, for the sake of Pañcaśikha the Gandharva...
The Gandharva King recites the mantra and hymns of praise of the Noble Tārā Bodhisattva; those who uphold them shall be able to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
*The Sutra of the One Hundred and Eight Names of the Noble Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva* (the ritual for worship and contemplation is the same as above).

Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Tian Xizai during the Song Dynasty. Spoken by the Buddha on Mount Potalaka, this scripture teaches that those who uphold it shall also be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
A Solemn Invocation to the One Hundred and Eight Names of the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī (the ritual for worship is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Fātian of Central India during the Song Dynasty. Spoken by the Buddha: The Dhāraṇī of the One Hundred and Eight Names of the Bodhisattva;
those who uphold it shall attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
Solemnly Invoked: The Sūtra on the Great Auspiciousness Dhāraṇī Spoken by the Buddha (to be viewed as above).

Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Central India during the Song Dynasty. When the Buddha was in the Buddha-field of Sukhavatī, Avalokiteśvara requested that he preach a dhāraṇī so that sentient beings might attain great wealth and nobility.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Twelve Mudrās and One Hundred and Eight Names of the Immaculate Great Auspicious Goddess (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Tang dynasty North Indian Śramaṇa Amoghavajra. The Buddha was dwelling in the World of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
To the fearless Avalokiteśvara, he spoke the thirty-eight auspicious names, as well as the twelve mudrās,
the one hundred and eight names, and the mantra of the stainless praise.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Twelve Names of the Great Auspicious Goddess (to be venerated as above), translated by Amoghavajra of Vast Wisdom.
When the Buddha was dwelling in the World of Ultimate Bliss, he spoke this mantra for the sake of Avalokiteśvara;
it is capable of eliminating poverty and all inauspiciousness.
I single-mindedly entreat you to accept the *Mahāyāna-aṣṭamahāmaṇḍala-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-aṣṭabodhisattvamaṇḍala-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Central India during the Song dynasty. Second, [translated by] the Śramaṇa Da... from Northern India during the Tang dynasty.
Translated by Guǎngzhì Bùkōng. There are praises for eight bodhisattvas. When the Buddha was on Mount Potalaka, the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha-Candraprabha requested him to speak [this teaching].
First, one should install the Buddha in the center; next, one installs the eight great bodhisattvas, namely:
Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, Ākāśagarbha, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, and Mañjuśrī.
The *Śrī-Ghanavyūha-Kṣitigarbha* contains nine mantras in total.
A single-minded invocation to the *Vimalaprabhāsa-mahādhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Mito-shan and others from the country of Tukhāra during the Tang dynasty. When the Buddha was in the city of Kapilavastu...
In the vihāra, it was foretold that the Brahmin Kapphiṇa Caṇḍa would meet his end after seven days.
A master of physiognomy informed him of this, and out of fear he came to see the Buddha. The Buddha commanded him to repair an ancient stūpa and to recite divine mantras;
thus his life-force would be prolonged, he would be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and eventually attain Buddhahood. Thereupon, the Buddha spoke on the stūpa.
And the dhāraṇī ritual.
With single-minded devotion, I reverently invoke the *Svalpākṣara-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Holy Mother of Buddhas (the method for prostration and viewing is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Tian Xizai from Central India during the Song dynasty. When the Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Holy Avalokiteśvara...
I entreat the Buddha to speak this. Furthermore, I shall recite the sublime and wondrous *Prajñāpāramitā-dhāraṇī*.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat [the Buddha to speak] the *Sarvabuddha-hṛdaya-mudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and the *Sarvabuddha-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (the ritual for prostration is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmadeva of Central India during the Song Dynasty. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Great Ci’en Monastery during the Tang Dynasty.
The Buddha, while in Tuṣita Heaven, preached two dhāraṇīs; those who hear them shall not be born into the realm of Māras and will swiftly realize Bodhi.
With single-minded devotion, I reverently request the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvavidyut-vighna-praṇidhāna-siddhi-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-cintāmaṇi-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang of the Great Ci’en Monastery during the Tang Dynasty. Second, [the version] from the Song Dynasty by the [monk] from North India...
Translated by Fenshi Hu. When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he spoke to Ānanda regarding the names of lightning in the four directions and recited divine mantras.
Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Brahmā, and Śakra each likewise recited mantras, and he also commanded the dragons to recite one mantra.
This is identical to what is taught in the middle fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
It appears to be the *Sūtra on the Inquiry of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha Concerning the Dhāraṇīs of the Seven Buddhas*,
the *Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Skillful Means and Mantras*, and the *Ārya-Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Appendix to the Liang Record. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta of North India during the Sui Dynasty.
Third, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmadeva of Central India during the Song Dynasty.

When the Buddha was atop Mount Vairaśikhara, one bhikṣu was afflicted by illness, and another bhikṣu was tormented by a ghost. Gaganagañja sought out the Buddha, and the Buddha manifested his spiritual power.
[The] Power. All seven Buddhas each spoke a mantra in mid-air. The Sui translation is the same.
In the Song translation, there is the account of a naked bhikṣu crying out and the occurrence of the mantras being spoken from the void.
With single-minded devotion, I respectfully request the *Buddhabhāṣita-yamāntaka-preta-tāraṇī-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-yamāntaka-preta-dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Tang Dynasty North Indian Śramaṇa Amoghavajra. Second: [Translated by] the Tang Dynasty [monk from] the Kingdom of Khotan.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda. While the Buddha was at the Nyagrodha Park, Ānanda was dwelling alone, reflecting upon the teachings he had received.
During the third watch of the night, he saw a hungry ghost with flaming mouth; terrified, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha then expounded for him the *Dhāraṇī of Immeasurable Majestic Virtue, Sovereign Radiance, and Supreme Wondrous Power*, which immediately transformed [the ghost].
The *Bhojana-mantra* (Food Mantra), along with the names of the four Tathāgatas—Prabhūtaratna, Suvarṇavarṇa, Vipula-kāya, and Abhaya-dāyaka—are recited.
If one performs the rite for hungry ghosts (*preta*), it is repeated seven times; for sages (*ṛṣi*) and others, fourteen times; and for the Three Jewels (*triratna*), twenty-one times.
Thus the *Yankou Fa* (Rite of Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) originated. In the second translation, the names of the four Buddhas are missing.
*The Ritual Manual for the Yoga-Collection Essentials: The Dhāraṇī of Teaching Ānanda, the Flaming Mouth (Yogajuyao jiao anantu zhou yan kou yi gui jing)* (To be consulted as above).
Translated by the Tang dynasty North Indian Śramaṇa Mahāprajñā Amoghavajra. It contains the method for invocation and the rite for breaking the earth.
One seal-mantra each for the prison, one seal-mantra each for summoning hungry ghosts, one seal-mantra each for summoning transgressions,
one seal-mantra each for destroying transgressions, one seal-mantra each for purifying karma, and one seal-mantra each for repentance.
One mudrā and one mantra for Amṛta; one mudrā and one mantra for opening the throat;
one mudrā and one mantra for the names of the Seven Tathāgatas and the arousal of bodhicitta; one mudrā and one mantra for receiving the samaya precepts;
one mudrā and two mantras for the offering of food; one mudrā and one mantra for universal offerings; and one mudrā and one mantra for the ritual dismissal.
With single-minded devotion, I respectfully request the Buddha to preach the *Sūtra of the Dharani of the Sublime Gate for Extending Life*,

the *Sūtra of the Divine Mantra of the Dharma-gate for Protecting Life*, the *Dharani of Skillful Means of the Good Dharma*, and the *Dharani of the Vajra Secret Sublime Gate* (the ritual of prostration and viewing is as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Central India during the Song Dynasty. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Bodhiruci of South India during the Tang Dynasty.
The third and fourth are appended to the records of the Eastern Jin. When the Buddha was at the site of his attainment of Perfect Enlightenment, Vajrapāṇi requested that he preach a sublime mantra.
The Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows, and the Buddhas of the ten directions assembled to offer praise and assistance. Next, the two [sections] are clarified.

Ten Merits. Second Translation. Many incantations, such as those of Vajrapāṇi, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Kings, Hārītī, Vajrapāṇi, Maheśvara, Kumāra Senāpati, Candraprabha Devaputra, Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, Himavat, Mahāyakṣa, and the Goddess Vajra-Śaṅkara.

With single-minded devotion, I respectfully request the *Buddhabhāṣita-saptakoṭi-buddhamātṛ-tāre-daśamahāvidyā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Recitation and Contemplative Practice; and the *Buddhabhāṣita-saptakoṭi-buddhamātṛ-hṛdaya-mahācundī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
The *Saptakoṭi-buddhamātṛ-bhāṣita-cundī-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be venerated as above), translated by the Śramaṇa Vajrabodhi of South India during the Tang Dynasty.
Second, [the version] by the Śramaṇa of Central India during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by Divākara. Thirdly, translated by the Tang dynasty North Indian śramaṇa Mahāprajñā Amoghavajra.
When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, he contemplated future sentient beings and preached the past seven-koṭi Tārā-tathāgata-dhāraṇī.

The Precious Repentance of the Dharma-Wheel for the Water and Land Rituals, Volume One, Part Two.
Solemn Invocation of the *Buddhabhāṣita-maitreya-bodhisattva-praṇidhāna-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Prostrations as before).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Fa-tian of Central India during the Tang Dynasty. The Buddha spoke this mantra for Maitreya; Maitreya made his vow;
he was delivered from suffering and received his prediction of enlightenment.
With a single mind, I reverently entreat the Buddha to speak the *Śatasahasra-mudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).

Appended to the Eastern Jin Records, secondly appended to the Liang Records. The mantras are somewhat more numerous; [this section] concerns the suppression by a Caṇḍāla woman.
To delude Ānanda, [the demon] used incantations to destroy him.

Mantra. A Solemn Invocation to the Buddha’s Discourse on the Great Protective Vidyā-Mahādhāraṇī Sūtra (Prostrations as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmadeva of Central India during the Song Dynasty. The Buddha was staying at the village of Malada. He went forth...

[It contains] the section on "The Swift Attainment of Siddhi through the Assistance of the Master and His Companions," wherein the Bodhisattva Subāhu achieves accomplishment through recitation.
The question was posed regarding non-attainment. Vajrapāṇi replied: "One should abandon the afflictions, give rise to deep faith, resolve upon bodhicitta, revere the Triple Gem, and have faith in me.
One should take refuge in the Great Vajra Family, distance oneself from the ten unwholesome karmas, and always remain free from delusion and false views. One must enter that great maṇḍala of samaya."
Relying upon the empowerment of that holy power, you must further give rise to a courageous mind and awaken the bodhicitta.
Believe only in me, and do not believe in external paths, celestial māras, or the like.
First, you must seek out an ācārya who is most excellent in terms of preceptual virtue, purity, and merit—just as one who sows crops requires fertile soil. If there is residual karma...
One must select an excellent location to construct a stūpa and enshrine an image, performing offerings, praises, repentance, and recitation.
Furthermore, one must have companions, like the two wheels of a chariot. This consists of: the section on selecting an excellent site;

the section on distinguishing the rosary and maintaining the mind while remaining free from obstacles. Whenever performing recitation, one should employ mantras and mudrās to withdraw and collect the mind, [freeing it] from greed.
If hatred, delusion, and so forth are prevalent, one should practice the meditations on impurity, loving-kindness and compassion, dependent origination, and so on.
All wholesome dharmas should be dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi, just as all rivers flow into the ocean. Furthermore, one should not allow the small to obstruct the great.
One should also remain far removed from the eight worldly concerns. Moreover, one must not consume food that has been offered as a remnant of a ritual, nor...
The *piśāca* remains as the leavings of the spirits; this is the portion for Vajrapināyaka. First, the method for the *vajra* is distinguished;
next, it is explained that there are four classes of obstructing *pināyakas*, who can only be repelled by the Great Mantra (*mahāvidyā*).
Furthermore, when performing recitation, offerings, *homa*, and so forth, if one does not act according to the ritual law, and...
If there is a deficiency in ritual procedure, or if the practitioner’s mind harbors doubt, or if they discuss mundane worldly matters, those who create obstacles will find their opportunity.
Next, the method for protecting the body shall be explained so that they may not find such an opportunity.
Regarding the section on distinguishing the signs of *siddhi*, one must not add or subtract anything from the mantras or the maṇḍala.
Regarding the transmission: furthermore, one must not exchange this dharma for that dharma. One must possess two qualities for *siddhi* to be accomplished:
first, the practitioner must be fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts, be diligent and energetic, and be free from greed and envy.
One must not be stingy. Second, the syllables and phrases of the mantra must be complete; the vocal characteristics must be distinct, and the recitation must be neither too slow nor too fast.
The sound should be harmonious and flowing, neither too loud nor too silent. Furthermore, one must not allow the mind to dwell on other objects or be interrupted by miscellaneous speech.
This is known as the stage of attaining proximate *siddhi*. To fully attain the primary *siddhi*, one must first be equipped with these [requirements].

Observe the eight precepts for four days, or three, or two full days and nights; furthermore, one must abstain from food before seeking *siddhi*. The Section on Explaining Accomplishment (*Sādhana-bhāga*).

Translated by the Śramaṇa Śīlaskandha Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty at Yuhua Monastery. Part One: Chapter One, the Prologue. The Buddha...
Dwelling on Vulture Peak, the Buddha, together with the fourfold assembly and the bodhisattvas, sat upon lion thrones that he himself had spread with *niketa* mats.
He sat cross-legged and entered the sublime samādhi known as the King of Meditative Concentrations (*samādhirāja*). Upon arising from this absorption, he surveyed the ten directions;
from every pore of his body, countless rays of light issued forth, illuminating the great trichiliocosm as well as all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
In every buddha-field, those who encounter this light will certainly attain bodhi. Furthermore, he manifests his constant radiance and extends his broad and long tongue;
various colored lights appear as precious lotus flowers, upon which transformation-buddhas preach the Prajñāpāramitā. Those who hear it will certainly attain bodhi.
He further entered the *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*, causing this great trichiliocosm and the lands of the ten directions to shake in six ways.
Those in the evil realms were freed from suffering and reborn among gods and humans, all coming together for the Buddha’s assembly.

The Buddha manifested his original form-body (*rūpakāya*), enabling all sentient beings in this realm to behold him. The devas scattered flowers that formed flower pedestals, equal in size [to the Buddha].

A thousand [times]. The adornments of this land are like those of Sukhāvatī. Furthermore, light is emitted from his face and eyes, illuminating the lands of the ten directions, so that sentient beings here and there may see one another.

Great Bodhisattvas from the various lands of the ten directions each receive the Buddha’s command and present a thousand stalks of golden lotuses. The Buddha accepts these flowers and scatters them back across the named lands.
The Buddhas upon the lotus pedestals preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā; one will certainly attain Bodhi.
This realm is like the assembly in the Pure Land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma in the world Padmāvatī.
Chapter Two: On the Study of Contemplation. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain perfect awakening to all phenomena and all their characteristics, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
that is, by taking non-apprehension as their power and means, they are able to fulfill the six perfections. To speak in brief: all worldly and world-transcending phenomena are merely names."
In reality, nothing can be apprehended. Regarding both the name and that which is named, the bodhisattva finds nothing to be grasped, because they do not perceive them and thus lack attachment.
Such wisdom is incomparable to the wisdom of the śrāvakas, for it accomplishes superior tasks.
The śrāvaka is like a firefly, while the bodhisattva is like the sun. From the first generation of the mind of awakening...
Bodhi constantly serves as the true field of merit for those of the two vehicles; thus, it has already repaid the kindness of all donors.
Chapter Three: Correspondence. This refers to being in correspondence with the emptiness of all aggregates, bases, and elements, up to and including unsurpassed bodhi;
it is in correspondence with the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet one does not perceive any sign.

Whether in association or dissociation, one should skillfully establish sentient beings in the realm of nirvāṇa so that Māra finds no opportunity, afflictions are subdued and extinguished, and one is protected by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Should there be karmic offenses, they will be transformed so as to be experienced lightly in the present.
One does not perceive phenomena as corresponding with emptiness, nor does one perceive emptiness as corresponding with phenomena; ultimately, [such conceptualization] does not arise.
The obstructive states of mind— namely, stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, indolence, distraction, and faulty wisdom—
will naturally give way as the six perfections manifest spontaneously and without interruption.
Chapter Four: On Rebirth. Śāriputra asked: "Where do Bodhisattvas of Prajñā pass away to be reborn here?
Having passed away here, where will they be reborn? The Buddha answered him: "A bhikṣu offered new, clean robes to the Buddha and resolved upon the unsurpassed mind.

Chapter Sixty-one: On the Non-duality of Many Questions. When a bodhisattva does not conceptualize form and so forth, at that time they are able to increase the roots of virtue they have planted and are able to bring the pāramitās to fulfillment.

This is because such a bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma within which they might give rise to attachment or abide. Prajñā is the root of all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*);
if one regresses from prajñā, one thereby regresses from and loses all pure dharmas. [This is] the profound prajñā...

Just as a skilled charioteer guides other excellent dharmas along the right path to reach the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), so too does Prajñāpāramitā follow wherever it goes and lead all other virtues to that same destination.

The path of benefiting others; the path of the knowledge of all modes; the path that does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa—this is the bodhisattva path.

Profound prajñā can accomplish this great task: it reveals the characteristics of what is the path and what is not the path, enabling bodhisattvas to know them and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
The Buddha Śāntaprajña remained as a transformation body for half an eon, performing [these deeds].
Regarding the various deeds of the Buddhas, one should have faith that all phenomena are like magical transformations. Subhūti asked:
"If all phenomena consist merely of names and signs, for what purpose does a bodhisattva generate the mind of enlightenment and practice with diligent austerity?
The Buddha replied: "Because all phenomena consist merely of names and signs, they are provisionally designated; yet the nature of these names and signs is empty."
All classes of sentient beings cling to perverted views and fail to escape from birth and death;

therefore, the Bodhisattva resolves to practice the path, realizes the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and delivers them by means of the three vehicles, causing them to transcend birth and death.
They enter the realm of nirvāṇa; yet, all names and signs are without arising and without cessation, nor can any designation of abiding or change be found.
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is shared with the two vehicles; the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) is shared with bodhisattvas;

and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the sublime, unshared wisdom of the Tathāgata. The Buddha said: "I speak of this by relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) for the sake of verbal expression."
[The Buddha] said: It does not rely on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Within the ultimate truth, there is no path for language.
Chapter Sixty-two: On Speaking the Truth. The Buddha said: "For example, it is like planting trees in a fertile field.
Although a person does not see the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of these trees, nor anyone who receives them, once the trees have been planted, they are irrigated."
When watered and protected, it gradually grows and flourishes so that all people may enjoy its fruits, their illnesses cured and they find peace. It is the same for the Bodhisattva:

although they do not perceive the existence of sentient beings or a Buddha-fruit, they seek enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, cultivating and perfecting the path until they realize it, so that all sentient beings may enjoy the Buddha-tree. Regarding the suffering of the evil realms, those who benefit through the flowers are born among humans and devas; those who benefit through the fruit abide in the fruits of the three vehicles.

Within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no conceptual differentiation whatsoever.

If all phenomena are like dreams and illusions, in what location do the sentient beings to be converted reside, such that they are extracted and delivered? The Buddha said: They reside in the false conceptualization of names and signs;
they are extracted and delivered from this. These [beings] are adventitious and provisional; although they are taught to abide in the realm of signlessness (*animitta-dhātu*).
He does not cause them to fall into the two extremes of grasping— namely, that "this is a sign" or "this is signless"—
