Chapter on the Vajra Body: The body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and indestructible, due to the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma in the past.
Chapter on Names and Merits: Explaining the meaning of the Great Parinirvāṇa.
The Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature has four meanings: first, self-correction; second, correcting others; third, the ability to answer questions as they arise;
and fourth, skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions. Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One, you possess only secret speech."
There is no secret treasury; it causes all sentient beings to fully know and see. The Buddha spoke of one hundred phrases of liberation.
He further spoke of four types of people as the refuge of the world. He also clarified the characteristics that distinguish the sūtras and vinaya spoken by the Buddha from those spoken by Māra.
Furthermore, he stated that those who know the eternally abiding know the Four Noble Truths. Again, he spoke of the four...

These are the characteristics of perversion. Furthermore, there are the parables of the poor woman and the golden treasure, the ointment on the breast and the washing of the breast, the jewel on the forehead of a strong man, and the medicinal flavor of the Snowy Mountains. The Vaipulya sutras are like nectar, yet they are also like poison;
when digested, they are like dew, but if not digested, they act as poison. In the Mahāyāna, there is no differentiation regarding the Three Refuges.

This is its characteristic. Furthermore, the nature of non-duality is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*). Moreover, there is the analogy of using a golden probe to remove a cataract so as to reveal two or three fingers;
and there is the extensive explanation of the analogy of a bodhisattva on the tenth stage seeing but a small portion of the nature.

The ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) are identical to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, he speaks of the metaphor of the sword in the royal treasury; he also speaks of the fourteen vowels as being called "phonemes" (*mātṛkā*).
Next, he clarifies the teachings of the "half-syllables" (*ardhamātrā*) and the "full-syllables. He further speaks of the metaphor of two birds flying together.

Furthermore, he cites the metaphors of the moon having neither half nor full phases and its rising and setting, as well as the metaphor of the sun’s varying lengths during the three periods of the day.
He further states that while this sutra benefits all beings, it alone cannot benefit those who are icchantikas.
Next, he explains the metaphor of the single name "Sampadā" which has four actual meanings, using it to illustrate how the Tathāgata’s esoteric speech is difficult to understand. He then clarifies...

One who knows for themselves that they possess Buddha-nature is called one with the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Furthermore, for the sake of Mañjuśrī, he explained the verses on "that which was originally non-existent but now exists.
In the "Chapter on the Questions of the Entire Assembly," light radiated from the Buddha’s face, illuminating the body of Cunda, who then received it.

He made offerings to the manifested buddhas and the Sangha. Accepting the offerings of the great assembly, he expounded the meanings of all the sūtras—both those with remainder and those without remainder—for the sake of taming all sentient beings. Desiring to manifest illness, he lay down on his right side.
Chapter on Manifesting Illness: Bodhisattva Kāśyapa exhorts the Buddha to arise; light illuminates all things, and he then proclaims the secret teaching.
Furthermore, he speaks of five types of persons who manifest illness: namely, those of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path and the pratyekabuddha, but not the Tathāgata.
Chapter on Noble Conduct. There are five types of conduct: first, noble conduct; second, Brahma-conduct; third, celestial conduct; fourth, infantile conduct; and fifth, sickly conduct.
Furthermore, there is one type of conduct which is the Tathāgata’s conduct, namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Next, the noble conduct is clarified: one guards the precepts as one would guard a life-preserving float, without relying on Māra at all.
[He] divided [it] into halves, quarters, and portions the size of a hand, down to even a single thread.

Furthermore, it is said that he attained the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), dwelt on the stage of endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), contemplated the Four Noble Truths, and eventually dwelt on the stage of fearlessness (*abhaya-bhūmi*), attaining twenty-five samādhis and destroying the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
Next, in response to the question concerning dwelling in the King of the Stainless Treasury (*vimalagarbharāja*) who emerged from the ox:
The Parable of the Milk; and the account of how, in the past, he sacrificed his body to seek half a verse.
From the Chapter on the Holy Life (*Brahmacarya-varga*), spoken for the sake of Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: by abiding in the seven wholesome dharmas, one attains the fullness of the holy life.

He knows the Dharma; he knows the meaning; he knows the time; he knows contentment; he knows himself; he knows the assembly; and he knows the distinctions of rank. Furthermore, there is the holy life (brahmacarya), namely:

loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. By means of explaining the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness of kindness and compassion, he causes all sentient beings to see various spiritual responses, yet the Tathāgata never moves. Moreover, he again explains that which "originally existed but is now absent."
The meaning [of this] is as follows: Furthermore, it explains that while all worldly beings do not know, see, or realize, the Bodhisattva alone is able to know, see, and realize its meaning.

It also clarifies the Dharma-gate of the Six Recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). It further recounts the account of King Ajātaśatru’s meeting with the Buddha, and elaborates upon the celestial conduct (*divyacara*) as described in the *Saṃpuṣpita* Sūtra.
Chapter on the Infant’s Conduct: One who is unable to rise, stay, come, go, or speak is called an infant.
The Tathāgata is also like this.
Chapter on the Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue Whose Radiance Shines Universally: The Buddha addressed King of Virtue: "As for the practice..."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra possesses ten meritorious qualities. Those of the four fruits, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who hear these words shall all attain entry into nirvāṇa;
those who do not believe shall wander through birth and death.
The Chapter on the Lion’s Roar. The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda asked: "By what reason is it called 'Buddha-nature'?
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not see it? Why do those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) not see it clearly, while the Tathāgata sees it clearly?
The Buddha said: "It is because [the former] lack the wisdom that fully contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*)."
There are four kinds: the inferior attains the state of a śrāvaka; the middling attains the state of a pratyekabuddha; the superior attains the ten stages (daśabhūmi);
and the most superior attains the bodhi of a Tathāgata. Therefore, the twelve links of dependent origination are called the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).
This is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). It is called the Middle Way; it is called the Buddha; it is called Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, because all who possess a mind will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Moreover, one must not say that there is no Buddha-nature simply because there are those whose minds regress; for if there were [no nature], there could be no cultivation.
Those who have accumulated the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks are called non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas.

Next, the true cultivation of the characteristics of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) is clarified. Next, the cause for entering *nirvāṇa* at the city of Kuśinagara is answered.
Next, the question regarding which bhikṣus adorn the twin trees is answered. Finally, it is stated that *nirvāṇa* is devoid of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and birth.

Because one dwells having abandoned the ten signs of male and female, it is called "signless" (*animitta*). From time to time, by cultivating the signs of concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), one is able to sever these ten signs.
Next, in response to the question of how to achieve the ten dharmas that enable one to see the signless *nirvāṇa*:
first, the perfection of faith; second, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*); third, associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); fourth, delighting in solitude; fifth, diligence...

1. Progressing forward; 2. Being fully endowed with the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*); 3. Using gentle speech; 4. Protecting the Dharma; 5. Providing for one's fellow students; 6. Possessing wisdom.
Next, it clarifies that one who is able to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom is called a wise person. Such a person can cause heavy karma to be experienced lightly;
otherwise, light karma would be experienced heavily. Next, the seven types of people are explained through the analogy of the Ganges. [The assembly...]
The Parable of the Blind Men Touching an Elephant. Next, it clarifies that a bodhisattva should test their own mind through ascetic practices.
Next, it clarifies that the great ocean possesses eight inconceivable qualities; the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise so.
Next, it answers the reason why the Tathāgata manifests as being born from a womb.
The Chapter on Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: He inquires about the matter of the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, and the Buddha answers him.
He asks about various divergent teachings that he has not yet understood, and the Buddha explains them in full. Furthermore, it clarifies that such disputes are the domain of the Buddha.
This is not something known by those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). If one can give rise to doubt regarding this, one is still able to destroy immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one were to develop a fixed conviction within this, it would be called attachment (*abhiniveśa*).

Furthermore, it is clarified that those who sever their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are neither inferior, dull-witted persons, nor are they among the gods or the [three... [The text here appears to be truncated].
The evil realms. Next, it clarifies that Buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent, yet both existent and non-existent. Next, it clarifies the twelve divisions of the scriptures:
some are spoken according to one's own intention, some are spoken according to the intentions of others, and some are spoken according to the intentions of both oneself and others.
Next, the parable of the seven sentient beings in the Ganges is explained. Next, it is explained that because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
and because space is non-existent, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time. Those who cultivate the ten perceptions of impermanence are able to attain nirvāṇa.
The Chapter on Kauṇḍinya. The Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya: "Form is impermanent; one must extinguish this form and attain the eternally abiding liberation of form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity are likewise so.
Apart from the Buddha-dharma, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor are there any who truly qualify as śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
The Dharma. At that time, having heard this, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) were filled with resentment. They went together to Ajātaśatru and requested a debate with Gautama.

The king and the non-Buddhists came together to the Buddha’s dwelling. [The Buddha] first answered one person, enabling him to cross over, leave the household life, and realize the fruit [of the path].
This began with the Brahmin Śreṇika and followed with the brahmacārin Vāseṭṭha.
The Brahmin Śreṇika, the Brahmin Kāśyapa, the Brahmin Pūrṇa, the Brahmin Viśuddha, the Brahmin Vātsīputra, the Brahmin Nāmatika, and the Brahmin Mahāgovinda all realized the fruits of the path.
Thereupon, he commanded Mañjuśrī to shatter Māra with a mantra and summon Ānanda; he then ordered him to go to the place of the Brahmin Subhadra.
He was exhorted to come and see [the Master], who questioned him on the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). He also realized the four fruits of the śramaṇa path.
With a single mind, he reverently requested the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in its Southern Recension (the protocol for prostration and viewing is as above).
The Śramaṇa Shi Huiguan of the Liu Song dynasty, together with Xie Lingyun, re-edited it. This includes the "Preface Chapter" and the "Cunda Chapter."
The Chapter on Sorrowful Lamentation; the Chapter on Longevity; the Chapter on the Vajra Body; the Chapter on the Merit of Names; the Chapter on the Four Marks;
the Chapter on the Four Reliances; the Chapter on the Correct and the Erroneous; the Chapter on the Four Truths; the Chapter on the Four Perversions;

the Chapter on the Arising of the Tathāgata-nature; the Chapter on Letters; the Chapter on the Parable of the Bird; the Chapter on the Parable of the Moon; the Chapter on Bodhisattvas; and the Chapter on the Questions of the Entire Assembly.
The Chapter on Manifesting Illness; the Chapter on Noble Conduct; the Chapter on Brahma-like Conduct; the Chapter on Infant-like Conduct;
the Chapter on the King of Sublime Virtues, Universally Radiant Light; the Chapter on the Lion’s Roar; the Chapter of Kāśyapa; and the Chapter of Kauṇḍinya.
A Solemn Invocation to the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty, together with Buddhabhadra.
It consists of eighteen chapters and concludes with the Tathāgata manifesting illness.
A Solemn Invocation to the Latter Part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra (Veneration as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānabhadra of Nanhai in the Tang Dynasty, together with Huìníng and others.
At the end of the *Kauṇḍinya-parivarta*, Subhadra cremates his body and manifests supernatural transformations. In the *Śāsanānuśāsanī-parivarta*, the Buddha entrusts [the Dharma] to Ānanda.
He exhorted the great assembly to protect and uphold the Dharma of the Great Parinirvāṇa. Āniruddha directed Ānanda to inquire about certain matters.
The Buddha, through the correct contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, instructed Chandaka: "The precepts of the *śīla-pāramitā* are your great teacher;
dwell with a mind adorned by the four foundations of mindfulness. At the beginning of all sūtras, establish the words: "Thus have I heard."

I have heard that at one time the Buddha was staying in a certain place. Furthermore, it is answered that making offerings to the śarīra with a profound mind, even if only as much as a mustard seed, is no different from making offerings to a present Buddha.
It also answers the method for cremation, which should follow the rites of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).

Moreover, it answers regarding the sites for erecting stūpas after cremation, including the architectural styles for the stūpas of Pratyekabuddhas, those of the four fruits of the path, and Wheel-Turning Kings; this is permitted by the Emperor.
The Buddha revealed his single-tooth relic, removed his robes to display his golden body, and emitted light as he made three proclamations.
Twenty-four times he ascended into the void, earnestly exhorting [the assembly] in the "Chapter on Returning to the Source.

The World-Honored One then transcended into various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), preaching the Dharma for the multitude three times. At midnight, he entered the fourth *dhyāna*, remaining in profound stillness.
There was no sound, and he then entered parinirvāṇa. The eight trees turned white, and the ten directions were plunged into great darkness.
Mahābrahmā, Śakra, Nandika, and Ānanda praised him in verse. [This concludes] the Chapter on the Miraculous Response of the Cremation.

The golden coffin rose of its own accord and circumambulated the city of Kuśinagara, awaiting the arrival of Kāśyapa. When the coffin opened and his body was revealed, it was bathed and wrapped; the coffin door then closed immediately.
Furthermore, his two feet reappeared, and flames surged from his chest; after seven days, his body was consumed by fire. The noble form was vast and moistened.
The kings of the seven kingdoms raised their armies and surrounded the city of Kuśinagara. The brahmin Dhūma proclaimed that it should be divided into eight portions, and each erected a stūpa.
A Solemn Invocation for the Buddha’s Discourse on the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Prostrations as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty. Chapter on Lamentation: Ānanda Relates His Dream.
The Venerable Aniruddha praised him in verse, and the great assembly wept with grief. [This concludes] the Chapter on the Manifest Birth of the Four Youthful Bodhisattvas:
the Bodhisattva Bhadramati from the east manifested birth as the prince Ajātaśatru; Priyadarśana-viśuddha from the south as the son of the elder Siṃha;
Gaganāmala from the west as the son of the elder Puṇyabhadra; and Ṛddhipuṣpa from the north.
The Lion King’s minister and son was born already sitting in the full lotus posture and reciting verses;
this is the "Chapter on the Four Youthful Disciples Who Guide All Beings to See the Buddha. The Buddha proclaimed the virtues of the four youthful disciples in verse for Ānanda;
this is the "Chapter on Entrustment. The four bodhisattvas spoke verses to console Ānanda; the Buddha then entrusted Ānanda and Rāhula to one hundred thousand [beings].
Bhikṣus, furthermore, he entrusted [the teaching] to five hundred Buddhas of the northern direction.

In the "Chapter on Delivering from Hell," the Buddha’s body emitted countless rays of light, and within these lights, emanated Buddhas preached the Dharma. He further emitted light that illuminated three categories of hell-dwellers:

first, causing them to be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and realize the first fruit; second, causing them to be reborn in Tuṣita and realize the third fruit; and third, causing them to be reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Chapter on the Entry into Nirvana and the Manifestation of All Buddhas: The Buddha emits light that illuminates the ten directions, reaching all Buddhas of the same name who have likewise entered nirvana;
these are beyond counting. He causes everyone in this assembly to see them and also hear the sutras they preach.
Furthermore, in the Chapter on the Purity of the Buddha-lands, he manifests this realm as pure and adorned, no different from the Land of Peace (Sukhāvatī).
The Chapter on the Devas and Bodhisattvas of the Sukhāvatī-kṣetra: The various devas come to the assembly; Aniruddha speaks verses in lamentation;
Bodhisattvas from the ten directions arrive together and present great offerings. The Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Transformation and Preaching of the Dharma.

Ānanda praised the Buddha; the Buddha first entered samādhi and manifested immeasurable transformation Buddhas preaching the Dharma, and afterwards further explained the various kinds of samādhis and supernatural powers of the Buddha.
*The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Ones Invoked with Single-Minded Devotion* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Sui dynasty North Indian śramaṇa Jñānagupta. This is identical to the aforementioned scripture, except that it concludes at the sixth chapter.
A Solemn Invocation to the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Narendrayaśas of Udyāna in the Gao Qi dynasty, together with Fazhi. Chapter on Brahmā:
[The Buddha] commanded Ānanda to spread out his seat and lay down on his right side; his radiance eclipsed the great trichiliocosm and reached the Great Brahmā.
The King Questions on the Dharma and Attains Faith; the Buddha Entrusts the Great Trichiliocosm to Him. Chapter on the Merchant Leader:
The merchant leader, son of Māra, requests the Buddha to remain in the world, and the Buddha bestows upon him the prediction of becoming a Pratyekabuddha. Chapter on Śakra:
The Buddha teaches Śakra the method of empowerment and transforms the Asuras, causing them to cease their strife. Rāhu.
The Chapter on Rāhu. Rāhu could not bear to witness the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, so he went to the presence of the Buddha Duṣpradharṣa in the eastern direction.

That Buddha consoled and exhorted him. He then went to the presence of the Buddha Śreṣṭhidatta in the zenith, where that Buddha further consoled and exhorted him, commanding him to return to this land.
Śākyamuni then preached for him the "Chapter on Seeing the True Dharma," and the great assembly attained the benefits of the three vehicles. Kāśyapa.
The Chapter on the Leaves. Ānanda wept with grief. The Buddha consoled him by explaining that Kāśyapa was capable of widely propagating the work of Dharma transformation.
The Chapter on Upholding the True Dharma clarifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there would be many who propagate the Dharma:
first, the bhikṣu Vidiśa; second, the bhikṣu Tīkṣṇaka; third, Upagupta; and fourth, Aśvagupta.
1. Bāhula; 2. Pañca-Uttara; 3. Śreṣṭha-Śātaka the Elder; 4. Vīthika and Sañjaya—these two;
5. Mahā-vīrya; 6. Mātaṅga; 7. Kāśyapa; 8. Gṛhapati Jñānika; 9. Dharmavardhana the Upāsaka; 10. Keśava the Bhikṣu.

Chapter on the Relics: King Caturmahāpradāna. This chapter clearly elucidates the merit of making offerings to the relics, even down to the scattering of a single flower or a single recitation of the Buddha’s name; such merit will surely result in the great fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Chapter Eight: On Prostration. The Great Makara Fish, upon hearing the merchants’ cry of "Namo Buddhāya," reached the end of its life and was reborn.
Within the human realm, one may leave the household life and realize the four fruits of enlightenment; how much more so for those who plant deep roots of goodness?

Regarding the Chapter on Roots of Goodness, it first employs the metaphor of entrusting seeds to water to clarify that roots of goodness planted in the presence of a Buddha will never be lost or diminished.
Regarding the Chapter on the Merit of Giving, it states that by giving to the Buddha as a field of merit, even if one does not seek nirvana, one will nonetheless certainly attain nirvana.
The Chapter on Planting Roots of Goodness: The wondrous retribution for manifesting five flowers as an offering to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
The Chapter on Entrusting the True Dharma through Various Similes: Clarifying the deeds of the Buddha making offerings to various Buddhas after [the time of] Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
the Buddha personally took Ānanda by the hand and entrusted him with the circulation of the precious treasury of the True Dharma. Question:
Section on the Teachings. A preliminary announcement regarding the compilation of the Dharma, together with an exhortation not to be negligent.
A single-minded invitation to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra and the Buddha-spoken Sarvavaipulya-śikṣā-saṃgraha Sūtra (to be viewed as above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Vinayavadraśīla of Northern India. Second, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
As he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, [the Buddha] entered the *yathā-dharma-samādhi*, causing the great trichiliocosm to be universally adorned.
A great assembly gathered like clouds. The Buddha extended his tongue, covering the entire great trichiliocosm, and commanded:
*Maitreya Questions on Resolving Doubts regarding the Dharma*. Invited by the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven to preach the Mahāyāna *dhāraṇī* dharma, the Buddha told Maitreya:

"All dharmas are spoken by the Buddha. One should not arbitrarily give rise to discrimination regarding what to reject or accept, nor cling to the Small [Vehicle] while abandoning the Great, or cling to the Great while abandoning the Small. If one slanders the Dharma, the transgression is immeasurable. This was stated as an explanation.
Due to the past causes of Amitābha, there exists the distinction between pure and impure Buddha-lands. Furthermore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the six perfections;
one must not speak of prajñā alone. Moreover, a bodhisattva must not slander other bodhisattvas, for such a transgression is extremely grave.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat you to accept this copy of the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccayasamādhi-sūtra* and the *Samantaguṇasaṃcaya-gāthā-samādhi-sūtra* (to be venerated as above).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of India during the Yao Qin dynasty. Second [copy], from the Yuezhi kingdom of the Western Jin.

Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa. Three months before the *Nirvāṇa*, the World-Ruler Nārāyaṇa Bodhisattva questioned the Bodhisattva Rakṣa regarding the Dharma of protection. The Buddha then expounded for him the name of a samādhi.
At that time, the Malla Vīrabhadra approached with pride; the Buddha manifested his innate power born of his parents to him, whereby [Vīrabhadra] gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Nārāyaṇa again requested the meaning of the samādhi, and the Buddha answered him with his unsurpassed mind.
Next, it clarifies that in cultivating this samādhi, one should achieve the three kinds of adornments: generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning.
Next, it clarifies the accomplishment of various fourfold dharmas, through which one can realize non-arising. Finally, he bestows the prediction of bodhi upon the Malla.
The various Great Bodhisattvas each expounded the Dharma-gates of the practices of bodhisattvas.

With single-minded devotion, they requested the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra* (to be venerated as above), also known as the *Sūtra of the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanyao of the Xiao Qi dynasty.

Translated by Jìng: While the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he emitted light and manifested transformations; he also commanded Mañjuśrī to invite his mother so that they might meet, enabling her to realize the first fruit of the path.
He then preached a divine mantra for her. Subsequently, descending from heaven, he gradually transformed and delivered beings through successive stages.
Upon receiving the invitation of Māra, he entered *nirvāṇa*. When Māyā arrived at the site of the coffin, the coffin opened and revealed a thousand transformations.
Buddha. Solemnly Invoking the Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Sūtra (Prostrations and Viewing as Above).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty. The First Division of the Mahāmegha: The Great Assembly Section.

The first [chapter] on Deliverance. The great assembly emerges from meditative concentration and proceeds to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. The Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-guhya-nidhi raises a multitude of questions like rising clouds;
the Tathāgata grants his approval and, for their sake, preaches the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*.

[It contains] the ocean of dhāraṇīs, the ocean of samādhis, the Tathāgata as the Dharma-preacher, the Dharma-city of all Buddhas, and the profound Dharma-realm which is eternally abiding and immutable. Not...

It is inconceivable: eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Within this sutra are four hundred inconceivable gates of liberation (*vimokṣa-dharmaparyāya*), which, when extrapolated, extend to the infinite.
Furthermore, it sets forth divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*) that cause sweet rain to fall and shake the world.

Chapter One: On Single Dharmas The veil of ignorance; the fetter of craving.
In a single kalpa, the bones of one’s body, the mind, and its defilements lead to rebirth in the evil realms; when the mind is pure, one ascends to the good realms.
All this arises from one’s own karma; the mind is the precursor. The schism of the Saṃgha; the reconciliation of the Saṃgha; the severing of a single fetter.

At that time, other [defilements] are also abandoned: namely, the conceit "I am," lack of heedfulness, and the abandonment of greed, the abandonment of desire, the abandonment of hatred, the abandonment of malice, the abandonment of delusion, the abandonment of concealment, the abandonment of vexation, the abandonment of anger, the abandonment of resentment, the abandonment of envy, the abandonment of stinginess, the abandonment of craving, the abandonment of pride, and the abandonment of harmfulness.
One recollects the Buddha, recollects the Dharma, recollects the Saṅgha, recollects the precepts, recollects generosity, and recollects the teachings.

Mindfulness of rest; mindfulness of ānāpāna (breathing); mindfulness of the body; mindfulness of death. Knowing greed, hatred, delusion, concealment, affliction, anger, resentment, envy, stinginess, attachment, pride, and harmfulness.

regarding internal powerful conditions, none is like right attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*). The fruit of giving; the retribution for violating the precepts.

Vipaśyanā, wisdom, and liberation; ignorance and wisdom—these turn toward evil and supreme goodness.
Through the turning away from ignorance and craving, the Wheel of Dharma is turned. Those who shave their heads and beg for alms [attain] two fruits;
two types of sentient beings fall into hell: first, those who break the precepts; second, those who slander others. The kindness of parents is difficult to repay.
Karma and wisdom are never deceptive; parents should be honored and supported. There are material gifts and the gift of Dharma;
there are material sacrifices and Dharma sacrifices. Regarding speech and silence, each has its own good and evil aspects.
Through the power of discernment and the power of cultivation, karma and lifespan follow one another, whether that lifespan be short or long.

Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Three Dharmas Sentient beings with inferior resolve and those with sublime resolve mutually associate throughout the three periods of time.
There are three causes and three conditions that can induce future existence (*punarbhava*): ignorance, karma, and craving;
the greedy attachment to enjoyments and the failure to see their faults; and the arising of many faults through these three causal conditions; and the three types of desire.

The heavens do not transcend birth and death; three [types of people] are like the braying of donkeys. One should increase the three higher trainings: the discipline of the Dharma and wisdom that tames and perfects;
the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the three kinds of pleasant matters, one should maintain pure precepts.
The three kinds of incense are not equal to the fragrance of the precepts. One should cultivate [the path regarding] the equal son, the superior son, and the inferior son.
The three roots of goodness and so forth can be lost through three types of seeking: first, for kinsmen; second, for gain; and third, out of envy for others’ excellence.
Furthermore, there are three [factors that lead to loss]: first, worldly affairs; second, idle talk; and third, sleep.

When pure faith, the gift, the object of giving, and the field of merit—these three factors—come together and manifest, immeasurable merit is produced. There are three things that are not firm, which are easily exchanged for one another.
The three things to be made firm—body, life, and wealth; the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*); the three types of sentient beings with whom one should associate:
the inferior, the equal, and the superior. The three enemies—old age, sickness, and death; the three meritorious actions—generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation;
the three most excellent ones—Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; the three great masters: first, the Buddha; second, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); and third, those in training (*śaikṣa*).
At the three times, the devas assemble and rejoice. First, they take the vow to leave the household life; second, they maintain the precepts according to the Dharma;
third, they realize the fruits by relying on the Dharma. In these three matters, the devas surpass humans: they possess long life, physical beauty, and happiness.

The exposition of the meaning of the scripture opens with ten general gates. First is the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; this refers to ten meanings being opened up for each of the causes and conditions.

Second is the inclusion within the scriptural collections (piṭaka); this refers to its inclusion within the Sūtra Piṭaka among the three piṭakas, while also including the other two. Regarding the two collections (pitaka)...
It is included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Furthermore, while provisional teachings do not encompass this, this [teaching] simultaneously encompasses the provisional.

Among the five teachings, it is subsumed solely within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), yet this also encompasses the others. Third, regarding the demarcation of its principles and scope, there are briefly four sections.
First, the substance of the single basis; second, the subsumption into ultimate reality; third, the manifestation of its non-obstruction; fourth, the universal inclusion and containment.
Each of these further comprises ten gates to reveal their inexhaustibility. Fourth, there are ten [aspects] regarding the capacities of sentient beings who are the recipients of this teaching.

The first five [categories] exclude those who are not suitable vessels; the latter five clarify those for whom [the teaching] is intended. Those lacking faith, those who oppose the truth and deviate from reality, and those who are narrow-minded, inferior, and cling to expedient means—all these are not suitable vessels.
It is primarily for the sake of those with the perfect capacity for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); secondarily, for those who have faith and inclination so as to establish the seeds [of enlightenment];

thirdly, to lead those Bodhisattvas of expedient teachings; fourthly, for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*); and finally, for ordinary people, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and those of indeterminate nature (*icchantika*). Thus it is ranked.
Regarding the five levels of teaching and their varying depths, ten bases are briefly elucidated: first, sound; second, names, phrases, and syllables;

third, the comprehensive inclusion of these four factors; fourth, the inclusion of the signified meaning; fifth, all phenomena manifesting the meaning; sixth, the inclusion of objects as being solely mind.

Seventh is the entry into reality through the conditions of phenomena; eighth is the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; ninth is the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena; tenth is the brilliant manifestation of the ocean-seal.
The final two are the true core of this scripture, which harmoniously incorporates the preceding eight without omission.

Regarding the sixth point, the general and specific tenets, there are ten schools in total: first, the school that asserts both the self and phenomena exist; second, the school that asserts phenomena exist while the self is non-existent.
1. The three dharmas have no coming or going; 2. the present manifests both the provisional and the real; 3. the conventional is false while the ultimate is true;
4. all dharmas are merely names; 5. the three natures are both empty and existent; 6. true emptiness transcends all marks; 7. emptiness and existence are unimpeded; 8.
they are perfectly interfused and endowed with all virtues. Now, this sutra [expounds] the principle of the causal origination of the inconceivable Dharma-realm.

third, it elucidates the subsidiary types; and fourth, it analyzes the commentaries. Chapter Eight concerns the transmission, translation, and spiritual responses. Chapter Nine provides a general explanation of the title of the scripture.

Now, sentient beings seeking liberation possess manifold capacities (*indriya*), and the sages who arise to respond likewise manifest manifold responses.

In this discourse on the Sahā world, where the Buddha’s work is carried out through sound, the gate of the ambrosia (*amṛta*) is opened; therefore, it is interpreted by means of the provisional teachings (*yathā-vāda*). If one preaches in accordance with these capacities...

The fundamental is high; its height cannot be measured to the limit. Day and night one enumerates the treasures of others, yet one’s own person possesses not even half a coin’s worth.

One should simply contemplate the loftiness and vastness of one’s own mind and strike upon the infinite response of the Sage. When the capacity is perfected, resonance is achieved, and one attains one’s own benefit.

It clarifies that the triple world consists of only two kinds of consciousness. The first is manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), which is the fundamental...

Consciousness is twofold: first, manifest consciousness; second, discriminating consciousness, which is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Manifest consciousness gives rise to discrimination, and discrimination gives rise to perfuming (*vāsanā*);

first, the perfuming of the habit-energy of attachment to the nature of conceptual construction increases the *ālayavijñāna*; second, the observation of the habit-energy of the true nature [counteracts it].

The four meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), dhāraṇīs, the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),

It is established that if one clings to the view that there is no cause and does not accumulate merit, giving rise to defiled attachment, one will experience rebirth in the evil realms.
A wise person who, in accordance with reality, has faith, understanding, respect, and reverence [for this truth], shall immediately obtain the most supreme mass of merit.

There are four greatnesses of generating the resolve: greatness of valor, greatness of skillful means, greatness of benefit, and greatness of transcendence.

There are four distinctions: the generation of the resolve by those practicing through faith, the generation of the resolve based on pure reliance, the generation of the resolve obtained as a result of maturation, and the generation of the resolve free from obstructions.

The Chapter on Faith and Understanding and the Chapter on the Description of Seeking [clarify the path].

As the verse says: "The Bodhisattva who studies the *Lotus Sūtra* fulfills two kinds of practice: first, the practice of signlessness (*animitta*), and second, the practice of signs (*sanimitta*).
The four types of peaceful bliss of signlessness are profound and wondrous meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). One observes the six sense faculties (*indriya*)..."
The Dharma is originally pure; the nature of sentient beings is stainless. There is neither origin nor purity;
without practicing remedial actions, one naturally transcends all sages. Awakening occurs spontaneously without a teacher, not through gradual cultivation. The commentary states:
Regarding the practitioner of signlessness (*animitta-carin*): within all phenomena, the characteristics of the mind are quiescent and ultimately non-arising.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; eating, drinking, or speaking; in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), the mind is constantly in samādhi.

As for other meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they follow the sequence of the three realms, from the stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhūmi*), through the stage of access (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), the first dhyāna stage (*prathamadhyāna-bhūmi*), and so on, up to the [stage of] neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

In the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are eleven distinct varieties. There is the existence of dharmas and the non-existence of dharmas;

these two paths constitute the distinction according to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-vyākhyā* on the noble practices. However, this is not the case for the profound and subtle meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) within the practice of peaceful abiding (*sukhavihāra*).
Such [concentrations] do not rely upon the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nor do they abide in the practices of the form or formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*). Thus it is.
Dhyāna-concentration is the universal practice of this bodhisattva. Because he is ultimately without mental activity, it is called "practice without marks" (*animitta-caryā*).

As for the "practice with marks," it is as described in the *Pravaraṇa-parivarta*: single-mindedly recollecting the words and letters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, practicing with diligence, and not lying down to sleep.
One must act as if one's head were on fire. If one practices with such accomplishment, one will immediately behold Samantabhadra and others and attain the three *dhāraṇīs*.
If, however, one is concerned for body and life or covets the four types of offerings, one will be unable to practice diligently and shall not attain them even after the passing of kalpas.

Composed by Zhiyi. Those who wish to study the Dharma must first maintain pure precepts and diligently practice meditative concentration; only then can they attain it.

The immeasurable merits and virtues of the Buddha-dharma all arise from meditative concentration. This is followed by a section of questions and answers to resolve doubts, after which the text provides a comprehensive explanation.
Each of the four foundations of mindfulness is fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat you to contemplate the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (the ritual for prostration and contemplation is as above).
The Master of Wisdom (*Zhìzhě*) spoke thus: Tiantai transmitted the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* from Nanyue: first, the gradual, which is the explanation of dhyāna.
The Dharma-gate of the Sequential Stages of the *Pāramitās* (1); the Two Indeterminate [Stages], which are the Six Sublime Gates (*ṣaḍ-sukhama-dvāra*), now lost to memory (2);

and the Perfect and Sudden [Stage], which is the present *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (3)—all of these belong to the Mahāyāna, all take the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as their object, and are equally termed "calm abiding and insight" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
In the gradual approach, the beginning is shallow and the end is deep, like the rungs of a ladder; in the indeterminate approach, the sequence may vary further.
Mutually, it is like a vajra jewel placed in the midst of the sun; the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) is non-dual from beginning to end.

Like a practitioner of supernormal powers soaring through the air, [the Buddha] expounds three Dharma-gates for the sake of the three types of root-natures. Now, as for the Perfect and Sudden, one initially takes the true aspect (shixiang) as the object of focus.
To encounter objects is itself the Middle Way; there is nothing that is not reality. To be bound by conditions is the Dharma-realm; in a single thought-moment, the Dharma-realm is present.
A single form, a single fragrance—none are not the Middle Way. One’s own realm, the Buddha-realm, and the realm of sentient beings are likewise so.
The aggregates and sense bases are all suchness; there is no suffering to be abandoned. Ignorance and the afflictions are themselves bodhi; there is no accumulation to be severed.
The extremes and the heterodox are all the Middle Way; there is no Path to be cultivated. Birth-and-death is itself Nirvana;
there is no extinction to be realized. There is no suffering and no origin [of suffering]; therefore, there is no mundane world. There is no Path and no extinction;

therefore, there is no supramundane world. It is the single, pure true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Outside of this true reality, there are no other dharmas. The quiescence of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called *śamatha* (calming); being quiescent...

Constant illumination is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Although it is spoken of in terms of beginning and end, there is neither duality nor distinction; this is termed "Perfect and Sudden" (*yuan-dun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

This Bodhisattva, having heard the Perfect Dharma, gives rise to perfect faith, establishes perfect practice, abides in the perfect stage, adorns himself with perfect merit, and utilizes perfect power to establish all sentient beings. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "The Snowy Mountains..."
There is a grass called "Patience. If a cow eats it, she immediately obtains the finest cream (mṛdvīkā). It is also said:
For example, if a person bathes in the great ocean, one should know that they have thereby used the waters of all rivers; thus should one understand śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The Teacher of all Buddhas is eternal because the Dharma is eternal; therefore, the Buddhas are also eternal. The same applies to bliss, self, and purity.
This chapter is divided into ten sections: first, the general purport; second, the explanation of the names; third, the essence and characteristics; fourth, the inclusion of dharmas;
fifth, the partial and the perfect; sixth, skillful means; seventh, correct contemplation; eighth, retribution; ninth, the arising of the teaching; tenth, the ultimate intent.
Returning to the beginning, I shall first explain the general meaning. Encompassing the beginning and end, crowning the initial and subsequent stages, I now summarize them into five points:
namely, generating the great mind, cultivating the great practice, realizing the great fruit, tearing the great net, and returning to the great place. First, generating the great mind.

This refers to distinguishing what is not [the true path] by means of the ten types of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*). Generating the bodhicitta is *vipaśyanā* (insight); the cessation of deviant and perverse minds is *śamatha* (calm abiding).
This is clarified by means of the Four Truths, the Four Great Vows, and the Six Identities (*ṣat-yukti*). Second, regarding the practice of the Great Vehicle:
it encourages progress through the four kinds of samādhi and entry into the stage of a Bodhisattva: first, constant sitting; second, constant walking.
Third, half-walking and half-sitting; fourth, neither walking nor sitting. Regarding the third point, those who attain great fruits:

if one practices in accordance with the Middle Way, there will be a superior and wondrous retribution. Even if one has not yet transcended the stage of conditioned existence (*bhavāgra*), the provisional rewards (*puṣpaphala*) obtained are already superior to the seven kinds of expedient means, let alone the true retribution. This principle is addressed later in the eighth section.

This shall be explained in detail. Regarding the "tearing asunder the great net": if a person skillfully employs *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to observe the mind, their internal wisdom becomes clear and lucid, and they penetrate all gradual and sudden teachings. It is like opening a great scroll from within a minute particle of dust;
the Buddha-dharma, vast as the sands of the Ganges, is understood within a single moment of mind. This meaning shall be explained at length in the ninth section.
This is also briefly indicated within the *Shefa* (Compendium of Dharmas). Regarding the "five points of ultimate resort" (*wǔ guī dà chù*):

one directs oneself toward the three virtues and leads others to enter them together; thus they are called the "ultimate resorts. Entering the Secret Treasury will be explained in detail in the tenth section.
The commentary states: "These five brief [sections] are simply the ten extensive ones. The first five chapters are simply the arousal of the bodhicitta..."
Focus the mind on a single point. Skillful means and correct contemplation are nothing other than the four samādhis.

The chapter on "Fruition and Retribution" clarifies only contrariness and compliance: contrariness refers to the retribution of the two extremes, while compliance refers to the sublime and wondrous retribution.
The chapter on "Arising of the Teaching" involves transforming one's own mind to benefit others; it may manifest as the body of a Buddha to bestow both the provisional and the ultimate.

Alternatively, it may manifest as the images of the nine realms, responding to and expounding upon the gradual and sudden teachings, transforming the gradual and sudden, and broadly disseminating the gradual and sudden;

this is the chapter on the ultimate aim. Since these all converge within the Great Abode of the Secret Treasury, one should know that the intent of both the concise and the extensive versions is identical.

Second, the explanation of the names "śamatha" (calm abiding) and "vipaśyanā" (insight). Briefly, there are four aspects: first, mutual dependence; second, transcendence of dependence; third, reconciling differences;

and fourth, penetrating the three virtues. First, regarding mutual dependence: śamatha and vipaśyanā each have three meanings. As for the three meanings of śamatha, they are: the meaning of cessation (*śama*).

The meaning of "stopping" (*ting*) is contrasted with the meaning of not stopping or stopping. Regarding the three meanings of "contemplation" (*guan*): it is the meaning of penetrating through, the meaning of reaching through by contemplation, and it is contrasted with the meaning of non-contemplation versus contemplation.

As for the two types of "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*): they involve horizontal and vertical subversion of the three aforementioned forms of stopping and contemplation, such that they cannot be described;
yet because there are causes and conditions, they can also be described. When viewed from the perspective of the six stages of identity (*liujie*), the initial mind is [empty].

Regarding what is lost: the sacred realm is free from confusion. Third, regarding the differences among the assemblies: this refers to the various names for the assemblies found in different sūtras and śāstras.

Fourth, regarding the three virtues being common to two characters: either the three virtues are collectively common to the two characters, or each of the three virtues is individually common to the two characters.

The explanation of the essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* consists of four parts: first, the characteristics of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*); second, vision and wisdom; third, the objects of focus (*ālambana*);

and fourth, gain and loss. First, regarding the characteristics of the teachings: *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are names of teachings that apply universally to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*).

One must not seek their distinct essence based on these common names; therefore, they are distinguished by their characteristics. This distinguishes them from the three preceding teachings (*yāna*) and reveals the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*paripūrṇa-akṣepaka-yāna*).
Cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are the essence. Second, regarding the two eyes of wisdom: cessation and contemplation are the cause, while the eye of wisdom is the fruit.
By employing the inconceivable eye of wisdom, one attains the essence of perfect and sudden cessation and contemplation. Third, regarding the objective realm:

if one has attained the intended meaning within the eye of wisdom that can manifest [reality], there is no need for further discourse on the truths (*satya*) as the manifested realm. For those who have not yet understood this, [the following is provided]...
Regarding this section: those who practice through faith value extensive learning; thus, they employ discernment to realize the perfect and subtle.
Those who practice through the Dharma take profound contemplation as their core; thus, they rely on reflection to perceive the true realm. As for the four points regarding gain and loss:
"loss" refers to the conceivable, while "gain" refers to the inconceivable.
The four clarifications of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) universally encompass all phenomena: first, they encompass all principles;
second, they encompass all delusions; third, they encompass all wisdoms; fourth, they encompass all practices; fifth, they encompass all stages;
and sixth, they encompass all teachings.

Regarding the five aspects of the partial and the perfect within the Five Sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): these distinguish the partial in order to reach the perfect. First, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles; second, the distinction between the Half and Full Teachings;
third, the distinction between the partial and the perfect; fourth, the distinction between the gradual and the sudden; and fifth, the distinction between the provisional and the real.

Sixth is the clarification of skillful means (*upāya*). This refers to skillful cultivation by which even a minute root of goodness can cause immeasurable practices to reach fulfillment and realization, leading one to enter the stage of a bodhisattva.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the five grades of provisional names and the stages of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) and so forth are still far removed from the truth and are thus called "distant skillful means" (*yuan fangbian*).
When the six sense organs are purified (*liu gen qingjing*), one resembles and neighbors the truth; this is called [the proximate skillful means].
Regarding the proximate preparations (*upāya*): prior to the five stages (*pañca-varga*), within the provisional stage (*prajñapti-pada*), we further distinguish between remote and proximate.
Twenty-five factors constitute the remote preparation, while ten types of objects constitute the proximate preparation. These encompass both the horizontal and vertical dimensions;

when the ten contemplations (*daśa-vipaśyanā*) are fully realized, one enters the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā-bhūmi*), capable of giving rise to the true and the semblance [of realization]. Now, I shall explain the remote preparation.
Briefly, there are five [stages]: first, possessing the five conditions; second, reviling the five desires; third, abandoning the five hindrances;

fourth, regulating the five matters; fifth, practicing the five dharmas. Regarding "possessing the five conditions": first, purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, sufficiency of robes and food;
third, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place; fourth, ceasing all worldly involvements; fifth, obtaining virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Reviling the five...
"Desires" refers to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. "Abandoning the five hindrances" refers to sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
"Regulating the five factors" refers to food, sleep, the body, the breath, and the mind. "Practicing the five dharmas" refers to [the following]...

These are: desire, diligence, mindfulness, skillful wisdom, and one-pointedness of mind; the above all involve both the understanding of phenomena (*nīta-artha*) and the understanding of meaning (*neya-artha*).
Seventh, regarding the correct cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: in the preceding six stages, one has opened up sublime understanding by relying upon the sūtras.
Now, relying on sublime understanding to establish correct practice, the unguent and the light depend upon one another; the eyes and the feet mutually assist each other.

When both practice and understanding are diligent, the three obstructions and four māras arise in chaotic competition; the heavy darkness and vast dispersion obscure and disturb the clarity of meditative concentration.
One must not follow what is unwholesome, nor fear what is wholesome. To follow it leads one toward the evil realms; to fear it hinders the cultivation of the True Dharma.
One should observe the turbid with observation, so that through turbidity there is clarity; one should still the distracted with stillness, so that through distraction there is tranquility.
It is like a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold; it is like the various rivers flowing into the sea; it is like fire fueled by wood;

it is like the wind increasing the roar of the ocean. Opening up *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are ten [topics]: first, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*); second, afflictions (*kleśa*); third, illness; fourth, the characteristics of karma.
1. The five demonic activities; 2. the six dhyānas; 3. the various views; 4. overweening pride; 5. the two vehicles; 6. bodhisattvas.

These ten objects are all capable of obscuring and obstructing. Beginning from the primary retribution of ordinary beings and extending to the skillful means of the sages, the object of the aggregates and sense bases is constantly manifest before one and is perpetually available as an object. As for the remaining nine objects, they arise...
They can serve as objects. If they did not arise, what would there be to contemplate? Furthermore, the eight objects are far from the correct path;

by guarding against them deeply, one returns to the right track. The two objects are close to the correct path; when reaching this stage, one need not worry about a lack of contemplation, for through slight cultivation, realization is attained.
Moreover, if one does not understand how these various objects mutually induce one another, a great web of doubt will arise. As it says:

When one is on the path of doubt and does not know where to proceed, if one has previously heard [the teachings], one may allow for their various transformations and wonders; yet the mind remains as tranquil as space.

First, regarding the entry into the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*): these are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. As for the elements (*dhātu*): [they are as follows].
All internal and external aggregates and sense bases arise from the mind. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "One dharma encompasses all dharmas;
that is to say, the mind. The mind is the root of delusion; if one wishes to investigate it, one must cut off its root."
It is like cauterizing a disease until the correct point is hit. Now, one should move from the *zhang* to the *chi*, and from the *chi* to the *cun*.

Setting aside the four aggregates such as form (*rūpa*), one contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). As for the aggregate of consciousness, it is the mind (*citta*). One contemplates the mind as possessing ten dharma-gates.
1. Contemplating the inconceivable realm; 2. Arousing the mind of compassion; 3. Skillfully establishing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;

4. Pervasive breaking of phenomena; 5. Recognizing the open and the obstructed; 6. Cultivating the factors of the path; 7. Applying remedies to assist in opening; 8. Knowing the stages and positions; 9.
Being able to practice patient endurance; 10. Having no craving for dharmas. These ten layers of contemplation encompass [all practices] both horizontally and vertically.

This collection is subtle, exquisite, and ingenious. At the beginning, it distinguishes between the authenticity and falsehood of meditative objects; in the middle, it combines the primary and auxiliary practices; and at the end, it establishes patience and non-attachment.
Its intent is perfect and its methods are skillful, encompassing all things with complete thoroughness. It provides a standard for beginners and guides practitioners to reach the state of *sāyujya*.
This is not something that could have been achieved by a Chan master who relies on dark realization or a Dharma teacher who merely recites texts.
It is known. As for the statement that "a single contemplation of the mind is the inconceivable realm": if there were no mind at all, it would be so;
yet, as soon as there is even a momentary thought, the three thousand realms are immediately present.

Furthermore, one does not say that the single mind comes first and all phenomena come later, nor does one say that all phenomena come first and the single mind comes later. If they arise from the single mind...
"All dharmas" refers to the vertical dimension (*tiryak*). If the mind were to contain all dharmas at once, this would refer to the horizontal dimension (*pārśva*).
Neither the vertical nor the horizontal is tenable. It is simply that the mind is all dharmas, and all dharmas are the mind;
therefore, it is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither one nor different. It is wondrous, profound, and utterly transcendent. It is not—
That which is cognized by consciousness is not that which can be expressed by words; therefore, it is called the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
What dharma is there that this inconceivable realm does not encompass? What wisdom is there that this realm does not give rise to? Relying on this realm, one gives rise to vows;
even until the point where there is no longer craving for dharmas (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*), what vow would not be fulfilled, and what practice would not be perfected?
Yes. Regarding the sequence of explanation: when practicing, a single mind encompasses all minds. Second, as for those who give rise to the correct and true bodhicitta:
having already deeply realized the inconceivable realm and knowing that one suffering is all sufferings, they feel compassion for themselves and others, giving rise to two vows:
"I vow to deliver infinite sentient beings" and "I vow to exhaust all afflictions."
The Vow of Severance. Furthermore, one contemplates the inconceivable mind of consciousness: "May there be joy for all, both for myself and for all sentient beings.
Although we have sought happiness in the past, we did not know its cause; only now do we understand it. Therefore, giving rise to great compassion, one makes two vows:
"I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma gates" and "I vow to attain the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha. (3)
"Skillful in settling the mind" means skillfully settling the mind within the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

According to faculties, according to ailments, turning [the practice], self-cultivation, and transforming others—there are sixty-four methods for settling the mind (*anxin-fǎ*). Regarding the "fourfold pervasiveness in shattering phenomena":
the inconceivable single object is all objects; the single mind is all minds; and so forth, across all horizontal and vertical dimensions.
All phenomena ultimately converge upon the mind. By breaking the mind, everything is broken; therefore, it is said to be "pervasive.

Within this, one first employs the gates of emptiness and non-arising to break things sequentially, thereby revealing the sudden and perfect breaking. Subsequently, one uses a single gate to break [all things], using that as an analogy for breaking through the other gates.
The text is extensive and the meaning profound; one must investigate it minutely. [Next is] the five consciousnesses: their penetration and obstruction.
1. Breaking Obstruction and Preserving Penetration: Like removing the film to nurture a pearl, or defeating the enemy to protect the general.
2. The Sixfold Path Factors for Balanced Adjustment: By means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one enters the three perfect gates of liberation.
3. Aids to the Path as Countermeasures: Because their faculties are dull, they cannot immediately open the three gates of liberation; therefore, they employ these to provide protection.
Therefore, it distracts and destroys the contemplation of the mind. For this reason, one must apply the path of cultivation to counteract and break through these obstructions.
Regarding the aids to the six perfections, if one understands them merely as individual acts, they cannot assist the path;

one should contemplate these aids as inconceivable, encompassing all dharmas. Eighth, regarding the clarification of the stages: in the two stages of the True and the Counterfeit, there is liberation.
One’s knowledge and vision are clear and distinct, like the differentiation between crimson and purple; one will never erroneously claim what has not been attained as having been attained.
How could an ordinary person, upon merely forming a thought, declare themselves a supreme sage? This would surely not be free from overweening pride—whom else could such a claim be attributed to?

Next, I shall clarify the progression from the five repentances through the stage of sympathetic joy, up to the ten stages of faith, the forty-two positions, and finally to the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment.
To be free from arrogance and overstepping one's bounds is called "knowing the sequence of stages. Regarding the "nine types of patience":
if fame, profit, or kinsmen come from without to cause disruption, one should remember these three methods and endure with clenched teeth.

Even if entreated by thousands or myriads, one remains firm and difficult to dislodge. "Let it be! It is hidden! It shall depart! If afflictions, karma, fixed views, pride, and so forth arise from within...
As for "shattering," one also recollects the three principles: emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle. Regarding the "attachment to dharmas" within the ten non-dharmas:

when practicing the nine preceding matters, one transcends internal and external obstacles and ought to enter the Truth; yet, if one does not enter, it is because one is hindered by dwelling in attachment to dharmas and cannot proceed further.
If one shatters this attachment to dharmas and enters the three gates of liberation, one gives rise to the true Middle Way.
The entire body of wisdom is not realized through another; it naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
These ten kinds of dharmas are called the Mahāyāna contemplation. One who studies this vehicle is called a follower of the Mahāyāna, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
It is practiced while speaking; seeing forms, hearing sounds, smelling odors, tasting flavors, feeling tangibles, and cognizing mental phenomena.
It may be cultivated within all conditions and amidst all objects of experience.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming in the Song Dynasty. First, he briefly clarifies the general meaning, stating:

"The perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of fruition is precisely the nature-virtue possessed by us ordinary beings; therefore, all the practices expounded in the various teachings [are for its realization]."
There is nothing that does not manifest this essence of awakening; therefore, the four samādhis are collectively termed "Buddha-remembrance" (nien-fo).

However, their contemplative methods differ according to their respective gateways. This present contemplative gateway, as well as the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, relies upon the objective realms of the Pure Land’s environment and its inhabitants, employing subtle and wondrous contemplation to focus exclusively on Amitābha to reveal the true body of the Buddha. Although...
Entrusting oneself to those environments, one must know that the environment (the dwelling) and its inhabitants (the supported) coexist within a single mind. The nature of the mind is all-pervasive;

there is no phenomenon it does not create, and no phenomenon it does not possess. By relying upon the nature of the mind, one contemplates the environment and its inhabitants, whereby the environment and its inhabitants become clearly manifest.

By entrusting oneself to that environment and its inhabitants, one contemplates the nature of the mind, whereby the nature of the mind easily manifests. What is called the "nature of the mind" possesses everything.
As for the Dharma: in reality, there is neither that which possesses nor that which is possessed, neither the creator nor the created. Mind itself is the Dharma;
the Dharma itself is the mind. Both the causal conditions that create and the phenomena that are created are, in their very place, entirely the nature of the mind.

Therefore, the present contemplation—whether regarding the environment (*āśraya*) or its inhabitants (*sattva*)—is the mind of the Dharma-realm contemplating the objects of the Dharma-realm, giving rise to the form and mind of the environment and inhabitants within the Dharma-realm.

Thus, the character "contemplation" (*guan*) is explained by means of the "three contemplations in one mind," and "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*) is explained by means of the "three bodies as one essence.
Regarding essence, school, power, and function, these meanings all follow the Perfect [Teaching]. As for the classification of the teachings, it belongs to...

The Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is worthy of veneration and esteem; its essential substance is termed "Gold. It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating. Its...
The essence is called "light" (*prabhā*); because great compassion benefits all beings, its substance is termed "clarity" (*prakāśa*).

Thus, one knows that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is fully endowed with the "Golden Light," which is the ultimate realization of the true meaning of the name. This sutra takes "Golden Light" as its title.

It takes *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its essence, takes *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its principle, takes *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its function, and takes *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its doctrinal manifestation (*śāstrasaṃjñā*).
Alternatively, these three characters may be treated individually to obtain five chapters:

taking "Gold" (*suvarṇa*) as the essence, taking "Light" (*prabhā*) as the principle, taking "Radiance" (*uttama*) as the function, taking the three together as the title, and explaining the three names separately.
Thus, it constitutes the characteristics of the teaching. Since the essence of the Dharma is thus, its substance and its qualities are likewise unified.

"Profound" is the quality of light, for it exhausts the depths of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). "Immeasurable" is the quality of radiance, for it reaches the limits of the nature of phenomena.
The non-duality of these two is the quality of gold, for the nature of phenomena is ultimately noble and precious. Alternatively, there may also be three meanings.
All are profoundly deep, all are immeasurable, and all are non-dual. The virtues of these five chapters are none other than thus.

and are able to purify the mental karma of the practitioner.
Next, perform the mudrā for inviting the assembly of noble ones: Interlace the two hands with palms facing upward.

Join the tips of the two index fingers together like the pole of a carriage. While reciting the mantra, use the two thumbs to respectively push the tips of the two middle fingers toward oneself, beckoning them.
Do this either three times or seven times. The mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ siddhye (1) dvīkane (2) sarvatathāgatānām (3) oṃ (4) vajragīte (5) krasaye svāhā (6)
Visualize this carriage arriving at the presence of the principal deity—whether a certain Buddha, a certain Bodhisattva, or a certain Vajra.
The principal deity and their retinue mount this carriage and descend to the ritual site, each taking their respective seat.
Next, visualize yourself as the practitioner, wearing a *kāṣāya* robe and holding an incense burner, kneeling with both knees on the ground to the right of the Buddha.
(Alternatively, kneel with hands interlocked). With single-minded devotion, gaze up at the Honored One and recite the Text of the Five Repentances:
I take refuge in the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the ten directions, The most supreme and wondrous Dharma, And the Great Assembly of Bodhisattvas.
With my body, speech, and mind purified, I reverently prostrate with earnest devotion. I repent for all sinful karma Accumulated throughout many lifetimes.
The Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra, the Vajra-samādhi, and all the roots of goodness produced and arisen from them—
belonging to the pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and all types of sentient beings— I rejoice in them all.
When the World-Honored One attained the Way and his light illuminated the three thousandfold world-system, I first entreated him to turn the wondrous Dharma.
When the world had been matured by his transformation, the Buddha was about to enter nirvana; I exhorted him to remain long, out of compassion to save all beings.
Through repentance, exhortation, and sympathetic joy, may all roots of goodness not obscure my bodhi, so that I may always encounter true friends.
May I leave behind hardships in future lives, with a body adorned by the marks and signs of excellence, entering the web of the Avataṃsaka and attaining the pāramitās.
His power and function are vast and abundant; his retinue is refined and excellent. The force of his conditions is boundless;
he summons all according to his will, taking the realm of space as his domain. He dwells in celestial palaces, manifesting wondrous lotus flowers throughout all lands.
Possessing the six supernormal powers and four analytical knowledges, he manifests an eightfold body of mastery, appearing everywhere without fixed location to fulfill the vows of sentient beings.
To introduce the Buddha-wisdom, inexhaustible and manifold, like a vajra-banner that none can move—
With a single mind, we reverently entreat you to enter the maṇḍala. The Mantra of the Greatly Powerful Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin Vidyārāja (Prostrations and Contemplation as Above).

The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, having accepted the invitation of the celestial king Maheśvara, immediately entered the samādhi of the Great Wrathful Universal Joy of the Terrifying Vajra and proclaimed the mantra of the vidyārāja Ucchuṣma.
All bhūtas saw their bodies completely overwhelmed and suppressed by Ucchuṣma, as if encountering the conflagration at the end of a kalpa; they were utterly bewildered.
One will feel as if one were on the verge of fainting from distress. Regarding this mantra-dharma: if one hears it even briefly, all undertakings will be fully accomplished;
there shall be no untimely or violent deaths; those who see one will feel reverence and affection; enemies will keep their distance; all secret mantras will attain efficacy;
and all Vajra-dharmas will be spontaneously realized. If one maintains this vidyā (vidyā refers to a mantra) for a full...
Ten thousand times over, one immediately ascends the altar for the complete consecration (*abhiṣeka*), as if receiving the transmission from an enlightened master.
One forms the *Puyen-in* (Universal Flame Seal): first, place the backs of the hands together with the fingertips hanging down; this is called the "lower joined palms.
Next, deeply interlace all the fingers (raise both hands, crossing them internally without clenching them into fists). The two little fingers are like needles, and the palms are opened wide. Two.
Interlace the thumbs and press them against the sides of the index fingernails.

The mantra is: Oṃ (1) hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ (2) ugraśūrapāṇi (3) hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ (4) phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ (5) oṃ raudriṇāna (6) hūṃ hūṃ (7) (The *phaṭ* at the beginning of the second phrase is pronounced with a half-syllable.)
HŪṂ (7) PHAṬ PHAṬ PHAṬ (8) OṂ OṂ OṂ (9) MAHĀMĀLA SVĀHĀ (10). First, regarding the painted image:
using a square white woolen cloth measuring two cubits in length and breadth, commission a skilled artisan to depict an image of the Tathāgata.

Seated upon the lion throne, his hands form the gesture of preaching the Dharma (joining the tips of the thumbs and index fingers of both hands; extending the middle, ring, and little fingers together; the right hand likewise;

and with the left hand, palm facing upward, held horizontally across the heart; placing the wrist of the right hand against the tips of the left hand’s middle and little fingers, with the palm turned outward and the three fingers splayed—this is the gesture of preaching the Dharma).

To the left of the Tathāgata, paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, holding a vajra in his right hand and making the gesture of inquiring about the Dharma with his left (placing all five fingers [against the heart]).
Slightly bend [the body]. Extend the hand forward, with the palm facing toward the Tathāgata. Next, paint the Great Powerful Vajra-uṣṇīṣa Vidyārāja in the form of a great wrathful deity.
His eyes are red (like those of a wildcat), his canine fangs are bared and sharp, and his yellow hair bristles upward. His entire body is a deep indigo-black.
Flames erupt from his whole being, and he has four arms: the upper right hand holds a sword, the next below it holds a lasso, and the upper left hand strikes a chariot.
A staff and a trident below; from these weapons, flames rise upward on both sides. To the right of the Tathāgata, one should paint Māmakī, the Mother of the Vajra Family.
She has abundant hair and a beautiful countenance, her entire body is azure in color, and she kneels with her right knee on the ground, palms joined in reverence, respectfully addressing the Buddha.
To the right of the Mother of the Family, the practitioner kneels on his right knee, holding an incense burner in his hand to make offerings to the Buddha.
Before this image, facing east, he recites the mantra while abstaining from food and remaining silent, as motionless as a withered tree.

Upon completing six hundred thousand recitations, there is nothing among all mundane and supramundane dharmas that will not be accomplished (for accomplishment, the homa rite is frequently employed; homa is like a fire sacrifice).
If one performs *homa* one hundred thousand times using non-glutinous rice mixed with cow’s ghee, one will give birth to a son endowed with auspicious marks.
If one performs *homa* one thousand and eight times using fennel flowers mixed with the three sweets for seven full days,
one will obtain one hundred gold coins.
Add one *liang* of blue lotus flowers to milk and honey, and perform thirty thousand *homāḥ*. All hidden treasures will appear.
Recite the mantra over the root of *achyranthes aspera* one thousand and eight times and hold it in the mouth; one will prevail in legal disputes.
If one treats the disease of insanity, join two earthen bowls together, form the *nāḍa* mudrā, and recite [the mantra] seven times by the patient's ear.
Then, smash the bowls apart; the illness will be cured immediately. *Nāḍa* means a staff. As for that mudrā:
with both hands, press the thumbs against the middle fingers and little fingers to form two rings. Clasp the two rings firmly together and extend the index fingers.
It is accomplished just like sealing a knot.
If one wishes to treat abdominal tumors or chronic enlargement, one should empower black sesame oil seven times and apply it to the abdomen; the ailment will immediately be cured.
If one empowers the right thumb seven times and seals five locations with the mudrā, it will immediately become a protection for the body, warding off [harm].
Regarding lions, tigers, wolves, and all such fears, or if one is imprisoned or bound, by holding this mantra, one shall be released from the shackles.
