If treating leprosy, empower red sandalwood incense one thousand and eight times and apply it; the disease will be cured immediately.
If one takes the root of *achyranthes aspera* mixed with honey and, having empowered it one thousand and eight times, consumes it, it cures cold-natured abdominal tumors (*śīta-jaṭhara*).
If one performs *homā* seven times using tiger claws, one will not be harmed by tigers.
If one prays for rain, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, by the side of a great river, one should fashion a dragon from the soil of an anthill.
Cover it entirely with leaves, mustard seeds, and oil, then place one's foot upon the dragon’s head and empower it by binding the *nāga-mudrā*.
Thus, one will obtain sufficient rain throughout the entire day.
If there is evil rain, snow, thunder, or hail, the Vidyādhara shall form the *vajra-mudrā* or the *nāḍa-mudrā*, and it will immediately cease.
To form the *vajra-mudrā*: interlace the two hands internally to form fists, then extend the middle finger of the left hand and the index finger of the right hand like a seal.
If one takes fertile soil and ashes, mixes them with honey, and consecrates the mixture to apply it to all sores, the flesh will grow back.
If there is an epidemic, one should perform *homa* one thousand and eight times using boiled rice mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*); the plague will then cease immediately.

If one is treating a case of possession by malevolent spirits, construct a square altar and sprinkle it with scented water. Burn frankincense and sit before the patient, performing empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) over them.
Furthermore, empower water seven times and sprinkle it on the patient's face; they will cry out loudly and be cast down.
If [the spirit] does not speak, sprinkle water again and it will speak. If [it is] deceitful, fashion the form of the patient out of earth from an anthill and empower it seven times.

Strike the head of the form with a ritual mallet; if it speaks truthfully and does not abandon this person, then take a knife made of the five metals and cut the form limb by limb from the feet until it is completely gone. Blood will flow from the air, and the spirit will die.
When the illness has subsided,
if one performs one hundred and eight homas using salt, or *kirimāla* wood, or mustard oil,
the host of spirits will be immediately extinguished and the illness will be cured.
If one does not eat on the anniversary of a deceased person's passing and makes offerings at a stupa or temple, sitting alone in a pure room and reciting [the mantra] one hundred times,
the deceased will appear as if they were still alive.
If one wishes to know the future, one should recite this mantra while falling asleep; the tutelary deity will then speak to one within the dream.
If, like a pregnancy that has exceeded its term, one consecrates rice one hundred and eight times and causes it to be consumed, one will immediately give birth [to the knowledge].
This mantra teaching makes no distinction between the pure and the impure, and constantly manifests a wrathful aspect. One attains efficacy upon completing three hundred thousand recitations.

With single-minded devotion, one should invoke the Great Maṇḍala along with the hand-seals (*mudrā*) and visualizations of the mantras of the five Tathāgatas (the ritual for prostration and visualization is as described above).

The World-Honored One Vairocana, having perfected his body through the five stages of manifestation (the *saṃbhogakāya*), attained manifest perfect enlightenment within the celestial palace of the King of Akaniṣṭha.

He was endowed with the Great Bodhicitta of Samantabhadra common to all Tathāgatas and received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by means of the great *maṇi* jewel born of the space of all Tathāgatas. He attained all...
The Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, through the wisdom of the Dharma, has reached the further shore. He accomplishes all the non-empty activities of all Tathāgatas without obstruction.

Having attained Buddhahood, he proceeded to the summit of Mount Sumeru and entered the Vajra-samādhi, giving rise to the thirty-seven wisdoms and stabilizing the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu. This...
Within the maṇḍala are five great lunar discs. The World-Honored One Vairocana is seated at the center of the lunar disc within the altar, upon a lion throne, in the full-lotus posture.
He possesses great majestic power, and his color is like that of a white goose.
His form is like the pure moon; all his marks and signs of excellence are perfectly complete. He wears a jeweled crown upon his head, with locks of hair hanging down adorned by silk ribbons.
Light and exquisite celestial garments wrap around his waist and serve as his upper robe.

His very essence consists of all vidyā-mantras, and he is able to perform immeasurable miraculous transformations. His hands form the mudrā of the Great Wisdom Fist: the two hands are joined to form fists.
Place the first phalanx of the index finger of the left hand flat inside the right fist and grasp it; stand up and form the mudrā. Recite the mantra: Oṃ vajra ḍaṭṭa gaṃ.

Next is the Honored One Akṣobhya. In the eastern direction (as the Vairocana maṇḍala faces east), before the moon disc of the central altar of Vairocana, he sits in the center of a great moon disc upon a throne supported by elephant kings.
He sits in the half-lotus posture with his left leg pendant. His body is the color of a great blue jewel.

His face is like the autumn moon; he is endowed with all the marks and signs of perfection. He wears a wondrous blue robe, from which emanate countless rays of light that illuminate all manner of adornments.
His right hand forms the earth-touching mudrā; his left fist grasps the corner of his *kāṣāya* robe, resting it upon his navel.
His right palm rests over his knee, its fingers hanging down and touching the ground. He utters this mantra:
Oṃ (1) Akṣobhya (2) Hūṃ (3). Next is Ratnasaṃbhava, who is in the moon disc to the right of the Tathāgata Vairocana, seated upon a horse-king throne.
He sits in the full-lotus posture. His body is the color of the sun; his face is like the full moon. He wears a jeweled crown and is clad in garments of yellowish-white.
His hands form the mudrā of boon-granting (*varada-mudrā*); his left fist rests upon his thigh, while his right hand is held at the level of his breast with the palm facing outward.
He assumes the mudrā of bestowing boons. The mantra is recited as follows: Oṃ ratna-sambhava traḥ.
Next, the Honored One Avalokiteśvara appears within a moon disc behind the Tathāgata Vairocana, [holding] a peacock.
Seated upon the royal throne in the full-lotus posture, his body is golden in color and his face is like the full moon. His topknot is magnificent and his crown is ornate.
He wears red garments and has the light of a moon disc behind him. With his hands turned back, he forms the mudrā of meditative concentration:
the two hands are in the vajra-bind, placed upward upon the lap; the two index fingers are held straight up with their backs joined, and the two thumbs [are likewise joined].
The fingers are held crosswise at its tip. The mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ (1) Lokeshvara (2) Rāja (3) Hriḥ (4). Next is the Honored One Amoghasiddhi, who resides upon a seat of the King of Garuḍas within the moon disc to the left of Vairocana.
He sits in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His body is a great green color; his face is like the full moon, radiating brilliant light, and he displays a smiling countenance.
His topknot is magnificent and his crown is exquisite. He wears blue garments and is adorned with various ornaments.

His hands form the *abhaya-mudrā* (gesture of fearlessness). His left fist is placed inverted upon his navel, while his right hand has the thumb and little finger joined together, with the [other fingers] held upright.
The three fingers are like a banner; with the palms raised beside the breasts, one assumes the posture of rescuing sentient beings.
The mantra is recited as follows: Oṃ (protracted) (1) Amoghasiddhi (2) Aḥ (repeatedly called) (3).
These five Tathāgatas each abide in one direction as the lords of the five families. Vairocana enters...
Within the Vajra-samādhi, sixteen great Bodhisattvas are successively produced.
They abide in their respective positions—front, right, left, and rear—within the moon-discs of the Tathāgatas in the four directions.
The first to be produced is Vajrapāṇi, who holds a five-pronged vajra; Vajrarāja, who holds a hook; Vajrarāga, who holds a bow and arrow; and Vajrasādhu.
"Excellent! Manifesting a joyful appearance, excellent sound! (The fourth Bodhisattva holds nothing in his hand). These four belong to the maṇḍala of Akṣobhya.
Next, those who are produced are Vajragarbha, holding a *māṇikya* jewel; Vajraprabha, holding the mark of a solar disc; Vajraketu, holding a banner;
and Vajrahāsa, manifesting a smiling expression. These four belong to Ratnasambhava.
Next, those born from the maṇḍala are the Vajradharma, who holds a lotus; the Vajratīkṣṇa, who holds a sword;
the Vajrahetu, who holds a wheel; and the Vajrabhāṣa, who manifests the appearance of recitation. These four belong to the maṇḍala of Avalokiteśvararāja.
Next, those born from it are the Vajrakarma, who holds a *karmavajra* (action-vajra) shaped like a cross, all of which have sharp edges.
Vajrapāla is clad in armor; Vajrayakṣa wields fang-like weapons; and Vajramuṣṭi manifests the gesture of the vajra-bind.
These four belong to the maṇḍala of Amoghasiddhi. Each arises individually, having first entered the samādhi of the sixteen great bodhisattvas of all Tathāgatas.
Having spoken their mantras, they immediately become vajras, hooks, and bows.
The arrows and other insignia return to the heart of Vairocana and abide within his palms;
from each of these insignia, various miraculous manifestations and playful activities appear.
The sixteen bodhisattvas are: Samantabhadra, Amogharāja, Māra, Pramuditarāja, Gaganagañja, Mahātejas, Ratnaketu, Nityapramuditamūla, Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, and Dharmacakrapravartin.
Silence. Skillful action. Invincible diligence. Subduing all māras. The fist of the wondrous bond. These bodhisattvas each possess their own rational nature.
The sixteen mantras that are taught are as follows: Vajrasattva, Rāja, Rāga, Sādhana.
Vajra-ratna, tejah, ketu, hasa, vajra-dharma, tiṣṭhāna, hīdu, vasa, vajra-karma, lokaya, yakṣa, sandhi.
These self-mantra seals all arise from the gateway of the Vajradhātu.
The essential nature of those bodhisattvas is firmly and wondrously united within the Vajrasattva samādhi;
from this, the bodies of the sixteen great beings, such as Vajrapāṇi and others, emerge from the heart of the World-Honored One Vairocana.
Descending, they abide within the lunar disks of the four Tathāgatas.
Thereafter, they are bestowed with insignia such as the vajra and given names, each being crowned with the title "Vajra.
At that time, the sixteen Great Beings, holding their respective insignia, perform various activities before all the Tathāgatas; this constitutes the manifestation of the sixteen.

This is the Dharma of the Great Bodhisattvas. Then those four Tathāgatas each individually entered a samādhi, giving rise to the four bodhisattvas—Vajrapāramitā, Ratnapāramitā, Dharmapāramitā, and Karmapāramitā—who abide within the moon-disc of Vairocana in the center.
Their mantras and mudrās are identical to those of the four Tathāgatas; this is their emergence.

The four pāramitā bodhisattva-dharmas are generated. Next, for the purpose of making offerings to the four Tathāgatas, Vairocana Tathāgata generates the goddesses Vajralāsyā, Vajramālā, Vajragītā, and Vajranṛtyā.
They abide within moon-discs at the four inner corners; this is called the inner offering. Next, the four Tathāgatas...
In order to perform the offerings to Vairocana, he brought forth the vajra-incense, vajra-flower, vajra-lamp, and vajra-unguent goddesses, who dwell within moon discs at the four outer corners;
this constitutes the outer offering. Finally, the Tathāgata Vairocana brought forth the vajra-hook and the vajra-noose.
The Vajra-Lock and Vajra-Bell messengers abide within the moon discs at the four gates; these are called the four messengers of attraction (*saṃgraha*).
As for the thirty-seven deities mentioned above, they all emerge from the body of Vairocana.
If there is one who maintains and recites the mantras of the five Tathāgatas, they should, according to the ritual, draw the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu and the images of the deities.
Having first established themselves in samādhi and generated the great bodhicitta, they should then enter the maṇḍala.
Facing the images before them, they should wash away the defilements of the mind and recite the mantra for purifying the three karmas for one *kṣaṇa*.

Within that state, the defilements of the mind are purified. Through the power of the mantra, one awakens the bodhicitta and contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, empty by their very nature from the beginning, and devoid of any solid reality.
Based on this thought of bodhicitta, one visualizes a moon disc. Upon the moon disc, one visualizes the syllable Oṃ in the Brāhmī script as the Vajra Body. Next, one visualizes...
Visualize the Sanskrit letter *A*, which becomes the Vajra of Speech. Next, visualize the Sanskrit letter *Hūṃ*, which becomes the Vajra of Mind.
Once these three letters have thus formed the vajra body, speech, and mind, visualize the Sanskrit letter *Praṃ* transforming into a lotus.
Mounting this lotus, endowed with all the marks and signs of perfection, visualize yourself assuming a majestic and haughty posture. This is [the practice of]...
The Tathāgata Vajradhātu is adorned with all ornaments and radiates a perfect light;
such a physical form is itself the ultimate bodhi and great wisdom. Furthermore, one should visualize all Buddhas filling the void, performing great miraculous transformations.
These five Tathāgatas expound the truth of Yoga, the Four Noble Truths, the Six Pāramitās, and so forth. Thus they act.

This brings great benefit and delivers all sentient beings. Then, visualize that each of the Buddhas sits upon a lotus flower, their various marks (*lakṣaṇa*) complete and adorned with every ornament.

These lotus seats then merge into one; this signifies that the Buddha’s body is neither one nor many, where principle and phenomena are non-obstructive, and all share the same essence within the *dharmadhātu*.
Thereafter, according to the ritual, present the eight offerings (including music, garlands, song, and dance).

Having offered incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments, one should immediately engage in recitation with body and mind in right concentration, free from all distraction. Neither too slow nor too hurried, the words and phrases should be perfectly precise.
Thus, according to the ritual, one should perform visualization and recitation, like the full moon in the sky, without waning or waxing.
Before long, he realized great bodhi. Next, its efficacy shall be explained:

by forming the mudrā of the Fist of Great Wisdom and reciting the mantra of Vairocana Tathāgata, one immediately attains the great bodhi of the equal radiance of the three vajra-actions and achieves the three bodies (trikāya), which are firm and indestructible. By forming the earth-touching mudrā and reciting [the mantra of] Akṣobhya...
By reciting the mantra of Ratnasambhava Tathāgata while forming the mudrā of the vow of giving, one immediately attains the samādhi of non-movement of body and mind,
and realizes the manifestation of the jeweled banner (*ratnaketu*) that gathers in sentient beings through the mark of non-abiding,
thereby accomplishing all vajra offerings and activities throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Through the wisdom of the selflessness of *bodhi*-dharmas, by forming the *samādhi-mudrā* and reciting the mantra of the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara,
one immediately attains the equal radiance of adamantine life-span and preaches the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
By forming the *abhaya-dāna-mudrā* and reciting the mantra of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi, one immediately attains the adamantine...
The Vajra-Abhaya-Equanimity Radiance gives birth to the auspicious ocean of wisdom. It benefits sentient beings and frees them from all fears.
With single-minded devotion, I invoke the Maṇḍala Dharma of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi (the ritual for viewing is as above).
This Bodhisattva is the eldest son of the Tathāgatas of the Secret Division; therefore, he is treated first.

The Tathāgata Vairocana, within the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, entered the Samādhi of Universal Goodness (Samantabhadra) of all Tathāgatas and gave birth to the Sattva (the great moon disc, which is the manifestation of the perfected bodhicitta). Within that Sattva-moon disc...
In the center, there appeared the form of a five-peaked vajra of radiant light, which remained within the Buddha’s palm.

Having performed a miraculous transformation, because its vajra-nature was in perfect union with the sublime samādhi of Vajrasattva, the head [of the Buddha] then produced the body of the Great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi (who received his office and name as previously described). He became the eldest son of all the Tathāgatas.
This is the bodhicitta of all Tathāgatas. Having received the commands of all Tathāgatas, he acts as the supreme sovereign within the secret Dharma.
This Bodhisattva manifests a posture of loftiness, the majestic power of Vajra-pride;
with both hands he forms the vajra-fist, placing the left hand beneath his hip and playfully tossing the vajra with the right hand.
Place the vajra at the center of one’s own heart and assume the posture of heroic valor;
this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā). Recite the mantra: Oṃ vajrasattva aḥ. Furthermore, for the root mantra, form the Great Wisdom Seal (mahājñānamudrā).
Oṃ (1) Mahāsukhava-jra-sattva (2) Jjaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ (3) Suratasatva (4).
Only by practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva and realizing wondrous enlightenment can one truly fulfill the original vow for the benefit of sentient beings. Sentient beings...

They are submerged; they are exceedingly deep, most deep. If one does not enter the maṇḍalas of the five families and five secrets, and does not receive the empowerment of the three kinds of secrets, how could one’s own body of the three tainted karmas cross over them?

Those classes of sentient beings in the two upper realms (the realm of form and the realm of formlessness) are comprised within the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*). In the desire realm there is no dhyāna; it is the stage of non-concentrated virtue (*vyutthāna-kuśala-bhūmi*). Even if—

If one wishes to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must first rely upon the dhūtas and the seven stages of expedient means (*pañca-vipaśyanā-sthāna*, *sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*, *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*, *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgra-dharma*).
Because their faculties are weak and inferior, even the fruit of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha is difficult to achieve;

how much more so the stage of the Great Samantabhadra, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), and the stage of Vairocana’s three bodies, the Universal Radiance? This is true even for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), though—

Having realized the fruits of the path, they are unable to benefit infinite sentient beings. In the practice of the Exoteric Teachings, they spend three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before finally attaining the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]. During that interval, they advance ten times and retreat nine times;
or they may realize the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) and, with the merit and wisdom they have accumulated, dedicate them toward the fruits of the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Nevertheless...
One cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

However, in the Secret Teaching, by hearing the Dharma of the internally realized, self-awakened noble wisdom as taught by the *svasaṃbhogakāya* of Vairocana, as well as the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* of the great Samantabhadra-Vajrasattva stage, one shall enter the maṇḍala in this very body and become fully endowed with the ritual actions (*karma*). By means of this—
Through the Samādhi of Samantabhadra, Vajrasattva is summoned to enter within one’s body.
By the power of his majestic empowerment, in a mere instant, one shall realize immeasurable samayas and immeasurable dharanī-gates.
By means of inconceivable dharmas, one shall be able to transform the seeds of innate clinging to a self and clinging to phenomena at that very moment.
Having accumulated within one’s own body the merit and wisdom gathered over one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one is then born into the family of the Buddhas.
One is born from the mind of all Tathāgatas and born from the mouth of the Buddha, attaining the wealth of the Buddha-Dharma (referring to the teachings on the three mysteries and the bodhicitta).
If, upon merely seeing the maṇḍala, one can give rise to pure faith for even a brief moment with joy—
Beholding with a joyful mind, one plants the seeds of the Vajradhātu within the ālayavijñāna; from this, one immediately transcends the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Amidst the four modes of deportment, one practices without interruption, such that the two emptinesses of person and phenomena are entirely equal.
One realizes the first bhūmi in the present, gradually ascending until, regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, there is no...

Unstained by attachment, they extensively bring benefit to infinite worlds. Manifesting ten billion emanations, they travel through the various realms of existence to mature sentient beings, causing them to realize the state of Vajrasattva. The practitioner should, before the ācārya, [proceed as follows].
Within the Great Vajra Family, one receives the dharma of the four kinds of wisdom; within the Great Ratna Family, one receives the dharma of equal correspondence;
within the Great Padma Family, one receives the subtle and secret dharma of the three vehicles; and within the Great Karma Family...

One receives the ritual for all activities of making offerings for the sake of perfecting the precepts (*samyak-saṃvara*). Having received the rite, one practices according to the Dharma to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
For those without a protector, one acts as their protector; for those seeking liberation, one causes them to attain liberation.
Abiding in the *samādhi* of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one contemplates the syllable *kaṃ* within the moon-disk of the mind.
Polish the vajra and, with a mind imbued with compassion, extend it throughout the realm of sentient beings to bestow immeasurable happiness (one may use the previous mudrā).
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) Mahā-maitrī-sphara (2). Next, with a mind of great compassion, one cuts off the suffering of all sentient beings and contemplates the karma-wheel pervading the entire dharmadhātu.
Universally Saving and Delivering (one may use the aforementioned mudrā). The mantra is:
Oṃ mahākāruṇyā-sphara. Next, with a joyful mind, one should mobilize the karma-cakra to pervade all sentient beings throughout the entire dharmadhātu, bestowing upon them bodhi.
[Hold] the previous seal (mudrā). The mantra is:
Oṃ sarvaśuddha-pramocana-spharaṇa. Next, extend the karma-cakra throughout the realm of sentient beings.
Accomplish great equanimity (*upekṣā*), with the mind abiding in equality, seeing nothing [dualistic].
Self and others are of this very nature and characteristic; this is the Great Bodhicitta of Samantabhadra (still using the previous mudrā). The mantra is: Oṃ (1) Mahākāśasphara (2).
Then, one should visualize oneself as Vajrasattva, situated within a great moon disc, seated upon a great lotus, [surrounded by] the five Buddhas.
Wearing a jeweled crown, his countenance is radiant and joyful; his body is like the color of the moon, transparent both within and without, and its magnitude is equal to space.
This constitutes the accomplishment of the Dharmakāya. Then, before one’s body, one should visualize the wisdom-body of Vajrasattva, surrounded by the four mudrās.
They share a single lunar disc and a single lotus, each abiding in their original majestic posture, holding their respective insignia. Each...
He wears a jeweled crown of the five Buddhas.

Regarding the four mudrās: the Desire Vajra holds a vajra bow and arrow, shooting all the contaminated seeds within the *ālayavijñāna* to realize the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). The Vajra-Ketukīla embraces the Vajra.

*Sattva* signifies the purification of the seventh consciousness (*manas*) of its deluded attachment to the eighth consciousness as a self—namely, self-delusion, self-view, self-pride, and self-love—which results in the attainment of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
It holds the Vajra and the Makara banner, and is able to purify the mental objects of the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
Regarding the defiled and pure, out-flowing minds, it becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Through the two *vajras*, Vajra-Pride...

Placing the clenched fists at the hips symbolizes the purification of the five consciousnesses and the obstructive body. Arousing great diligence and valor, one causes all sentient beings without exception to suddenly attain Buddhahood.
Thus, one is able to purify the body of the five consciousnesses and accomplish the Wisdom of Accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The practitioner focuses intently on Vajrasattva before the body, as if facing a reflection in a mirror;
with the mind undistracted, they cause him to appear clearly and distinctly within meditative concentration. Then, one recites the four-syllable mantra: Oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ.
Recite *Jah Hūṃ Baṃ Hoḥ* to cause the wisdom-body of Vajrasattva to be summoned, bound, and delighted, merging into a single essence with the yogin’s meditative body.

Whether holding a rosary or not, focus one-pointedly on the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) and perform recitation four times a day without limit, without becoming weary. By abiding in samādhi, recite this mantra:
Because of these words, one realizes immeasurable *samādhis* in the present life and is able to manifest the body of the Principal Deity (*mūlamantra*).
If one desires to seek the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*), one should first arrange the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and depict the holy image of the Tathāgata in its center.
Together with the four classes of preeminent bodhisattvas, they reside within the lunar disc. At its four corners, one should paint the deities and sages of their respective families.
Before these images, the practitioner should extensively arrange offerings and recite the mantra with a sincere mind for a full four months.
Thereafter, one should recite throughout the night. At the time of dawn, one will immediately attain the method for the supreme siddhi of all Tathāgatas.
If one wishes to seek the accomplishment of the mudrā, the practitioner, before the image, should bind the Sattvavajra-mudrā.
According to whatever one seeks, if one does not understand this seal (*mudrā*), one should recite and maintain the great mantra (*mahāvidyā*) for one hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, one should recite and maintain it with a sincere mind throughout the entire night until, at last, a blazing light appears and the image of the Buddha utters a voice.

Only then should one release the aforementioned seal-binding; immediately, one will obtain a form according to one’s desire, attain mastery over invisibility, and all undertakings will be accomplished.
One is able to accomplish all things.
If one wishes to seek the accomplishment of *samādhi*, one should first visualize the subtle vajra according to whichever *samādhi* gate one prefers,
and practice the preliminary cultivation using the corresponding heart-mantra for a full four months.
Thereafter, throughout the night, sitting upright in the full lotus posture, with a straight mind and concentrated mindfulness, he dwelt in tranquility.
When morning arrived, he immediately attained the accomplishment of all samādhis, such as those of the Tathāgata.
If one wishes to seek the accomplishment of *karma*, one should recite according to the ritual for one month while aspiring for accomplishment;
thereafter, by reciting throughout the entire night, one will immediately attain all accomplishments of *karma*.
The Ritual Method for the Maṇḍala of the Bodhisattva Vajrāyuṣ (to be viewed as above).
Vairocana, with Mahādeva prostrate face-down upon the ground on the verge of death,
entered the Samādhi of Vajrāyuṣ within the Samādhi of Compassionate Great Pity and spoke the Vajrāyuṣ Mantra.
Having spoken thus, he formed a mudrā: with both hands in vajra-fists, the index fingers hook together, the right pressing down upon the left, and the gesture is placed upon the crown of the head.
Through this empowerment, Maheśvara was restored to life and his lifespan was further increased.
He took refuge in all the Buddhas, received the seal of consecration, and attained the eighth bhūmi. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajrayuṣe svāhā. If any man or woman receives, maintains, and recites this [mantra] three times each day, one thousand times per session, then by the power of this mantra,
all past karmic causes and conditions for short life or premature death shall be [purified] through their faith.

Purified, the karmic obstructions are extinguished. If one practices the gate of samādhi, one should sit in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), straighten the body, close the eyes, and place both hands one upon the other below the navel. One should clearly and vividly visualize all the Buddhas throughout the expanse of space.
Then, within one’s own body, one should contemplate the mind as being like the full moon, its radiance pure and translucent, with [a syllable] above it.
The form of a five-pronged vajra gradually increases in size until it is equal to his own body, transforming into the Bodhisattva Trailokyavijaya.
He has four faces and eight arms; his beard and hair are red and bristling upward. His brows are knitted and his fangs are sharp. His primary face is blue, and his right face is yellow.
The back is red; the left side is green. His entire body is ablaze with majesty like the fire at the end of an eon.

His two central hands form vajra-fists, the right pressing down upon the left, with the two little fingers hooked together and the two index fingers extended upward with their backs touching, in the manner of a piercing strike.
The upper right hand holds a vajra; the second [right] hand holds an arrow; the third hand holds...
[He holds] a sword; his upper left hand holds a hook, the second hand holds a bow, and the third hand holds a lasso. He sits upon a blue lotus flower.

Upon his crown is Vairocana Buddha, from whose every pore flows nectar for consecration, which pours over his own body and enters his heart. Thereupon, he binds the *vidyā* of the Bodhisattva Vajrāyuṣ.

Using the same mudrā as before (the Ni-mudrā), recite the mantra seven times and place it upon the forehead. Then, with hands separated, bind them behind the neck and extend the two index fingers straight out.
Rotate [the hands] all over the body in the manner of donning armor. The mantra is as follows:

Oṃ (1) Kaṭa (2) Vajra (3) Kāma. By means of this mantra and mudrā, one attains a body as indestructible as vajra, is freed from all calamities and misfortunes, brings joy to those who behold it, and inspires great reverence.
For the homa to eliminate calamities and establish the life-consecration altar, one should prepare a pure chamber. Within it—
To the east, place an image of the Bodhisattva Vajrāyus. Hang various banners and canopies. Before the image, construct a square altar three cubits on each side.
In its center, draw a vajra armor one and a half cubits in size using white powder.
In the middle, pierce a fire-pit half a cubit deep, with a rim surrounding it. If one does not wish to pierce [the ground], it is also permissible to simply set up a fire-pit.
The practitioner sits before the fire pit and presents various offerings. Vases are placed at the four corners, and charcoal is lit within the pit.
First, prepare twenty-one pieces of milky wood, each ten finger-widths long and as thick as a thumb, with both ends smeared with ghee.
Recite the mantra and cast it into the fire. Once it has blazed up intensely, visualize an eight-petaled lotus within the fire.
Within the heart of that lotus, visualize the letter *A* in the Brahmī script, which transforms into the Bodhisattva Vajrāyus.
Next, with the four-syllable mantra, invite the Bodhisattvas to enter the fire pit and receive the various offerings.
Next, sprinkle water upon the fire to purify it. Then, take *śara* grass stalks dyed blue and soaked in clarified butter; reciting the mantra once for each, cast them into the fire.
After performing this one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eight times, again offer three full ladles [of clarified butter].

Offer ghee to the Honored One; do so likewise at the beginning and the end. If one can perform such an offering on the three long fasting days, or on one's own birthday, it will be able to eliminate calamities and extend one’s lifespan.
The land will be peaceful and stable, free from all disasters and epidemics, and winds and rains will arrive in their proper seasons. All sages and worthies will protect that person.
The Ritual for the Mandala of the Four Buddha-Mothers (Worship and Contemplation as Above).
The Tathāgata Vairocana-Vajra, having entered the Samādhi of the Supreme Vajra of Quiescent Dustlessness Arising from the Transformation of Great Wisdom,
brought forth the Buddha-Mother, the Great Auspicious Vajra Consort, and spoke this mantra:
It is said: It can accomplish all vidyās and fulfill all aspirations; it extinguishes sins and generates merit; it causes all sentient beings who see it to rejoice;
it swiftly brings about the Cakravartin of all families, which is most supreme and peerless; it accomplishes all matters that are difficult to resolve;
it can perform the rite for pacifying calamities for the world; and even for those who wish to relinquish their life-span.

By the power of this illumination, one’s lifespan is further increased. One is able to assist the majesty of the five profound and secret divisions (*pañcakula*), attesting to them all simultaneously.
With both hands, join the palms with the hollows facing upward; bend the two index fingers so they rest upon the upper joints of the two middle fingers, forming the shape of a smiling eye.
Each of the two thumbs presses against the marks on the middle joints of the two middle fingers, likewise [forming a seal].
Form the shape of a smiling eye. Slightly separate the two little fingers so that they also form the shape of a smiling eye.
With this mudrā, wipe the eyes and the eyebrows, while simultaneously holding the fingers upright to wipe between the brows. Visualize the five eyes emerging.
Then, while maintaining the mudrā and reciting the mantra, circumambulate the face three times while wiping it. All who see this will be filled with joy. The mantra is as follows:
Namo bhagavatyai (1) śrī-saṃghāya (2) oṃ (3) ru-ru (4) sarva-ru (5) jvala-tiṣṭha (6) siddha-rocani (7) sarvārtha-sādhanaye (8) svāhā (9)
At that time, the body of the Mother of All Buddhas dwells upon a great white lotus;
her body radiates with the luster of a white moon, her two eyes smile, and her two hands rest at her navel as if she had entered *śamatha*.
From all her limbs, ten *nayuta-koṭi* of Buddhas are born. Each Buddha pays homage to the one from whom they were originally born. In an instant—

At that moment, he transformed himself into the One-Syllable Cakravartin King. Holding the wheel-seal in his hand and emitting light from the crown of his head, he gazed with a haughty look and manifested great supernatural powers.
He then returned to pay homage to the Mother of All Buddhas from whom he had originally arisen.
The various Cakravartin Kings of the Buddhas each placed a vajra-wheel beneath the feet of the Buddha-mother, so that two wheels were formed:
one supporting her feet and one covering the crown of her head. At that time, the Buddha-mother addressed all the Tathāgatas, saying:
"If one constantly recites this vidyā-mantra, one shall be like that Vajradhātu Tathāgata and like that Sattvavajra-padmapāṇi."

The Vajra-Ākāśa-ratna Viśvakarman, like those four pāramitās, sixteen great bodhisattvas, four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and eight great offerings, performs all activities identical to those of all Tathāgatas.
Whatever words he utters become mantras; his every movement and limb become great mudrās; and wherever his eyes gaze becomes the Great Maṇḍala.
In the Vajradhātu, wherever the body touches becomes the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).

If one wishes to act as a Great Ācārya and instruct others in the mudrās and other aspects of the Secret Dharma, one must first recite this mantra one thousand times before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
All were filled with joy. All sentient beings who saw him regarded him as their own parents. His merit was like that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), fully endowed with the seven treasures.
His lifespan was long, lasting for many millions of *koṭis*. [He was attended by] Vajrasattva and all the other bodhisattvas.

They shall constantly follow and protect you. On days of urgent distress, like the sun rising in the sky, all karmic obstacles from past lives and the influences of the seven planets and twenty-eight lunar mansions shall be unable to destroy you;
you will attain great peace and happiness. If you recite this one million times, you will attain the state of Great Nirvana.
The practitioner should always contemplate their own body as having the form and appearance of the Honored One, the Buddha Eye, abiding in great whiteness.

The lotus gradually unfolds, pervading the entire realm of space. Alternatively, by forming the root mudrā and empowering one’s own body, one abides in the samādhi of the dharmadhātu and shall swiftly attain the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Regarding the method for painting an image: take pure white woolen cloth and paint upon it a size equal to one's own body. In all yoga practices, the images should be depicted with the deity seated;
they must be painted to this same proportion. Within the center, one should paint a three-tiered eight-petaled lotus. In the center, paint the Honored One Locanā.
Directly in front of the central deity, on one of the lotus petals, paint all [the deities].
The Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin holds a golden wheel with eight spokes, which rotates clockwise; around it are arrayed the messengers of the seven luminaries.
In the second flower court, directly in front of the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, one should paint the eight great bodhisattvas, beginning with Vajrasattva.
Proceeding clockwise to the third flower courtyard (*puṣpakaraṇḍa*), draw the eight Great Vidyārājas (also known as the Vajrarājas) in clockwise order.
Furthermore, outside the flower courtyard, draw the eight offerings and the four *saṃgraha-viṣaya* messengers;

all of them wear golden lion crowns. [The Cakravartin is in the east. In the south-west is the Sun, and in the west is the Moon. Continuing thus through the northeast, there are Fire, Water, Mercury, Venus, and Earth. Outside the Sun is Mañjuśrī, and outside the Moon is Ākāśagarbha. Continuing thus, there are Dharmacakrapravartaka Avalokiteśvara and Gaganagañja.

The Vajra Fist subdues all māras. Outside the [mandalas] of fire, water, wood, metal, and earth are the eight Vidyārājas: Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, Takkirāja, Prajñāntaka, Nīladaṇḍa, Padmāntaka, Mahābala, Vighnāntaka, and Acalanātha.
Furthermore, there are the eight goddesses—Gandhā, Lāsā, Pāśā, Mālā, Śṛṅkhalā, Gītā, Dīpā, and Ghantā—who likewise extend from the east to the northeast in eight directions.
If one does not use an image but employs only a maṇḍala, the arrangement is likewise as described above.
On a day when the moon is in conjunction with the four lunar mansions of Citrā, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, or Rohiṇī, the practitioner need not select an auspicious or inauspicious date;
having fasted for one day, they should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times. All their heart's desires will be fulfilled at that very moment, and they shall attain great siddhi.
By performing the ritual before the image altar, one will immediately attain the accomplishment of the Mother [Tārā] and behold her manifest form.
Furthermore, the mantra for accomplishing all vidyās is said to be: Oṃ (1) ṭa ṭa ṭa u (short) (2) dhīdhī ṭa u (short) (3) ṭau ṭau.
(Tā-u)(4) Vajrasattva (5) Jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ (6) Hrīḥ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ (7) Hūṃ (8). This mantra is capable of accomplishing all vidyās, subduing all devas, and achieving [all aims].
Regarding all matters: if one wishes to know future events, one should immediately form the *Acala-khaḍga-mudrā* (the sword mudrā of Acala;
see the entry for the sword mudrā), place it against the left side of the body, and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, while maintaining the mudrā, one should sleep.
The deity *Avīśa* will then manifest all matters of good and ill fortune within the dream. (The *khaḍga-mudrā* is the sword mudrā.)
The Vajra Mother Bhagavati Bodhisattva— arising from the Tathāgata Samantaprabha’s entry into the supreme,
blazing samādhi of the Vajra-samādhi, as the Great Holy Mother Prajñāpāramitā, the foremost consort of the Vajra— spoke this mantra.
It is constantly in accord with the Vajra protection dharmas and is capable of extinguishing [all evils].
All sinful obstructions are purified; all activities are accomplished; one is able to perform rites of subjugation for the world;
and may cause all beings everywhere to be free from fear. Form the vajra-bind with both hands, and extend the two middle fingers.
With the two index fingers, pinch the third joint of the middle fingers, forming the shape of a vajra. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo ratnatrayāya | Namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye | Mahāyakṣasenāpataye* || 1 || 2 || 3 ||
E (3) Oṃ (4) Śaṅkari (5) Śāntikari (6) Ghuṭa ghuṭa (7) Ghuṭini (8) Gada gada (9) Ghuṭini hūṃ phaṭ svāhā (10)
This Bodhisattva dwells in the form of a young maiden, of a pale violet-blue hue, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, seated upon a lotus flower.
Her physical demeanor is tranquil; she is neither too tall nor too long, her countenance is pleasing, and the color of her eyes is like the radiance of a blue lotus.
Her right hand holds a Buddhist scripture (brahmapustaka), and her left hand holds a cintāmaṇi jewel, making the gesture of granting boons (varadamudrā). All...
All that is performed accords with skillful means. She is not only the mother of all Vidyārājas, but also the mother of the Vajras of all Buddhas.
The Honored One in White Robes is the Samantaprabha Tathāgata, who has entered the transformation-vajra of the infinite lotus of the Mahāyāna.
In the samādhi of the Mother of the Lotus-Birth Dharma, the foremost consort, spoke this mantra.
If one recites and visualizes it, one can accomplish all activities, provide excellent protection, and even increase the subtle treasury of the Dharma.
With both hands joined in *añjali*, let the tips of the ten fingers not touch one another. Slightly...
Bend it into the shape of a lotus. The mantra is as follows: Namo ratnatrayāya (1) Nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya (2) Bodhisattva...
VAJRA (3) MAHĀSATTVĀYA (4) MAHĀKĀRUṆIKĀYA (5) OṂ (6) KACCI (7) VIKACCI (8) NIKACCI (9) KAKAṆṬAKACCI (10) KIRUṬA VĪRYA SVĀHĀ (11)
[Invocation] (11) This Bodhisattva also dwells in the form of a woman. Her body is adorned with lotus garlands, and she wears a jeweled silk scarf draped over her shoulders.
She is white in color. In her right hand, she holds an opened lotus; upon the calyx of the flower is... [as above]
The *Cintāmaṇi* [mudrā]: With the left hand turned upward upon the left thigh, one bestows fearlessness (*abhaya*).
If there are wicked people who create obstacles against the yogin without cause, the practitioner should visualize those persons beneath his own feet and recite the mantra twenty-one times;
they will all be completely dispersed. Facing him with a mind of loving-kindness, they will be unable to obstruct him.
Oṃ (1) Śvete (2) Pañcaravāsini (3) Jaṭāmakuṭadhāriṇi Svāhā (4). If one is able to constantly recite this, all sinful karma will be entirely extinguished. [Recite] seven times...
Within the capital city of the sun [country], all the people shall revere and honor him. If one recites this for one month, one will obtain great wealth and nobility.
By reciting it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), one shall become equal to a Bodhisattva, with power no different from theirs.

The Honored Tārā is the Tathāgata Samantaprabha. Having entered the samādhi of the Great Bliss Vajra of Universal Radiance, she gave birth to the Great Mother of Buddhas, the foremost consort of the Karma Mahāsamaya, and spoke this mantra.
Throughout the realm of sentient beings, may one universally cause them to accomplish supreme and sublime deeds.
In a single instant, may one be able to cause all sentient beings to give rise to reverence and affection, becoming one's servants.

With both hands joined in *añjali*, the two index fingers press against the middle fingers, and the two thumbs are extended and inserted into the palms, forming the shape of an *utpala* lotus. The mantra:
It is said:
Namo ratnatrayāya (1). Namo ’ryāvalokiteśvarāya (2). Bodhisattva... (3)
VAJRA (1) MAHĀSATTVĀYA (2) MAHĀKĀRUṆIKĀYA (3) OṂ (4) TARE (5) TUTTARE (6) TURE (7) SVĀHĀ (8)
At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested in the form of a beautiful woman and dwelt in the samādhi of supreme and exquisite color.
Adorned with priceless miscellaneous jewels, she was like refined pure gold reflecting lapis lazuli gems. She addressed all sentient beings, speaking these words:
"Who is undergoing transformation and suffering? Who is submerged in the ocean of birth and death? I now vow to deliver them."
Having spoken these words, he traveled throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds and returned to the presence of the Buddha,
where he remained awaiting instructions. He contemplated the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual power, which, with its cool light, universally illumines all sentient beings—
just as the cool lunar orb in the world can dispel heat and affliction— and leaves no darkness unilluminated, causing all to rejoice.

He smiled, out of compassion for sentient beings like a loving mother. With the light of his loving-kindness and compassion, he universally illumined the Buddha-field, such that the radiance of all the devas became completely invisible.
If a woman wishes to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) or fulfill supreme worldly aspirations, she should, according to the ritual,
draw a maṇḍala and an image [with a *muṇḍa*-headdress], painting the body of the Bodhisattva greenish-yellow in appearance like that of a person in the prime of youth,
with a compassionate, smiling expression directed toward the practitioner, adorned with exquisite jewels, and with Avalokiteśvara upon her crown.
The Tathāgata Vaśavartin holds a blue utpala lotus in his left hand and makes the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with his right.
He sits in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) upon a lotus. Before this image, the practitioner should visualize a great lotus flower.
Upon the flower is a Brahmi syllable *tluṃ* (also written as *tluṅ*, or as the character *dang*). This syllable transforms into a blue lotus. Then...
Upon reaching the transformation into the Bodhisattva Tārā, as described above, one next visualizes the syllables of the mantra-gate being arrayed upon one's own body:
the syllable *Oṃ* is placed at the crown of the head; the syllable *Tā* is placed on the forehead; the syllable *Rā* is placed on the two eyes; and the syllable *Tā* is placed on the two shoulders.
The syllable *Ṭa* settles the mind; the syllable *Lri* settles the navel; the syllable *Ṭhu* settles both thighs; the syllable *Lri* settles the two shins; *Svā* settles the left foot;

and the syllable *Ha* settles the right foot. Having thus performed this distribution, one then uses the four vidyās to invite the deity into one’s own body, consecrating one’s own being so that it merges inseparably with the deity.
Next, one visualizes the true [mantra] being distributed within a pure moon disc.
Regarding the word: it should be rotated clockwise like a topknot, like crystal beads set in a clear mirror, with light penetrating both inside and out.
The sound should be like that of a ringing bell—neither too slow nor too fast—just enough to be heard by oneself.
After reciting this three hundred thousand times, one should again extensively arrange offerings. Take twelve finger-widths of agalloch incense and cut them into one hundred and eight pieces.
During the homa, one will see the Greatly Compassionate Holy One, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, coming from the east.
Clad in white robes, with a black deerskin draped across his right shoulder, and holding a staff, he appears before the practitioner.
Emitting great radiance that universally illuminates the suffering beings of the three miserable realms, those who encounter this light find their bodies at peace and experience happiness.
Having generated the bodhicitta, the practitioner shall grant all that is requested or wished for.

Whether it be soaring through the void, or the attainment of *āntardhāna* (invisibility), or the power of hearing and retaining [the teachings] and extending one's lifespan, or the restoration of impaired faculties to perfection—even those who seek hidden treasures or wish to enter the caves of the asuras shall be able to enter accordingly, as well as the palace of Avalokiteśvara. Such are the [attainments].
May all supreme aspirations, both mundane and supramundane, be fully accomplished.
The four aforementioned *upāsikā* Bodhisattvas all abide in female forms at the side of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha:
in the eastern corner is Locanā, belonging to the element of earth; in the southeast corner is Māmakī, belonging to the element of water; in the southwest corner...
The White-Robed Honored One belongs to the fire element. Tārā in the northwest corner belongs to the wind element.

These four Bodhisattvas are all capable of performing every rite of accomplishment (*siddhi*). If one wishes to perform a rite for averting calamities (*śāntika*), one should visualize the syllable *Laṃ* in the Brahmī script, which transforms into the Bodhisattva Locanā, complete with all marks and signs of perfection and every adornment, holding a sweet [fruit] in her hand.
Display the *kamaṇḍalu* and the rosary. With the *amṛta-kamaṇḍalu*, sprinkle it upon the crowns of those afflicted by calamities and obstacles;
it is as refreshing as wish-fulfilling nectar, capable of removing feverish afflictions and pacifying all disasters. Next, perform the rite of augmentation (*puṣṭi*).
Visualize the Sanskrit syllable *baṃ*, which transforms into the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsīnī, whose body is golden in color and who holds a jewel and a lotus in her hands.
Flowers fall as a sweet, divine rain, followed by a rain of precious jewels; these are able to perform the supreme rite of enrichment (*puṣṭi*). Next, one performs the rite of magnetizing (*vaśya*).
One should visualize the syllable *Dhāṃ* in the Brahmī script, which transforms into the Bodhisattva Tārā, her body red in color.
Holding a noose and a vajra hook in one's hands, one immediately uses the hook and noose to draw [the target] in, causing them to swiftly attain reverence and affection.
Next, perform the rite of subjugation (*abhicāruka*). Visualize the Sanskrit syllable *maṃ*, which transforms into the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
The body is green in color, with vajra-light pervading its entire form. It manifests a great wrathful aspect, raining down great celestial fire.
This fire burns the bodies of those being subdued, producing a state of terror. When one practices the visualization in this manner, within a mere instant, the person being subdued can be eliminated.
(Alternatively, it is said: "This is the form of the goddess Tārā; because she dwells in *dhāraṇī* out of her compassionate concern for many sentient beings...")
...the form of a *dhāraṇī*. It is so named because it reveals the essential points of the secret Dharma to them.
In the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*, there is a mantra for Avalokiteśvara’s granting of vows which states: *tadyathā garava du...* and so forth.
While this is not without efficacy, it is not the true mantra. This is what was transmitted before [Master] Baiyi (the White-Robed One).
Regarding the mantra: the first five phrases are words of taking refuge; the main body of the text consists of only twenty-odd characters following "Oṃ.
The subsequent twenty-character mantra is even more concise. This is truly a mantra for laypeople (baiyi), yet people do not know it.
It is a similar error as failing to study the Heart Sūtra or the Universal Gate Chapter, yet instead reciting the Gao Wang Guanshiyin Jing.
The collected scriptures and incantations in the *Gao-wang Guanshiyin Jing* all have their origins;
yet, when mixed with the "pickled fish of the five marquises," they are no longer the "eight delicacies" of the celestial kitchen.

Generally, those scriptures that lack a translator’s name, those incantations interspersed with vulgar vernacular, those scriptures interspersed with Chinese place names, and those Buddhist scriptures that incorporate Daoist terminology [are suspect].
Those who claim that the names of the teachings of Master Lü and the Immortals are included therein; those who draw upon Mahāyāna sūtras to fabricate associations with alchemical methods (dān-fǎ);
and those who annotate the scriptures without knowing the true causes of the entire Dharma-piṭaka—all such views are heterodox teachings and are not to be trusted.
Furthermore, what the common world calls the "Avalokiteśvara Image that Delivers Children" is actually the form of the Mother Hārītī, and is not Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, there are people in the southeast who fashion effigies of young women with arched feet and fine attire, worshipping them as Avalokiteśvara; this too is erroneous.
If one wishes to know the location of a lost object, burn incense and recite the mantra seven times, then go to sleep; do not speak of it to others.
Regarding human speech: Tārā manifests her divine form in dreams and comes to inform one of a person’s name, physical appearance, possessions, and location;

however, she must not reveal this to others. If wicked people come, recite the mantra of the Honored One Tārā seven times over [the water], sprinkle it around the bed on all four sides, and they will be unable to cause harm; it will also ward off mosquitoes.
Recite the Tārā mantra seven times over a sword or staff. When traveling at night, draw a circle around your lodging with the sword or staff;

then no wild beasts or thieves shall be able to approach. If one is bitten by a venomous snake and is on the verge of death, take a pinch of water, empower it seven times with the mantra, and drink it; one will immediately rise. Or, in the case of a wound...
If one recites [the mantra] twenty-one times while facing the afflicted area, a headache will inevitably arise; one should then wash the head with scented water.
For earache, empower oil twenty-one times and apply it to the painful spot. For other pains, empower the hand twenty-one times and press upon the afflicted area.

For pain in the eyes caused by [substances] entering the ears: take agallochum (śrīkhaṇḍa), blue sandalwood (sūcī), licorice (yaṣṭimadhu), and so forth, boil them into a decoction, empower it twenty-one times with mantras, and wash the eyes. For heart pain:
at dawn, take water from a well (jāhnavī-jala) mixed with rock salt (saindhava), empower it seven times, and drink it to induce vomiting. For swelling of the body: empower oil twenty-one times.
For swelling, smear [the medicine] over it twenty-one times. For sores, empower earth twenty-one times and mix it with clay to apply to the sore.
For dysentery, empower salt water thirty-seven times and drink it. For the disease of muteness, take dog’s milk, empower it seven times, and smear it on the mouth;
one will then speak. If rats disturb people, empower ashes seven times [and scatter them].
Recite [the mantra] seven times over water and pour it into the hole; do this for three days, and the rats will emerge and disperse, never returning again.
If a rabid dog has bitten someone, quickly recite the mantra seven times; the dog will be unable to move.
Recite it another seven times while facing the dog until it disperses, and its affliction will immediately be cured. Woman.
If a woman’s menstrual flow does not cease and continues day after day, empower non-glutinous rice (*śāli*), take its juice, mix it with honey, and recite [the mantra] twenty-one times;
she shall drink it. If a child dies in the womb, take water and place it in the hand;

add a small amount of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) medicine, empower it one hundred and eight times, and have her drink it, and the child will immediately emerge. For chronic hemorrhoids that do not heal, [perform the following].
Take one *qián* of white lead powder (*húfěn*), three *qián* of mercury (*shuǐyín*), and seven dried dates with their pits removed.
Pound these into pills and wrap them in thin cotton. Insert them into the lower part [of the body] and recite the mantra twenty-one times.
This will cure injuries from being stabbed by a blade or falling from a height; even when the pain is unbearable, apply the empowered mud (*niányī*) seven times.
If one recites [the mantra] thirty-seven times over clay and applies it, white leprosy, yellow leprosy, or wounds from being bitten by a mad dog,
or pierced by arrows or cut by blades, will be immediately healed.
In the past, in the kingdom of Sphatika, there was an elder whose family was very wealthy, yet he was by nature dull-witted.
His teacher, for seven days, made offerings according to the Dharma and prayed on his behalf; consequently, the elder attained intelligence and could recite a thousand verses daily.
Furthermore, there is the *Buddhamātṛ-catur-parṣad-rakṣā-mantra*. See page sixteen of the lower fascicle of the *Mayūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*.
A ritual for the five-syllable mantra maṇḍala of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva (to be viewed as above).
The Great Being, desiring to benefit future sentient beings so that they may swiftly achieve the accomplishment of Mahāprajñā, entered samādhi and manifested great supernormal transformations.
One hundred trillion Buddhas assembled simultaneously and, with one voice, proclaimed this mantra.
To recite it once is equivalent to having recited the entire Sūtra-piṭaka of all Tathāgatas. First, the two...
Form the Vajra-muṣṭi mudrā. Extend both middle fingers and bend their upper joints so that they touch each other like the shape of a sword.
The mantra is: *A-ra-pa-ca-na maṇḍala*.
The maṇḍala may be made as large or small as desired. In its center is the youth Mañjuśrī, his form the color of *uragasāra* gold. [He belongs to] the lineage...
Adorned with various necklaces, they grace their bodies. With the left hand holding a vajra sword and the right holding a *brahmapustaka*, they sit within a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*).
The lunar disc is surrounded on all four sides by the five-syllable mantra. Next, one should draw the eight offerings and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Once the practitioner has entered the maṇḍala and performed the recitation according to the ritual, they should form the seal of concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*) and contemplate the Bodhisattva with focused attention.
The Bhagavān then proclaimed the five-syllable mantra. Five-colored light rays issued from his mouth and entered the moon-disc within the practitioner’s heart.
The syllable *A* was positioned at the front, while the remaining four syllables were arranged in succession, circling to the right.
One should contemplate their meaning: the syllable *A* signifies non-arising; the syllable *Ra* signifies purity, being unstained and free from defilement.
The syllable *ya* signifies that even the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—the equality of all phenomena—is non-existent.

The syllable *va* signifies that all phenomena are devoid of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). The syllable *na* signifies that among all phenomena, intrinsic nature, characteristics, speech, and written words are all unobtainable.

Because the syllable *na* is without intrinsic nature or characteristics, the syllable *va* is without conditioned formations; because the syllable *va* is without [conditioned formations], [it is thus].

Because of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the syllable *pa* has no ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Because the syllable *pa* has no ultimate meaning, the syllable *ra* is free from dust and defilement (*rajas*).
Because the syllable *ra* is free from dust and defilement, the syllable *a* is the fundamental non-arising of phenomena (*anutpanna*).

Because the syllable *a* is the fundamental non-arising of phenomena, the syllable *na* has no intrinsic nature or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus one contemplates the mind as being primordially pure.
Pure, unstained by attachment, and free from the conceptual marks of "I" and "mine. Entering this gate is called the authentic cultivation of samādhi.
Reciting it once can eliminate all the hardships and sufferings of the practitioner; reciting it twice...

It eradicates the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over billions of kalpas. At the third repetition, samādhi manifests before one. At the fourth repetition, one attains dhāraṇī and does not forget.

At the fifth repetition, one swiftly achieves unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. (At this point, people cannot believe it; they do not know that among the four kinds of recitation, this is the true recitation.

If one contemplates and practices according to the meaning of these words, and is able to awaken to the fact that there is no self-nature or characteristics, even to the point that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, then this mind will be pure and undefiled, free from all conceptual discrimination. How could it not then eliminate suffering and extinguish sin, and swiftly [attain liberation]? )

Regarding the realization of Bodhi: some say that in the *Yogadharma-paṭala*, one recitation performed once results in ten million (*koṭi*) recitations, and two recitations result in twenty million; thus, the numbers differ according to what is taught for each individual capacity.
Having performed such recitation for a full month, Mañjuśrī will manifest in the air and preach the Dharma.

The practitioner will immediately attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajātismṛti-jñāna*), unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*), sovereign supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*), and the fulfillment of supreme vows, swiftly realizing the state of a Tathāgata.
Regarding the Vajra Dharma-body:
if one constructs a mudrā-maṇḍala, draw a sword in the center, and in each of the four directions, draw the eight offering mudrās and the four saṃgraha-mudrās.
If one constructs a samaya-maṇḍala, write the five syllables and the eight offerings in the center.
The seed-syllables of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*): If one constructs a *karma-maṇḍala*, place a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in its center.

Facing this maṇḍala, perform recitation according to the method of the revolving wheel of syllables (the method of the revolving wheel of syllables consists of circumambulating clockwise while arranging the five seed-syllables; furthermore, it involves reciting, visualizing, and contemplating them).
Additionally, for the Five-Crested Mantra (*Pañcaśikha*), join the ten fingers together and separate them to form five peaks; seal the heart, both shoulders, and the throat with this mudrā.
Finally, at the crown of the head, the five directional Tathāgatas are formed.
This is called the Five Topknots Seal (*pañca-śikhā-mudrā*). The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām* (1) *Aparājitāśayanām* (2) *Tadyathā* (3) *Oṃ* (4) *Rara* (5) *Sama-ra* (6) *A* (7)
*Pratihatasaunānām* (7) *kumāra-lupphadharini* (8) *hūṃ* (9) *sphoṭa sphoṭa* (10) *svāhā* (11).
The Heart Mantra of Vajrarāga-rāja for the Maṇḍala Rite (the ritual for prostrating and observing is as above).
The Tathāgata Samantaprabha entered samādhi within the heart-palace of Samantabhadra’s full-moon radiance and uttered this mantra of the King of Firm Attachment,
which brings benefit and purpose. It is the most honored and supreme among all yogas,
capable of causing all who see it to feel toward one another as they would toward their own parents, wives, or children.

Furthermore, for those whose mantras belonging to the Buddha-family, Tathāgata-family, Lotus-family, Vajra-family, or Karma-family fail to attain accomplishment, by reciting this mantra three hundred thousand times, one will swiftly obtain *siddhi*.
Form the *bandha* mudrā by interlacing the two hands with the palms facing inward, extending the middle fingers straight upward, and pressing the right over the left. In the center...
Divide [the lines] so they intersect crosswise. The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) mahā-rāga (2) vajra-senā (3) vajra-sattva (4) jaḥ (5) hūṃ (6) vaṃ (7) hoḥ (8).
Furthermore, there is the single-syllable heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*). Form the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*) with both hands, joining the two middle fingers upright.
Curve the two index fingers like hooks. Join the two thumbs and the two little fingers upright together, forming the shape of a five-pronged vajra. The mantra is as follows:

HŪṂ (1) | TĀKṢI HŪṂ (2) | JAḤ (3). On a day corresponding to the constellation Mṛgaśīrṣa during the bright fortnight, one should take a pure white woolen cloth and paint an image of the Honored One. His body is the color of the sun and he stands upon a blazing wheel.
He has three eyes on his face, which gaze with a wrathful expression, and his head is adorned with a lion-mantra-anger [crown].
Upon his crown, he wears a five-pronged golden vajra-hook and a flower topknot of five colors that hangs down to cover his ears.
His body has six arms: the first left hand holds a vajra bell, and the first right hand grasps a five-peaked vajra;
he abides in the form of Vajrasattva. The next left hand holds a bow, and the next right hand holds an arrow, as if shooting at a celestial star.
The light of the *kṣipta* mudrā forms the Great Dyeing Dharma (*mahārakta-dharmatā*). Lower the two hands, with the right above and the left below, holding lotuses in a striking gesture.
Adorn the body by binding and knotting various flower garlands. Sit in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) upon a red lotus.
Beneath the lotus, paint two precious vases emitting clouds of jewels. The image faces east. The practitioner [should visualize themselves] before the image.
First, form the *karmamudrā*: using two vajra-fists, assume the posture as if discharging an arrow.
Recite the root mantra while simultaneously displaying the *samayamudrā* and the one-syllable heart secret seal (*hṛdaya-guhyamudrā*). Evil-minded sentient beings shall be immediately annihilated.

Furthermore, if one binds the thirty-seven *karmamudrās* of the Vajradhātu (the three types of seals for the *karma-samādhi* should be carefully examined by cross-referencing them with the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*,
the first assembly, and the *Svalpabhāvanā-guhyasamāja-tantra*), and recites the mantras of one's own practice, one will swiftly accomplish all ritual activities.
If one performs the rite of attraction (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should take the filaments of a red lotus and perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings; after one night, attraction is attained.
If one wishes to subjugate all sentient beings, one should take white sandalwood and carve it into the form of the deity.
Measuring five finger-widths, wear it upon the body; all those [obstacles] will be subdued.
If one empowers food and drink seven times, all poisons will be eliminated as if one had obtained nectar (*amṛta*).

If the seven planets oppress, or if obstacles are created by water, fire, wind, māras, or malevolent beings who move through the crown of the head, one should draw their forms and place them within the mouth of a lion, and recite [the mantra].
Recite this one thousand and eight times; [the obstacles] will be swiftly extinguished and will not arise again.
Furthermore, for the practitioner who maintains the recitation, the primordial innate obstacles that have existed since beginningless time will suddenly manifest in the form of Vajrasattva.
Upon his crown there appears a vajra-wheel, and beneath his feet there appears a vajra-wheel; in each of his two hands, there likewise appears one.
A single vajra-wheel appears again upon the heart, emitting light from the entire body that touches the practitioner;
their mind becomes as if intoxicated, and they do not know where it has come from. One should then recite the one-syllable heart-mantra to extinguish this state.
If a practitioner of mantras gives rise to even a single moment of distracted thought, this obstacle will find an opportunity to act.
However, if one holds the mind upon a single syllable, forms the five-peak mudrā,
and constantly contemplates the sound of the syllable *HŪṂ* within one’s own heart throughout inhalation and exhalation, this obstacle will be immediately extinguished.

Not perceiving body or mind, but observing only the arising of the syllables, Abiding in this body which is equal to the great void— This is called the subtle concentration (*sūkṣma-samādhi*). The obscurations of one's own nature are all extinguished.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Honored One, Seven-Crore Buddhamātā Cundā (i.e., Juntì) Bodhisattva, and her mantra-maṇḍala.
[The Ritual for Veneration is as above.
The World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Great Ocean of Transformative Supernatural Powers Equal to Space,
from which he brought forth the Great Queen of Mantras, Mahācundī, and spoke this dhāraṇī, which enables both lay and ordained bodhisattvas to uphold and recite it.
Those who [practice this] shall extinguish all sins, become abundant in wealth and treasures, and be reborn in the realms of humans and devas.

They will be born as children of imperial or royal families, free from calamities, misfortunes, illnesses, and afflictions. They will encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and always attain renunciation. If they are renunciant bodhisattvas...
One who possesses all the prohibitive precepts and practices according to the teachings will swiftly attain the supramundane *siddhi* sought in this present life before them.
With the two little fingers and ring fingers interlaced and inserted into the palms, the two middle fingers are held straight and upright.
The tips of the two index fingers touch each other. The tips of the two index fingers are placed against the sides of the upper joints of the two middle fingers.
The two thumbs are each placed against the sides of the two index fingers; this constitutes the *mudrā*. The mantra is as follows:
Namo satvānām (1) Samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭīnām (2) Tadyathā (3) Oṃ (4) Cili (5) Culi (6) Cundhe (7) Svāhā (8)
Paint the principal deity with a body that is yellowish-white in color, seated upon a lotus flower, and adorned with a circular halo.
He wears garments of fine, light gauze, like those of a Bodhisattva of the ten pāramitās; both the upper and lower garments are white, and his waist is bound with a sash.
Dawn light entwines his body. He wears a white conch shell as a bracelet on one hand; his armlets are adorned with the seven precious gems. On each of his little fingers, he wears a jeweled ring.
He wears a jeweled crown upon his head and long necklaces hang from his body. He has eighteen arms and three eyes.
His two upper hands perform the gesture of preaching the Dharma (*dharmacakra-mudrā*). His second right hand bestows fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*). His third right hand...
[The deity holds] a sword in the [right] hand; the four [left hands hold] a rosary, a *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit, an axe, a hook, and a *vajra*;

the [remaining] left hands hold a jewel garland, a wish-fulfilling jewel banner, a lotus, a water vessel, a noose, a wheel, a conch, a *bhadraghaṭa*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra. Below the lotus, [the following are] painted:
There is a pond. The two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, together support the stem of the flower.

On the left side, paint the practitioner of recitation holding an incense burner and gazing up at the Noble Mother, Cundī. Out of compassion for the practitioner, she lowers her eyes and looks down upon him.
Above, paint two deities from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens making offerings with garlands. (Regarding this Cundī rite, there are visualizations of her with two, four, six, or eight arms.)

Regarding the differences of having ten, twelve, eighteen, thirty-two, or eighty-four arms, the *Yogamahārājatantra* states that Cundī has twenty-six arms. From Vairocana downward, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vidyārājas such as Vajrapāṇi vary in the number of their arms;
their eyes likewise vary in number. Since these all arise from the samādhi of the transformation of Great Wisdom, one must not become dogmatically attached to any single form.

Once the image is completed, it should be placed within the center of the maṇḍala. One should perform recitation three times daily and form the mudrā of the arranged syllables, with the two hands joined palm-to-palm inwardly.
Form the *viśvavajra* mudrā by joining the two thumbs, the two index fingers, and the two little fingers together and holding them upright; this constitutes the seal (*mudrā*).

From the crown of the head down to the feet, visualize each syllable of the mantra clearly defined in its curves and turns, emitting radiant light that illuminates all sentient beings suffering in the cycle of rebirth within the six realms.
Arising with profound compassion, bestow peace and happiness upon them. [Recite] the mantra nine times.
The syllable *oṃ* is arrayed upon one’s own body, thereby forming a body empowered by the Eight Great Bodhisattvas through the Seal of the Tathāgata.
The Sanskrit syllable *oṃ* is at the crown of the head, serving as the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Tathāgata; it is the color of gold and constitutes the signless *dharmadhātu*.
By touching it with the thumb, the Sanskrit syllable *vaṃ* is placed in the two eyes, forming the *uṣṇīṣa*.

The *sa* syllable becomes a great wheel, also golden in color. By touching it with the index finger, the letter *la* of the Brāhmī script appears upon the neck, and one becomes the Vidyārāja Acala, holding a conch and a noose, appearing deep black in color.
Again, by touching it with the thumb, the letter *dza* of the Brāhmī script appears at the heart, and one becomes the Bodhisattva Tārā, her body a deep blue color, manifesting in a wrathful form.
His features include protruding fangs and elephant hide for clothing. One hand holds a sword, and the other holds a skull-cup filled with blood, which he touches with his thumb.
On both shoulders are *li* script characters in the Brāhmī script.
He is formed as the Bodhisattva Amoghapāśa, with three eyes on his face, holding a lotus, a noose (*pāśa*), and a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*). Alternatively, he may be golden in color.
Alternatively, one may visualize [the deity] as red in color. Touching with the thumb, one places the venerable letter of the Brahmi script within the navel-cakra;
this becomes the Honored One, Krodhabhūti (Kruddha) Bodhisattva, whose body is white in color and from within whose body all Buddhas are generated.
Touching with the thumb, the Brahmi letter *ṇi* is placed upon the two thighs; this becomes Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, whose body is circular.

The light is like that of the sun at the end of an eon (*saṃvartakalpa*). Touching [the calves] with the little finger, one places the Sanskrit syllable *svā* on both calves (the term *chuǎn* refers to the lower part of the leg).
This forms the Bodhisattva Ekajaṭa, who has three heads and six arms.
His first right hand holds a jeweled staff (*yaṣṭi*), his second right hand holds a noose (*pāśa*), and his first left hand holds a *khaṭvāṅga*. His second [left hand]...
He holds a skull and his body is blue in color. He wears an elephant hide as a garment and touches with his little fingers.
The Sanskrit syllable *ha* is on both his feet. This is the Bodhisattva Vajranāga, whose body is the color of the moon.
His two right hands hold a sword and a battle-axe; his two left hands hold a noose and a lotus. This Bodhisattva is a horse.
This is the transformation of the Head Vidyārāja, which possesses great majestic power.
If there is one who has been bitten by the dragon Takṣaka, no power whatsoever will be able to rescue them; only the Vajranakha mudrā can provide salvation.
By touching [the victim] with the little finger and thus performing the empowerment through the binding of this seal, their body immediately becomes indestructible like vajra.
All obstacles are extinguished; there is immeasurable auspiciousness. When the recitation count is completed, immediately form the seal of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*).
With body upright and eyes closed, clarify the mind and still the thoughts. Visualize within the region of the chest a brilliant, luminous orb, like the disk of the full moon.
One will certainly be able to realize the originally pure mind. Within that luminous orb, visualize the Sanskrit syllable *Oṃ*, and the other eight syllables.

Rotate it clockwise (this method is most detailed in the version of the *Śūraṅgama-mantra-ṭīkā* carved by Wu Kunxiu). Arrange them upon the perfect luminosity, making them clearly and distinctly manifest.
With the mind undistracted, one enters into union with Prajñā (Note: This is according to the Wu edition; it includes the entire mantra along with the *bīja* syllables such as *oṃ* and so forth.

These nine characters of the Dharma are the most expedient; there is no need to contemplate the entire mantra at length. Brevity is swift). Regarding the visualization of these nine sacred syllables: first is *oṃ*; then to its left, *li*;
then *zu*; then *li*; then *zun*; then *nei*; then *svo* (a conjunct); then *ha*. When the visualization of the lunar disc is accomplished, one contemplates it.
Explanation of the Characters: *Oṃ*: The meaning of the three births; it also signifies that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen. *Ja*:
The meaning that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished. *Lī*: The meaning that the characteristics of all dharmas are non-apprehendable. *Bzu*.
All phenomena have no meaning of arising or abiding: *Ṣre*. All phenomena have no meaning of defilement: *Bhū* (also written as *Zong*).
All phenomena have no meaning of equal awakening: *Nī*. All phenomena have no meaning of grasping or abandoning: *Svā*.
(Combined) The meaning of the equality of all phenomena beyond verbal expression: *Ha*.
