The Buddha was dwelling in the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven. For the sake of protecting all sentient beings, he taught this mantra method of the practice-wheel of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
If one can receive and uphold it, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva will come to provide long-term protection;
whether in waking or in dreams, he will manifest his physical form and bring about various auspicious matters. This mantra is able to eliminate all [obstacles].
It can suppress calamities and obstacles, evil dreams, enemies, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, the ten non-virtuous actions, and other such sins.
This King of Mantras is capable of subduing all that is malevolent and accomplishing every virtuous deed; it is even able to summon Mañjuśrī himself.
How much more so for all other ordinary and noble beings (*pṛthagjana-ārya*) [hand gestures to be supplemented]. The mantra is: Oṃ (1) Dantī (2).
Upon a white cloth, one should paint a pool of water. Within the water, there arises a single-stemmed, three-pronged *utpala* lotus. In its center...
On a lotus branch, Mañjuśrī appears in the form of a youth with five topknots on his head. His body is adorned in golden hue, and he wears a blue robe.
Seated upon a lion throne in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), with his left leg hanging down supported by a lotus, he displays the gesture of preaching the Dharma (*dharmacakra-mudrā*).
All his marks are perfectly complete; his face bears an expression of both joy and gravity, and his eyes gaze upon the practitioner.

On the right branch is a lotus flower. Upon it is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, adorned with all ornaments, possessing the various marks and signs, his body greenish-purple in color, wearing a blue robe, and with a pearl necklace draped across his chest.
His left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), and his right hand holds a white lotus. To the left, paint the noble Avalokiteśvara, his body like the full moon of mid-autumn.
Her complexion is like the color of the moon; she is endowed with all the marks of perfection and adorned with every ornament.
She likewise wears a blue robe and has a necklace of pearls draped across her chest. Her left hand holds a white lotus, and her right hand holds a vajra-whisk.
Her face bears an expression of joy as she gazes up at Mañjuśrī. The stem of the lotus is the color of a great green jewel, and it is supported by two nāga kings.
[Place it] there. On the right, near the corner, paint the practitioner performing recitation. In the two upper corners, paint two *kusuma-devaputra* (flower-god sons).
If there is one who has resolved upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta, by reciting [this mantra] once, they can protect themselves;
twice, they can protect their companions; thrice, they can protect their household; four times, they can protect a village; five times, they can protect...
Reciting it one hundred times can protect a single city; reciting it one thousand times can protect the four continents.
This mantra method is foremost for healing illnesses and protecting the body; it is the most supreme secret. To speak briefly: whatever one undertakes will be entirely accomplished.
Even if one does not enter the mandala to perform the ritual, simply by reciting and holding [the mantra], when one touches another with the hand at that time—
Even if done at will, if one consecrates water with it in the early morning and washes one's face, it will cause those who see one to rejoice;
if one consecrates one's clothing, those who see it will feel love and respect.
If one suffers from toothache, empower a tooth-stick with mantras and chew it; rub it on the painful area of the teeth and the pain will immediately subside.
For eye pain, empower salt powder seven times and apply a small amount to the eyes; the pain will then cease.
For earache: take the mushrooms that grow upon a heap of elephant or horse dung, together with *kṛṣṇatilataila* (black sesame oil) and a small amount of salt.
Empower these seven times, then blend and grind them into a paste. Squeeze out the juice, warm it, and drip it into the ear canal; relief will be achieved in an instant.
When a woman experiences difficult labor, take the root of *aṭarūṣaka* or the root of *śatāvarī*.
Grind it into a paste with water free of insects, empower it seven times with mantras, and apply it below the navel; the child will then be born naturally.
Both mother and son were at peace.

However, the arrowhead had penetrated deep into the bone and could not be extracted. [The practitioner] took three *liang* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) ten years old and empowered it one hundred and eight times.
By consuming this butter and simultaneously applying it to the wound, the arrowhead was immediately removed.

For those with indigestion, abdominal knots and pain, upward transformation of the humors, downward diarrhea, or cholera that threatens death, one may take black salt or red salt, empower it seven times, grind it into a powder, and have the patient drink it with warm water; they will then be cured.
If diarrhea does not cease, grind the roots of the orange and the papaya together; empower them seven times with mantras and drink them mixed with water.
One will immediately recover.
If a woman has been unable to bear sons or daughters for five, ten, twenty, or thirty years, or if she herself is afflicted by illness, [this remedy shall be applied].

If a man suffers from illness, or is afflicted by spirits or poison, one should take one *liang* of ghee that is ten years old or older and one *liang* of peacock tail feathers, place them within the ghee, and empower it twenty-one times. Then, boil the mixture until it is reduced to a powder.
Combine this with one *liang* of rock honey and three large *harītakī* fruits, having removed their seeds, and recite the mantra over them.
Recite this one hundred and eight times. Always take it entirely on an empty stomach at the break of dawn; within seven days, one will become pregnant, though the menstrual flow does not cease.
Take a handful of the roots of *ālaṃbu*, pound them, mix with milk, and boil until thickened. Add [the aforementioned powder].
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and consumes it, the illness will immediately be cured.
For headaches, empower a raven’s wing feather seven times and brush it over the patient's head; they will immediately recover.
For malaria lasting from one day to seven days, or for chronic cases, prepare a gruel by boiling pure milk with one *liang* of clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over it and consume it; one will immediately be cured.

To state the essential point: if one wishes to compound various medicinal decoctions for the purpose of taking them as medicine, one must first, with a sincere mind, empower them twenty-one times; then one will quickly attain one's wishes.
The Ritual for the Maṇḍala of the Treasure Store Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva (to be viewed as above).

When the Buddha was in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, after his parinirvāṇa, in this Jambudvīpa, to the northeast, there was a land named Mahācīna (also known as Zhendan). In that land there was a mountain called Wuding (that is, Mount Qingliang Wutai).
The Youth Mañjuśrī wanders and dwells among them, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude and benefiting all living beings.
Within this treasury of Dharma is a true, supreme, and most excellent teaching, beyond compare, which can act as a wish-fulfilling jewel for sentient beings.
It protects all kings who uphold the ten virtuous paths, causing them to obtain their wishes and attain long lives, [and to be shielded from] armor and weapons.

Rest. The land is peaceful and secure. This eight-character secret mantra of great majestic power can act as a lamp of light within the great darkness for all sentient beings (the first six phrases are the homage). Regarding the mudrā of Great Vigor:
join the two hands in *añjali*; interlace the eight fingers and tuck them all into the palms; with the two thumbs slightly bent, place them side by side and press down.
Place [the hands] upon the knuckles of the two index fingers.
The mantra is as follows: Namo aparimitāyāḥ (1) rājñe viśvarūpiṇe śāntarāya (2) tathāgatāya (3) namo mañjuśriye (4) kū... (5)

Mārabodhaya (5) tadyathā (6) oṃ (7) āmīra hūṃ kṣaṇa (8). If anyone should see or hear this mantra, it is as if the Buddha were present in the world, or as if one were seeing Mañjuśrī. Or, if there should be any difficulty...
If one has resolved to recite [the mantra] but is unable to provide extensive offerings, or if one is a householder beset by various worldly constraints and cannot fully comply with the ritual rules,
it is still possible to achieve accomplishment simply by firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts and maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness.
If one wishes to lie down to sleep, by reciting this mantra one hundred and eight times, one will immediately have auspicious dreams and clearly discern good and bad fortune.
If one suffers from malaria, if someone faces the patient and recites this mantra one thousand and eight times, that [patient]—
The afflictions were immediately eliminated.
Kings, princes, queens, princesses, ministers, officials, and the common people— by writing this mantra and placing it within their dwellings,
those dwellings attained great wealth and nobility, abundant treasures, and children of keen intelligence.
One will possess clear and sharp wisdom; one's appearance will be dignified and handsome, such that all people love and respect them. Whatever words they utter will be honored and never opposed.
Elephants and horses will form herds, and servants and slaves will be inexhaustible. Calamities and misfortunes will be extinguished, and all things will be auspicious.
If one can recite this one hundred and eight times three times each day, all that is undertaken will accord with one's wishes and be fully accomplished.
Even at the moment of death, Mañjuśrī will personally manifest his sacred form and preach for them the profound and wondrous Dharma-treasury of the Mahāyāna.
One immediately attains the Samantamukha-samādhi. One shall be forever separated from the suffering of birth and death and shall long rely upon the Noble Ones.
One’s rank shall reach the third bhūmi.
Taking a pure white woolen cloth, one should paint Śākyamuni in the center, seated upon a precious lotus flower in the posture of preaching the Dharma; to the right, one should paint Mañjuśrī...
Distinctly adorned with necklaces upon his body and a *kaustubha* jewel hanging from his neck, he is arrayed in various exquisite garments. His complexion is like that of saffron (*uruvūka*).
Kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he gazes up at the Tathāgata, assuming the posture of requesting the Dharma.
To the right [of the central figure] are Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, Gaganagañja, and Akṣayamati; to the left are Maitreya, Vimalakīrti, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Candraprabha.

The Vajras (five on each side, left and right) shall each occupy their respective positions, with their original forms depicted in full detail. Furthermore, in the space above the Buddha, one should additionally depict the Seven Buddhas:

King of Thunder Sound Buddha, Buddha Who Removes All Obstructions, Amitābha Buddha, Buddha of the Abode of Merit, Universal Fragrance Buddha, Buddha of Difficult-to-Conquer Conduct, and Buddha Whose Mind is Immovable. Their bodies are all golden in color, and they are depicted in the act of preaching.

The *dharmavega* (Dharma-Force) [deity], the *puṣpavikīrṇa* (Scattering Flowers) Devaputra, and the *āśraya-dhara* (Supporting the Throne) Nāgarāja—all should be depicted according to the prescribed dharma.
Below Mañjuśrī, paint the wrathful king Yamāntaka looking up at Mañjuśrī, with his body bent in a posture of receiving instructions. Below Maitreya, paint the Dharma-holders;
do not lose their essential characteristics, and depict them in a posture of listening to the Dharma. To the left and right, paint the various attendants.
O Deva. [One must] not allow confusion [in this matter; one should examine it closely according to the original scripture].
Solemnly invoke the Maṇḍala Dharma of the Mantra of Mañjuśrī, the King of Garuḍas (the method for prostration and contemplation is as above).
When the Buddha was in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, he praised Mañjuśrī, causing all beings to accord with the Great Teaching of Mantras.
Birth. Entering the Samaya-maṇḍala, one thoroughly studies the five elements: earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
By knowing these, one attains mastery over the languages of all sentient beings, the inconceivable realm, and even those of all animals.
He also fully mastered the teachings on the bodies of all the Garuḍa kings. Having finished speaking, Mañjuśrī transformed himself into a Garuḍa king;
his physical form was vast and magnificent, surrounded by immeasurable retinues, as he expounded a hundred kinds of dharmas from the past.
Regarding the mudrā: intertwine the two thumbs; with both hands in the gesture of outspread wings, the body-mudrā is formed.
If any nāgas see this, they will not dare to disobey the command. The mantra is as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām. (1) Apratihata-śāsana-nam. (4) Tathāgata. (5) Oṃ śakuna mahā-śakuna vidanta pākṣa sarva-pañjara-ga. (9–10)
Nāga (11) | Khakha khahi khahi (12) | Samaya (13) | Manuṣyamāra (14) | Hūṃ tiṣṭha (15) | Bhagavate (16) | Jñāpaya ti (17) | Svāhā (18) ||
This mantra method can summon dragons, tame dragons, and seize dragons; it summons snakes and punishes snakes; it neutralizes all poisons so that one is not harmed by them.
One who maintains this dharma should construct a six-cubit altar on the bank of a river, draw an eight-petaled lotus, and in its center draw the Buddha in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
To the right of the Buddha, one should use colored powder to draw the Great Sage Mañjuśrī.
[The practitioner] joins his palms in reverence and gazes upward. To the left, he draws the god Nārāyaṇa, four-armed and holding ritual implements.

Near Nārāyaṇa, he draws the King of the Garuḍas, depicted in an extremely terrifying form with his two wings spread wide, wearing a flower garland upon his head, and possessing a divine face and a beak.
His right hand grasps a nine-headed, four-legged serpent-dragon king (*nāgarāja*), and his left hand holds a three-headed [serpent].
The Nāga King Pādaśarīra is depicted with garments like those of the devas, adorned with variegated colors. Near the Garuḍa King, one should paint the deity Rāvaṇa.
Behind Mañjuśrī, one should paint the Bodhisattvas Prajñākūṭa, Sudhana, and Subhūti, all standing with palms joined.
This constitutes the central maṇḍala. Next, in the outer enclosure, on the eastern side, one should mark the ground with white lime and paint a vajra.
At the southern edge, draw a sword with charcoal powder; at the northern edge, draw a staff with yellow pigment; at the western edge, draw a noose with red pigment.
Having drawn them thus, one should make offerings of the three sweets (ghee, honey, and sugar) in accordance with the Dharma.
Alternatively, recite the root mantra to invite all the noble hosts, and generate a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. Perform [the rite].

One should sit in the *nāga-āsana* (the posture of a dragon), sitting with the knees pressed together. Then, kindling a fire of *khadira* wood and using sticks of *ahi-kaṇṭaka* wood smeared with the three sweets (*trīmadhu*), perform one thousand and eight *homa* offerings.
Thereupon, accomplishment will be attained and signs will appear: a multitude of snakes will assemble and offer *arghya* water.
One should then make a vow for accomplishment, recite the root mantra to dismiss them, and thereafter perform whatever rites are required.
Accomplishment is achieved through recitation.

Furthermore, there is another method: by consecrating a clod of earth and casting it into a fire, the fire will not grow hot. If one wishes to release [the effect], one should consecrate grass and cast it into the fire.
Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra seven times to consecrate rivers, streams, and springs; then no fish will be caught by nets.
Moreover, if one plucks [an instrument] while reciting the mantra, one can summon all the fish.
For all those with illnesses, if one empowers the mantra twenty-one times and sprinkles it upon the crown of the head,
the disease will be immediately cured.
For those struck by a poisoned arrow, if one empowers water and splashes it [upon the wound], the arrow will be extracted.
For one who desires rain: following the aforementioned ritual, establish a mandala and kindle a fire with *nimba* wood.
Perform one thousand and eight *homa* offerings with white mustard seeds, and a sweet rain will immediately fall. If more is required, perform the *homa* again.
One will immediately obtain one's wish.
Having taken the *piṭaka*, empower it twenty-one times; holding it in hand, wherever one brandishes it in any direction, all frost and hail will immediately depart.
In the event of a house fire, perform the aforementioned rite; the fire will immediately shift away.
If one does not wish for snow, perform the aforementioned rite; the snow will immediately cease.
For those who have been bitten by a snake's venom, fashion four *garuḍas* out of clay, recite the mantra, and [sprinkle] water...
Sprinkle it upon his body, then immediately cast the garuḍas in the four directions; they will each come bringing snakes in their beaks.
The practitioner shall say these words: "Drink the poison of that person! The poison will then be purified and dispersed, and he will be able to rise up.
Take up a bow and empower an arrow; shoot it in the four directions. Immediately, a snake will coil itself around the arrow and return.
The practitioner should say, "Drink this poison. The person who was bitten will then rise. The arrow must not have an iron point.
Empower charcoal. Draw a snake on the ground and strike it with a staff made of *argha* wood;
the drawn snake will immediately depart and return carrying another snake in its mouth. It will drink its own venom, and the deceased will then rise.
By consecrating banners and parasols, one brushes away those who have died from poison; or by consecrating musical instruments, one plucks, ties, or blows them near the person’s side;
or by sprinkling water, fanning with a fan, or smearing mud [upon them], through the power of reciting the mantra, those who have died from poison are restored to life.
Furthermore, pound radish seeds and mix them with sesame oil, then burn them; this is the method for the incense of swift invocation.
With a single-minded mind, one should invoke the Maṇḍala Dharma of the Great Wisdom Bodhisattva’s Mantra for Increasing Wisdom (the ritual for prostration and visualization is as above).
Since many people forget [the rites], one should empower pure water with this mantra and drink it during the *yau* period (the morning/evening juncture), doing so every day.
This is so. Upon reaching the seventh or eighth month, one naturally recites a thousand verses daily; wisdom gradually increases, and the faculties become sharp and clear.
(Hand seal to be supplemented). The mantra is as follows:
Tadyathā (1) oṃ (2) bījo bījo (3) prajñāvartani (4) jara jara (5) mitāvartani (6) diri diri (7) muditāvartani (8) svāhā.
(Invocation) (9) The Ritual of the Maṇḍala for the Mantra of the Womb-Sanctuary of the Bodhisattva Mahāpratisarā for Peaceful Abiding in the Womb (Prostrations and Contemplation as Above)

All the powerful spirits and ghosts who constantly afflict sentient beings among humans and devour fetuses in the womb, upon hearing this mantra, shall all be struck with terror as if their bodies were ablaze.
Other ghosts will no longer devour fetuses, but instead shall provide security and well-being. (Seal to be supplemented). The mantra is as follows:

Oṃ (1) maṇidhari (2) vajriṇi (3) mahāpratisare svāhā (4). The Ritual of the Maṇḍala for the Mantra of the Youthful Kanyā Rāguli for Eliminating Snake Poison. (The method for prostration and visualization is as above.)

The World-Honored One was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, wandering upon Mount Gandhamādana (the name of the mountain). There he saw a young girl whose body was adorned with the marks and signs of a hundred merits;
she wore a garment of deer skin and used various venomous snakes as her necklace, including vipers and adders.
Surrounded by playful companions, one drinks poisonous gruel and eats poisonous fruit while reciting this mantra.

If it is maintained for a long time, no venomous insects or poisonous drugs shall be able to cause harm. Should a snake bite this practitioner of the mantra, the head of that snake shall split into seven pieces.
However, one must not recite this mantra in the presence of snakes; otherwise, the snake will surely [be destroyed].
Death. For one who cultivates this dharma, first recite the *Anurāgaṇa-mantra* ten thousand times as a preliminary practice (*pūrvaprayoga*).

Thereafter, perform the ritual. When removing poison, visualize yourself as the maiden Śāntikarī, green in color, resembling a nāga-girl, possessing seven heads, with a halo around the neck, and endowed with four arms; [visualize] the right...
The first right hand holds a trident; the second right hand grasps five or three peacock feathers. The first left hand holds a black snake;
the second left hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*). She is adorned with necklaces, earrings, armlets, and anklets.
Adorn his body and use various snakes as necklaces. Visualize flames streaming forth from all the pores of his skin.
Having performed this visualization, before the person who has been bitten, bind the root mudrā by interlacing the two hands.
In the manner of cupping an object, join the two little fingers together and extend the remaining eight fingers slightly apart and gently curved.
Then, form the *Anucitta-mudrā*: with the five fingers of the right hand extended and slightly bent, forming the shape of a lion’s claw, touch the five places of one's own body.
Take a vessel of well-baked copper, fill it with water, and empower it by reciting the *Anucitta-mantra*.
Seven times, scoop up water with the right hand and strike it upon the heart of the person who has been stung.
All poisonous vapors will gradually be extinguished. Then, recite the supplementary phrases within the mantra.
Again, take pure earth, empower it seven times, and encircle the person who has been stung on all sides. All poisons shall be extinguished at that very moment. (Furthermore, from the *Yogamahā...*)

The *Śrīparamādya-tantra-rāja* states: "Visualize all Buddhas filling the expanse of space, holding vases of nectar in their hands and pouring it over this person’s crown. Furthermore, visualize that within the person’s mouth is the Brahmi letter 'ĀṂ'; their poison will be extinguished immediately."

Furthermore, there is another method: before the person who has been bitten, bind the root mudrā and recite the single-syllable mantra *HŪṂ* many times, or visualize the single-syllable mantra *PHAṬ*.

Both can eliminate the poison. If a person upholds this method and recites it once daily, not only will all worldly poisons be extinguished, but the three poisons within their own body will also be eradicated at their very root.
The root mantra is as follows: *Tadyathā oṃ iri-mite (1) tirimite (2) iritirimite (3) nume numare (4) nut*.

(Above is the Bodhisattva Family; below is the Vajra Family).
Solemnly invoke the Vajrasattva Bodhisattva to enter the Wisdom Mantra Maṇḍala Ritual (the procedure for prostration and visualization is as above).
First, perform the mudrā: with both hands, form the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*); place the two thumbs inside the palms, resting upon the little fingers.
Between the ring fingers, join the two index fingers like a ring, also in the shape of a pincer. With the vajra speech, recite mentally according to one's intention.
Visualize that at a distance of one cubit in front, there is a white lotus flower, upon which is marked the syllable *AṂ* in Brahmi script.
A white light emanates from the syllable and flows into the heart, where it rests upon a white lotus flower. By this, one is able to give rise to subtle, wondrous wisdom.
Through this wisdom, one is immediately able to understand the minds of others as they truly are, know events of the past and future, and attain a firm mind.
One is thus able, within the teachings of all Tathāgatas, to bring to rest all sufferings and hardships.
Fearless. Accomplishing samādhi and fulfilling all aspirations.
The mantra is as follows: ĀRYA-TTASAMAYO VAJRAṂ (1) VAJRASATTVA (2) MĪTI-SAMITĀNĀVIŚAYATO (3) TĀYE VA (4)
VAJRAKIÑCAMANUTALAṂ (4) VAJRABAIŚAḤ (5). This is the mantra for the Maṇḍala Rite of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi for Stopping Malaria, [the method for which is to be observed as above].
The various ghosts of malaria subsist by consuming the vital radiance of humans; by reciting this mantra, one can sever the [power] of these ghosts.
"O spirits, flee and disperse quickly! (Hand seal to be supplemented). The mantra is: Oṃ vajrakarma viśodhaya sarvavaraṇāni dhvaṃsayaina samaya hūṃ.
(Invocation) (4) The Ritual of the Maṇḍala for the Mantra of the Great Compassionate King of Emptiness-Wisdom Vajra for Invoking Rain (Prostrations and Contemplation as Above)

Using a cord from a charnel ground, measure out the boundaries and paths of the mandala. At the center of the mandala, create the painted design using five-colored powders from a charnel ground (the five colors being:

white powder made from bone; black powder made from charcoal; red powder made from brick; yellow powder made from realgar; and green powder made from *bharu* leaves; if these are unavailable, substitute with malachite).

Within the Secret Mantra section, one employs malevolent rites and impure substances to overcome demons and evil influences; as I do not know the details of this, I dare not offer a hasty discussion. Furthermore, [one may employ] pride, anger, passion, and resentment as symbolic attributes, or [use] a skull-adorned staff, or a human...

The head serves as the rosary and so forth; likewise, one should double the visualization of the evil forms to subdue demons. One must by no means harbor heterodox thoughts or groundlessly alternate between doubt and faith. Faith must be entirely wondrous, and doubt must reach its very root; only then will power be gained.
If one uses talismans to seize objects, or employs mantras to become invisible, these do not possess the great compassion and upright light of this [practice].

One will inevitably suffer a strange downfall—be cautious! [Visualize] the Great Vidyārāja Khagarbha-Vajra: eight faces, four feet, and sixteen arms. Each face has three eyes, and he displays a wrathful expression, treading upon Āḥ.
Nanda Nāgarāja: One should fashion an image of Ānanda Nāgarāja out of fragrant clay (this nāga king has nine heads, his face is serene and joyful, and he resembles a celestial deity;
from atop his heads, further nāga heads emerge). For this nāga king and his consort, the seed-syllables are both *pau* and *aḥ*.
Bathe [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and scatter black flowers. Next, smear it with the sap of the nāga-flower tree (or substitute it with white wormwood juice).
Then, apply elephant ichor (the congealed secretion from the eyes) to the crown of the nāga-king’s head.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, take the milk of a black cow and fill a vessel with it. Have a black-skinned young girl join together threads of blue color. At...
In the northwest corner of the maṇḍala, dig a small pond and place the Nāga King Ānanda within it.
Recite this rain-invoking mantra with a stern voice according to the ritual rules (the hand seal is to be supplemented). The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) kuru kuru (2) kneḍa kneḍa (3) mardaya mardaya (4) kṣata kṣata (5) kuṭāya kuṭāya (6) ānanda (7) kṣobhakara (8) nāgadhipataye (9) hi hi ru ru kaṃ (10) sarva...
TAPATĀRAGAṂ (11) | NĀGANA KARIṢYA (12) | MARṢAYA (13) | GARJAYA (14) | PHUṬ (15) PHUṬ (16) PHUṬ (17) PHUṬ (18) PHUṬ (19) PHUṬ (20) PHUṬ (21) PHUṬ (22) HŪM (23) ||
HŪṂ (24) HŪṂ (25) SVĀHĀ (26). Recite this mantra. If rain does not fall, one should then recite this spell in reverse; immediately there will be heavy rain.
If it still does not rain, the Dragon King’s head shall split into seven pieces. If one wishes to stop the rain, take a garment from a cold forest and place it [in the water].
While remaining at the base of the seat, recite this mantra; the rain will cease immediately.
(This is the second mantra. The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) Arya (2) Śmaśāna-priyāya (3) Hūṃ (4) Hūṃ (5) Hūṃ (6) Phaṭ (7)
Furthermore, regarding the ritual for accomplishment: by reciting this mantra, *vilu ya vilu ya*, the elephant immediately flees;
by reciting this mantra, *manma manma*, the tiger immediately flees.
*Tiriya tiriya*—by reciting this mantra, the bear will immediately flee.
*Ilime lipu phu phu*—by reciting this mantra, the snake will immediately flee.
The Ritual for the Maṇḍala of the Mantra of Bodhisattva Amṛtakuṇḍalī (Prostrations and Contemplation as Above):

Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, through the skillful means of compassionate wisdom and in accordance with the Wheel of Command, manifests in the form of a great wrathful deity to subjugate all the retinues of asuras, ghosts, and spirits. He pours forth nectar to wash and purify the practitioner.
The seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* are perfumed by habitual tendencies; one swiftly accumulates merit and wisdom and attains the pure *dharmakāya*. As for the seal (*mudrā*):
interlace the two little fingers with their tips entering the palms, bend the two ring fingers to press against the base of the thumb, and extend both middle fingers together.
Bend the two index fingers like hooks and place them behind the first joints of the two middle fingers, forming the shape of a three-pronged vajra.
Extend the two thumbs together and press them against the backs of the two ring fingers, positioning them between the two middle fingers. The mantra is as follows:
Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo vajrakrodhamahākrodhāya. Oṃ. Huru huru. Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha. Bandha bandha. Haṇa haṇa.
(7) AMṚTE HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. (8) The ritual method for the *hṛdaya-mantra* (small-heart mantra):
Press the thumb of the left hand against the nail of the little finger; the remaining [fingers] form the shape of a three-pronged vajra.
This is called the *karma-mudrā*. The aforementioned mantra is named the *mahā-hṛdaya* (great-heart), and the mudrā is named *samādhi*. [End of] the mantra.
The mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ āḥ mṛte hūṃ phaṭ. The practitioner, having entered the maṇḍala and paid homage to the Buddha, sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) and visualizes himself within each of the [deities].

Before the Buddha, he made offerings of various incenses and flowers. Without rising from his seat, he took pity on sentient beings who drift through the six realms of existence due to the false imaginings of their own minds.
Deluded regarding the ultimate truth, they commit various unwholesome deeds and thereby invite the diverse fruits of suffering as karmic retribution.
Among the realms of humans and devas, they are addicted to the five desires; thus, they experience the suffering of not obtaining what they seek. Regarding all these...
In the heavens, one undergoes the suffering of transformation; by means of the *miao-jue* (wondrous awakening) flower, one opens the bodhicitta.
Contemplating the cold-hell realms, one uses the fragrant scent of Brahma-fragrance to distance oneself from the suffering of the cold.

Within the realm of hungry ghosts, one uses divinely wondrously empowered food and drink to cause them to be fully satisfied, wishing for them to distance themselves from the karma of stinginess. Contemplating the [asura]...

They are born as rākṣasas and take rebirth in the realms of form and formlessness; their mental faculties are more prone to deceit and malice, they engage in mutual slaughter, and they become addicted to the flavor of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
By means of my Prajñā and other illuminations, I shall completely eliminate all such entanglements of delusion for them.
Without departing from this visualization, cause all afflicted sentient beings to swiftly ascend to Bodhi.
Then, following the ritual procedures, perform the method of arranging the seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence, whereby one’s own body becomes the samādhi of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
Immediately above the crown of the head, visualize a red syllable *Oṃ* in the Brahmī script, possessing great radiance that illuminates the ten directions. Next, contemplate:
Visualize the Sanskrit letter *A* at the heart; its color is like white jade or snow, shining both inwardly and outwardly like a great lunar disk.
Next, visualize the Sanskrit letter *MṚ* on the two shoulders; its color is like a rainbow, illuminating all worlds.
Next, visualize the Sanskrit letter *TI* at the navel center; its color is pure white, with radiant and lustrous light.
It illuminates the boundless worlds and all evil destinies. Next, one contemplates the Brahma-script syllable *HŪṂ* at both thighs;
it is the color of gold, and its radiance touches and reaches the Avīci hell. Next, one contemplates the Brahma-script syllable *PHAṂ* placed at both necks;
it is the color of a silken cloud, and its radiance touches those asuras, swiftly causing them to realize the Right Path. Next...
Visualize the letter *Ṭha* from the Brāhmī script placed upon the palms of both feet;
it is white in color, shaped like a crescent moon, and emits light that touches all non-Buddhists, causing them to abandon false views and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Through this *akṣaravyūha-samādhi*, one’s own body transforms into the form of the deity. One should visualize [the deity] as having four faces and four arms, with the right hand holding a vajra.
He holds a *vajra* [mudrā] and his left hand forms the *pūrṇa-mudrā*. Both hands form the *karma-mudrā*. His body is adorned with a garland of majestic light and flames.
He dwells within a lunar disc and has the color of a blue lotus. He sits upon a rocky seat shaped like a lute. His front face is compassionate; his right face is wrathful;
his left face displays a great laugh; and his rear face is slightly angry with its mouth open. Visualize him in this manner and recite the mantra.
Having done so, one immediately binds the Vajrabandha mudrā and enters the samādhi of the true nature of the mantra-syllable wheel of the deity.
Then, upon the pupils of the eyes, one visualizes the Sanskrit syllable *raṃ*, the color of which is like the flame of a lamp.
Slightly bending the neck and closing the eyes, one uses the wisdom-eye of the mind to illuminate the path of the mind; one should then visualize it as being perfectly complete within the chest.

The moon-disc of the bodhicitta appears vividly and clearly; free from external distraction and movement, because the water of wisdom is limpid and pure, the reflection of the moon of bodhicitta manifests within it.

After a long while, with the mind focused on a single object, one should arrange the syllables of the heart-mantra in a clockwise sequence upon that luminous orb. Reciting them silently three or five times, one then contemplates.
First is the syllable-gateway Oṃ. Because all phenomena are fundamentally unobtainable (one contemplates only the principle with the mind, not the syllable;
the single path is pure and pervades the entire dharma-realm).
The second is the letter-gateway A; because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
The third is the letter-gateway Miḥ; because the self is unapprehendable in all phenomena (thereby constituting the self-nature of the equality of true suchness).
One accomplishes merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Fourth is the gateway of the syllable *Ti*: because the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is unapprehendable [within which lies the meaning of the subtle causal and conditional dharmas of subject and object].
The fifth is the gateway of the syllable HŪṂ. Because the cause of all phenomena cannot be apprehended (since the cause is unapprehendable, the fruit is likewise unobtainable).

The sixth is the gateway of the syllable PHA. Because the fruit of all phenomena cannot be apprehended (since the fruit is unapprehendable, one thereby accomplishes the ultimate, perfect Dharmakāya, the untainted Dharma).
The seventh is the letter-gateway *Ṭha*.
Because all phenomena are without contention, and because all phenomena are without contention, all phenomena are fundamentally unattainable.
Because all phenomena are unattainable, all phenomena are fundamentally unborn. Because all phenomena are unborn, all phenomena...
The self is unapprehendable, because all phenomena are without self. The suchness of all phenomena is unapprehendable, because the suchness of all phenomena is non-apprehensible.
The cause of all phenomena is unapprehendable, because the cause of all phenomena is non-apprehensible. The fruit of all phenomena is unapprehendable, because the fruit of all phenomena...
Because there is nothing to be obtained, all phenomena are free from contention.
Since all phenomena are without contention, one attains the samādhi of the pure, non-conceptual true nature. This process continues in cycles;
through its association with a single moment of pure mind, one attains unimpeded *prajñāpāramitā*. From beginningless time, all...
The karmic obstructions, retributive obstructions, and afflictive obstructions are extinguished all at once.
All Buddhas of the ten directions and their respective deities (iṣṭadevatā) appear before one. Before long, one shall obtain the mundane and supramundane siddhis as desired.

Accomplishment is attained in this very body, and the first stage of joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) is realized. Within sixteen great births, the state of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is realized.
Bodhi. If a woman suffers from constant menstrual discharge, or if any man or woman has bleeding from the nostrils,
one should take two *liang* each of the roots of *rasa* (the *śanana* plant) and *xiancai* (garden radish), along with the rinse-water of *taṇḍula* (non-glutinous rice).
Mix these together with honey to form a pill. Empower it twenty-one times, then divide it into small pills the size of a *wuzi* (walnut seed).
If taken according to the ritual method, the illness will be cured immediately.
If one suffers from nasal congestion or an obstructed, foul-smelling breath within the nose, take sugar, saffron flowers, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*);
grind them together until they resemble an ointment and instill it [into the nostrils]. It will be cured immediately.
If one suffers from a headache lasting half a day, rubbing it with the aforementioned medicine will cause it to be cured immediately.
If a person suffers from eye ailments, rubbing the upper and lower eyelids with the medicine will cause them to be cured immediately.
If a person suffers from jaundice and loss of appetite, abdominal gas and lumps, labored breathing, or severe pain in the throat, one should take these seven ingredients—
rock salt, asafoetida, *harītakī*, cumin seeds, dried ginger, *bījaka*, and black pepper— in equal parts, taking half a *liang* of each.
Grind them together into a powder and form pills with granulated sugar, [the size of]...
The size is that of a jujube fruit. Take one dose on an empty stomach; each dose consists of one pill. There are no dietary restrictions or prohibitions.
It can make the complexion healthy and radiant, and provide abundant physical strength.
All of the aforementioned medicines should be empowered one hundred and eight times with the Tooth Seal before being consumed.
Regarding those methods in various quarters that employ the Tooth Seal for empowerment, the form of the seal is as follows: using the little finger of the left hand.

Press [the thumb] against the dorsal root of the ring finger. Next, with the middle finger, bend it behind the ring finger and press down upon the dorsal surface of the little finger, bending its proximal phalanx so that it lies flush alongside the ring finger.

Next, with the index finger (the second finger), bend its middle phalanx and press it against the nail of the little finger, with the fingertip directed toward the palm, [aligning it] with the ring finger.

Place the fingers side by side. Next, press the thumb obliquely against the second phalanges of the index and middle fingers, which are likewise placed side by side. The ring finger is held straight and pointing upward.
The mantra is as follows (this is the mantra for the Fang-tooth Mudrā): Oṃ u hūṃ hana dhuna matha viśaya śayatsara.
If at night a person suddenly suffers from heart pain, spirit-possession (*guizhu*), or is struck by a malignant affliction (*zhong'e*), one should form this mudrā and seal the site of the pain,
reciting this mantra forty-nine times; the pain will then be immediately cured.
If a person dies suddenly from poisoning, one should press the ear with the hand, pull the mouth toward the ear, and recite the *Sakushi* (Small Heart) mantra twenty-one times.
One should empower water seven times and sprinkle it on the face; then, reciting the mantra twenty-one more times, give it to the person to drink.
They will immediately revive.
If a person suffers from the mental illness of losing their mind, they may run frantically east and west;

they may strip off their clothes and sit down, or dishevel their hair, or take up dust and soil to defile their bodies. They may further desire sexual intercourse or eat repeatedly, claiming at each time that they are not yet full.
Or they may strike and kill one another, showing no avoidance of water or fire. Such various manifestations are manifold; it is certain.
Knowing that a ghost has entered the body and caused this illness, the practitioner should construct a water mandala two cubits in size.
Holding an incense burner in hand, he should make offerings to the Buddhas, burning both agallochum and frankincense.
He should place a protection seal upon the patient’s head and recite the mantra repeatedly. Within one or two days, the illness will be cured.
If someone has been poisoned and the venom has entered their stomach, one should hold a knife in hand and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with a sincere mind.
Then, using this knife, one should draw lines from a distance upon that person's body; they will immediately recover.
For one who recites this mantra, when about to eat, they should set aside a small portion of food for Kuṇḍalī and recite the mantra seven times.

Wherever they may be, he will constantly follow and protect them. If this is performed daily, Vajra-Kuṇḍalī’s heart will be greatly pleased, and he will not depart from afar. This is highly efficacious for curing illnesses.
This Amṛta-vajra rite is most suitable for curing illnesses. However, if one does not obtain auspicious dreams, one must not depart.
Or, if a messenger from the patient’s household arrives while facing southwest or northwest, the illness will not be cured.
Or, if the messenger raises their left hand and repeatedly touches their face, these are all inauspicious signs. If one departs [under such circumstances], then—
One loses one’s reputation.
With single-minded devotion, one should invoke the Dharani and Mandala Rite of the Great Powerful Spirit-King Guhyapada (who is the Vajra of Impure Traces),
[the procedure for] prostration and contemplation being as described above.

When the Buddha was about to enter *parinirvāṇa* between the twin *śāla* trees on the banks of the Bahudā River, the Brahmā Śikhin, accompanied by celestial maidens, was indulging in amorous pleasures and did not come to pay his respects. Thereupon, the great assembly dispatched a minor *vidyādhara* to go there and bring him back;
as soon as he smelled the foul odor, he was bound and confined within the inner enclosure, whereupon they further urged a Vajradhara to take action.
He departed with incantations. For seven days, no one was able to recover it.

At that time, the Buddha of Fundamental Wisdom, who eternally delights in the light of quiescence, employed the supernatural power of the Great Omniscience of Subsequently Attained Wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) to manifest an indestructible vajra wherever his mind directed it.
He then leaped into the air from the abode of Brahmā and, pointing at the foul matter, transformed it into the great earth. II.
The various classes of mantra-siddhas each returned to their supernatural powers. Brahmā, having resolved his mind, came to the place where the Buddha was. (For the mudrā, use the vajra-fist, etc.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) [prolonged, read with a high tone; draw the sound from the chest to the throat. Popular tradition reads it as the sound of "wèng," but this is likely unreliable.
Bhrūṃ (2) Mahā-pra (3) Hana-ai (4) Kṣi-kṣi (5) He-maṇi (6) Viki-vi (7) Maṇākṣe (8) Oṃ-cakriṇa (9) Uṣmau (10) Bhrūṃ (11) Hūṃ.

HŪṂ HŪṂ (12) | PAṂ PAṂ PAṂ (13) | PAṂ PAṂ SVĀHĀ (14). (This is the ancient scripture; the original mantra consists of forty-three characters. During the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, many recited it, and there were numerous miraculous responses.
Later generations removed ten characters, whereby it lost its efficacy. To prevent its misuse, they have not been removed here.
At that time, there was a Brahmā King named Jiu-shi (World-Savior), who addressed the Great Powerful Spirit King, saying: "I pray that you may long remain in this world."
...extracting and rescuing all sentient beings from their various sufferings and calamities.

At that time, the King of Spirits remained for seven days, preaching the dharma of the signless Dharmakāya to the Brahmā Śikhin and the entire assembly gathered at the ocean. He taught: "Lust, anger, and false views obscure True Suchness (Tathatā).
It is like a clear blue sky where no objects exist, yet black clouds suddenly arise; these are all created by your own minds and do not come from without."
When the seven days had passed, he immediately entered a state of meditative absorption.
Next, a manifested spirit-king suddenly arrived through the air, carrying several *zhang* of *bīḍa* white woolen cloth, fragrant resin, alum powder, and various pigments.
With a brush held in his right hand, he drew the image of the Great Majestic Spirit-King with three faces, eight arms, and nine eyes, his body being dark blue-black in color.
The color is azure-blue. His red hair stands upright. Eight dragons coil around his arms as an adornment.
His right hands hold: first, the mountain-opening mudrā; second, a vajra; third, a jewel bell; and fourth, a jeweled trident. His left hands hold:
first, the all-gathering mudrā; second, a wheel of fire; third, a lasso; and fourth, a sword. His left foot presses down upon Jambudvīpa.
The realm. Treading upon the precious stones, the right foot stamps the air and lifts up; *HŪṂ* blazes with fierce flames, manifesting as great wrath.
Having thus painted it, further delineate the four great jewel seals and inscribe the forty-two spirit talismans.
Form the five mudrās with the fingers and entrust them all to the Brahmā King Śikhin to uphold and practice. At that time, the emanated king, together with...
The Brahma King Śaṅkhakuṭa placed his hand upon [the deity’s] head and conferred the prophecy of enlightenment, bestowing the name Tathāgata Pure Radiance (Vimalaprabhā).
Thereupon, he withdrew and entered the body of the original spirit-king. The original spirit-king, a mass of purple-gold light, then entered the golden coffin. The spirit-king said:
"In general, when reciting any mantra, one must first construct a maṇḍala; however, for this mantra, there is no need to construct a maṇḍala. One need only..."
Carve an *vajra-gadā* (the *vajra* being *vajra*, here translated as "diamond"; cf. the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*, which records the ritual for the *vajra-śaṅkara-maṇḍala-seal*:
"Draw a human face; upon the head of that face, draw the form of a *vajra* standing atop it; its body is drawn in the shape of a staff, like a mendicant’s staff) from agalloch and sandalwood.

Within a Buddhist stūpa or a quiet chamber, smear the ground with fragrant mud. Depending on the size [of the space], place a basin filled with pure water before the image of the deity and set a pestle upon it. Recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times as a preliminary practice.
Then, on the night of the full moon, arrange extensive offerings and maintain the recitation throughout the entire night.
Without interrupting the sound, one will see water gushing forth and the ritual mallet (kīla) vibrating, emitting light that illuminates all, or transforming into various strange objects;
do not be startled by these. Concentrate your mind and continue reciting. The mallet will then rise up, three feet from the ground, or five, six, seven, or even ten feet.
At that point, the practitioner must take refuge, repent, and make a vow, saying: "I..."
At that time, I shall manifest my true body and constantly serve as an attendant according to the practitioner’s wishes.
Whatever they desire or delight in, all shall be swiftly attained according to their intent. I shall then bestow upon them the prophecy of enlightenment (*bodhy-avyākaraṇa*).

If there should be thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, venomous dragons, sudden winds, or violent rains, one should immediately form the mudrā for stopping thunder and hail with the middle finger of the left hand.

With the ring fingers and little fingers bent together into the palm, extend the index fingers straight upward. Press the thumbs against the middle joints of the index fingers while reciting the mantra.
Point the mudrā from afar toward the location of the thunder and hail, and they will cease of their own accord.
If one wishes to cure the illness of another, perform the "Sudden Illness" mudrā: adorn the right hand [with ornaments], and for the left hand, position the index and middle fingers as follows...
The *Paryaṣa* Seal: Bend the [left] hand toward the palm; keep the remaining three fingers straight and upright. Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Strike the patient seven times with this seal, and they will immediately recover. If the patient is on the verge of death, form the *Pañcamārga-bandhana* Seal:
bend the ring finger of the left hand toward the palm; keep the other eight fingers all standing upright. Place it [upon the head].
Place it upon the heart and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times in a loud voice; the soul and spirit will return to the body.
If treating those with demonic illnesses, burn agalloch incense (guggulu) beside the head of the afflicted person and recite the mantra; they will be cured immediately.
If treating illnesses caused by sorcery or poison, write the name of the afflicted person on a piece of paper and empower it; they will recover at once. If treating those who are subdued...
Even for the sick, one should write down the name of the afflicted person and the name of the disease-demon, bury them beneath the patient’s bed, and recite the mantra.
That demon will quickly acknowledge its name and manifest its own form; one should then command that demon to observe matters of the three periods of time and report each detail to the person.
Thus, the illness will be swiftly cured. If there is an affliction by the plague (time-sickness), [the same shall apply].

When a practitioner sees [the affliction], it is immediately cured. If one wishes to prevent the kings of pestilence from entering a boundary, one should recite this mantra one thousand and eight times on the ten days of the *zhāi* (fasting) observances; this can eliminate calamities and ailments for ten thousand *lǐ*.
If one wishes to cause all ghosts and spirits to come of their own accord to submit and serve as messengers, take three *shēng* of water and place it in a copper vessel.
Within the vessel, surround it with pure ash. Then, form the *saṃharaṇa* mudrā: join the two ring fingers together, bent into the palms with their backs touching;
press the tips of the two middle fingers together; extend the two index fingers and the two little fingers like opening blossoms;
and press the thumbs against the middle joints of the index fingers. Silently recite the mantra one hundred times.
Eight times. All the spirits and deities within that world will gather like clouds and manifest their own forms, placing themselves at the disposal of the practitioner to be commanded.
If one wishes to subjugate a mountain, one should recite the mantra one hundred times upon reaching that mountain, utter three loud cries, and then form the mudrā:
bend the ring finger of the right hand into the palm, while the middle and index fingers [are held erect].
Place the thumbs side by side, pointing straight upward; this is the *śaila-mudrā*. Advance and retreat seven steps each time, performing one mudrā for every recitation of the mantra.
Surveying all directions—left, right, above, and below—all birds and beasts shall depart from the mountain.

This dharma of the mantra can cause withered trees to sprout branches, dried-up springs to gush forth water, barren mountains to grow timber, and wild beasts to submit; it also subdues yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Akṣobhya shall serve as his attendant; venomous snakes and malevolent spirits will not dare to harm him. Should he seek eloquence, he shall obtain eloquence;
should he seek precious jewels, he shall obtain precious jewels. Whatever he undertakes, he shall be able to accomplish it all. This applies to anyone who recites this mantra.

First, recite "Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha," "Namo to the Transformation Body Śākyamuni Buddha," and "Namo to the Great Empowered Spiritual King Buddha" ten times each, and then perform the recitation.
The Ritual of the Maṇḍala for the Mantra of the Sword-Mudrā of Acala’s Messenger (the method for viewing and worship is as above).
Regarding this sword-mudrā: with the left hand, press the tips of the ring finger and little finger with the thumb, and extend the index and middle fingers straight;
this is called the "sword-sheath. Then, with the right hand, press the ring finger and little finger with the thumb.
On the left hand: extend the middle and index fingers straight upward to form a sword. Place it within the palm of the left hand;
bend the left index finger to press down upon the thumb like a ring, and keep the tip of the middle finger pointing straight up. This is called the Sword Mudrā (Khaḍgamudrā).

Place it upon the heart and recite the mantra seven times to ward off all poisons and evils. Move it to the crown of the head. If there is one who has consumed poison and is on the verge of death, perform [this rite].

For this mudrā, it is sufficient to recite [the mantra] seven times. If one wishes to establish a boundary, ward off spirits and ghosts, or disperse evil clouds and the like, one should place it upon the left knee in the manner of drawing a sword.
Exerting force, draw it upward; then, circling three times clockwise above the crown of the head, extend it to whatever distance is desired.
Finally, plant the sword vertically between the eyebrows and pause for a short while. Then, none will dare [to approach].
The mantra for one who has committed an offense is as follows: Oṃ (1) ajarāgaṇapada-ṭṭhakā (2) hūṃ hūṃ (3) ke-i ke-i (4) e-taṃ (5) garhe (6) mahā-rviṣa-sakṣata-vaḥ (7) hṛt.
RĪṂ KHAṂ PHAṬ (7). Solely with a single-minded devotion,
I invoke the mantra of Ucchuṣma-vajra for reviving a deceased child, the mantra for stopping a child’s crying,
the mantra for purifying defilements, and the *maṇḍala* ritual (the method for worship and contemplation is as above).

There is a mantra for the mouth-dharma-mudrā offering. First, with the ring finger and little finger of the right hand, enter from behind the ring finger of the left hand into the space between the middle and ring fingers.
Press the tip of the right thumb against the nail of the right ring finger and little finger, grasping the left ring finger and little finger. Next, bend the left ring [finger].
This is called the little finger. Again, press the left thumb upon the nails of the left ring finger and little finger, forming a circular hooking gesture.
Straighten the tips of the right middle fingers so they touch each other. Bend the tip of the left index finger slightly backward behind the left middle finger.
Turn the head to the right, with the middle finger slightly bent forward.

If a woman gives birth and the child dies in the womb and cannot emerge, take water in the cupped hands, mix it with a small amount of asafoetida (hiṅgu) medicine, and recite the *Pūjā-mantra* one hundred and eight times before administering it to her;
the dead child will then come forth. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) Vajrakrodha (2) Mahāsara (3) Oṃ (4) Jvāla jvāla (5) Mahājvāla (6) Cūḍa cūḍa (7) Khira khira (8) Sara sara (9) Hara hara (10) Dhara dhara (11) Svāhā (12).
To stop a child’s crying: transcribe the mantra upon plain white silk. Consecrate five-colored thread to form a cord, and tie the mantra at its center.
Then, reciting the mantra once for each knot, tie one hundred and eight knots. Fasten this cord beneath the small child's neck;
they will not fear any ghosts or spirits, their crying will immediately cease, and the child shall also attain long life. The mantra: [Insert Mantra]

At the request of Wei, the Prefect of Shaoyang, the Master preached the Dharma at Dafan Temple. The Master first explained the account of how he attained the Dharma and his subsequent conduct; next...
He expounds the meaning of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, along with the Verses on Signlessness (*animitta-gāthā*). Next, he answers the doubt regarding the non-existence of merit.
Next, he answers the question concerning the aspiration to be born in the Western Land. He emphasizes that one must purify the mind to be born in the Pure Land;
it is not that he asserts the non-existence of the Western Land. Finally, he demonstrates that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are of one essence and non-dual.
Next, he shows the Samādhi of One Practice; next, he shows that the mind does not dwell upon dharmas, so that the Way may flow and circulate.
If the mind dwells upon dharmas, it is called self-binding. Next, he shows that the teaching has neither sudden nor gradual aspects, for people have sharp or dull faculties.
Next, he shows that in the essence of sitting meditation, one does not attach to the mind, nor does one attach to purity, nor is it the case that one does not [attach].

[The Master] moved. Next, he demonstrated the true meaning of seated meditation (*zazen*). Next, he transmitted the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body of self-nature (*svabhāva-pañcaskandha-dharmakāya-gandha*), conferred the formless repentance (*animitta-pratikramaṇa*), and inspired the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*). He conferred the formless precepts of the three refuges (*animitta-triśaraṇa-śīla*).
Furthermore, he expounded upon the single essence and the three bodies (*ekasvabhāva-trikāya*) along with verses.

The following is the same as the single person presiding over the ritual who makes the announcement.
The Sūtra says: "One enters samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Therefore, in seeking the realm of the Buddha, one must necessarily rely upon what the Buddha has spoken.
The merit of hearing and permeation can give rise to the true cause and can eliminate false views. In the past, there was a man who fell ill and did not seek treatment.

Suppose a person were to read aloud the names of medicinal herbs; every time a herb’s name was recited, the illness would respond accordingly. Yet, upon reaching the name of *leiwán* (thunder-bolt pill), it would dare not respond.
If one were to take this pill and ingest it, the illness would then be completely eradicated. The illnesses of sentient beings are many, yet they respond just as sound does to its echo.
How could the wondrous medicine of the Tathāgata be limited to the *leiwán* alone? One should therefore invoke each of these names one by one and pay homage.
[This shall be] so. Having planted roots of goodness in past lives, [the truth] shall gradually be revealed. The Dharma-lineage of the ten directions shall flourish from this point onward.
We, with deep sorrow, reflect that since beginningless time, we have not known that within our own bodies there is no self, yet within the expanse of emptiness there is the Sūtra.

Having lost our fundamental nature and undergone the cycle of rebirth, we have not yet ceased [this suffering]. Therefore, on this day, before these precious Dharmas, we deeply repent for our former transgressions and together resolve [to practice].
With a sincere heart, repent immediately of past transgressions (chanting aloud):

"For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, I vow to take refuge and offer my utmost sincerity; with a single mind, I repent.
(After one prostration, stand up, inquire after the assembly's well-being, and kneel long.)
The assembly of disciples (bows). May all sentient beings universally share this single mind, which fully encompasses the myriad dharmas.
The mind-dharmas of self and others are in truth neither different nor the same. From beginningless time, they have been clouded by confusion and suddenly become distinct;

yet as difference and sameness arise together, they give birth to that which is neither different nor the same—this difference is not other than sameness, and this sameness is not other than difference. Throughout kalpas and lands, whether horizontal or vertical, the primary and secondary realms interpenetrate one another.
To seek liberation from saṃsāra while remaining in such a state is impossible. One merely gives rise to further deluded views, debating what is practiced and what is not.
Though one strives diligently in the quest for the Way, one strays further and further from it. Phenomena and principle are not unified; phenomena and principle do not accord.

Principle is confused with principle, and phenomena contradict phenomena. Thus, the impartial and perfect penetration is completely lost. The true medicine is ever-present, yet one has been unable to take and apply it for a long time.
Yet we become increasingly ignorant and do not even hear their names. How painful it is to reflect upon our own kind:

though we are called ordinary beings, we have perhaps constantly served all Tathāgatas throughout boundless ocean-like assemblies, where the Dharma was preached in successive layers for hundreds of millions of faithful humans and devas.
Some attained the pure eye and gave rise to the unsurpassed mind; yet through many kalpas and successive births, we have eventually forgotten this matter. Now, at this time...
The Dharma-treasure, with its ten thousand volumes and thousand wheels, is that which I wish to speak and that which I am able to hear.
Yet, as merit is exhausted life after life, wisdom likewise perishes; there is nowhere to seek it, no day upon which to encounter it, no understanding through recitation, and no perfection in faith.

In my speaking, there has been much negligence; in my practice, there have been many errors. Like a blind man who is immensely wealthy yet injures himself by touching his treasures, all these are transgressions for which I now confess boundlessly.
With solemn reverence, I repent (bow). That which is the Dharma is the mind itself;

relying upon the spiritual grace of the Buddhas, light radiates from within—like a thread drawn from a precious gem, like the luster emitted by a pearl, and like a mirror that is one with space. As it is...
The sharp sword cuts through; it severs my deep delusions and empties the root of my karma. It transforms the *adāntaka* (unsubdued) and leads them into *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Auspiciousness first dawns, its fragrance wafting afar. The dragons and devas of the ten directions are simultaneously moved; sounds of joy erupt like thunder, and wondrous powers arise like clouds.
They perfectly protect the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and fulfill the vows of all beings. I, receiving this—
The Buddha’s wisdom transforms the ignorant masses; its precious moisture deeply penetrates, and its subtle sounds resonate in perfect harmony.

It causes the coarse to become sublime and the insentient to become enlightened, leading all to enter the True Doctrine and return to their original state. Body after body reflects within the land of the lotus;
thought after thought fully contains the fragrance of the campaka flower. Not a single person shall fall into ruin along the way. (Prostrate, circumambulate, and recite.)
Homage to the eternally abiding Buddhas of the ten directions. Homage to the eternally abiding Dharma of the ten directions.
Homage to the eternally abiding Sangha of the ten directions. Homage to the Vairocana Buddha currently seated at the site of enlightenment.

Homage to all Buddhas of the three bodies: the Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya. Homage to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya, wherein the entire realm of emptiness is fully manifested.
Homage to the profound twelvefold canon of sutras. Homage to Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi. Homage to Bodhisattva Vīradatta.
Homage to Bodhisattva Dharmarakṣa. (Recite three times; then perform inquiries. I take refuge in the Buddha.
May all sentient beings propagate the lineage of the Buddhas and give rise to the unsurpassed resolve. (Prostrate.)
I take refuge in the Dharma. May all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
(Prostrate) I take refuge in the Sangha. May all sentient beings lead and manage the great assembly, free from all hindrances.
(Prostrate) Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Avataṃsaka Ocean Assembly. (Recite three times) (Exchange greetings and withdraw to the meditation hall.)
The End of Volume Ten of the *Fǎlún Bǎochàn* (Precious Repentance of the Dharma-Wheel) for the Water and Land Rituals.
June, the third year of the Dīngchū era (1877). Bǎorén Shàngshàn consulted with the monks engaged in carving the scriptures regarding matters concerning the Dharma-treasure.
Bǎorén joyfully made a vow to oversee the carving of the *Fǎlún Bǎochàn*, according to the principles of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.

He benefited sentient beings. When he encountered a severe illness in the ninth month, he earnestly requested his mother, Wuyuan, and Shangshan to take the remaining assets and accumulated clothing and belongings he possessed, exhausting them all without exception, and to offer them as alms to fulfill this vow.
Layman Xiong, Benzhen, Shangshan, and others assisted him in making this request. Wuyuan complied.
Baoren then took leave, reciting the Buddha’s name as he departed. Thereupon, the carving gradually progressed;
from the year Wuyin to the ninth month of Jimao, the work was completed. After dedicating the merit to all those involved, their names were inscribed at the end of the scripture.
The transcription being complete, Wuyuan requested that the monks who carved the scriptures be invited.

He prayed that through the power of Bao-ren’s vows and the diligent efforts of Wuyuan, together with all the superior persons who contributed funds, these merits might be dedicated toward the adornment of the Pure Land, so that they might be reborn there together upon the high-grade lotus flowers.
Recorded by the scripture-carver Miaokong.
The entire *Dharmacakra-ratna-sūtra* Repentance Ritual. According to the size of what is offered by each person, both the living and the deceased shall obtain it;

each shall receive supreme retribution and attain wondrous liberation, together fulfilling their aspirations. Upon changing bodies, they shall go together to the lotus-flower pavilions in the void of the Pure Land, employing skillful means to transform and deliver all sentient beings.
